From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

British film director and producer (born 1944)

| Jamil Dehlavi |
| --- |
| Born | 1944 (age 81–82) [Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolkata "Kolkata"), [British India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_India "British India") |
| Education | [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") ([BA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts")) [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") ([MFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Fine_Arts "Master of Fine Arts")) |
| Occupations | Film director and producer |
| Notable work | _[The Blood of Hussain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Blood\_of\_Hussain "The Blood of Hussain")_ (1980); _Born of Fire_ (1987) _[Immaculate Conception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate\_Conception\_(film) "Immaculate Conception (film)")_ (1992); _[Jinnah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinnah\_(film) "Jinnah (film)")_ (1998); _[Infinite Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite\_Justice\_(film) "Infinite Justice (film)")_ (2006); _[Godforsaken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godforsaken "Godforsaken")_ (2010) |
| Website | [www.dehlavifilms.com](http://www.dehlavifilms.com/) |

**Jamil Dehlavi** ([Urdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urdu_language "Urdu language"): جمیل دہلوی) (born 1944) is a London-based independent film director and producer of [Pakistani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan")-[French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") origin.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-BFI-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-Habib_University-3)

Since he became a filmmaker in the 1970s, his work has been widely screened internationally, notable films including _[Jinnah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinnah\_(film) "Jinnah (film)")_ (1998),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-citwf-4) about the partition of India and the birth of Pakistan, which won the Grand Prize at the [Festival of the Dhow Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_the_Dhow_Countries "Festival of the Dhow Countries"), Best International Film at the World Film Awards in Indonesia, the Gold Award at Worldfest Flagstaff, Best Foreign Film at [Worldfest Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WorldFest-Houston_International_Film_Festival "WorldFest-Houston International Film Festival"), and was nominated for a Golden Pyramid at the [Cairo International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo_International_Film_Festival "Cairo International Film Festival").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TNI-5)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jamil_Dehlavi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Born in [Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolkata "Kolkata"), [West Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bengal "West Bengal"), to a [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people") mother and an [Pathan-Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathans_in_India "Pathans in India") father who was a diplomat and subsequently travelled extensively between Asia and Europe, Dehlavi is fluent in five languages (English, French, Italian, Spanish and Urdu).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-6)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TNI-5) He studied at [Karachi Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karachi_Grammar_School "Karachi Grammar School"), then at international schools in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") and [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), before going to [Rugby School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_School "Rugby School") and [Oxford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University "Oxford University").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2) He graduated with a BA degree in Politics and French Literature and an MA (Hons) in Jurisprudence. He was subsequently called to the Bar at [Lincoln's Inn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln's_Inn "Lincoln's Inn") but never practised, preferring instead to go into the world of cinema.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-BFI-1) Dehlavi studied film directing at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), where he was awarded an MFA degree.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-Habib_University-3)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jamil_Dehlavi&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

While studying in New York, Dehlavi trained as an actor with [Stella Adler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stella_Adler "Stella Adler") and made his first feature film, _Towers of Silence_, which he wrote, produced and directed. It won the Grand Prize at the Festival of the Americas. His next film, _[The Blood of Hussain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Blood\_of\_Hussain "The Blood of Hussain")_ (1980),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-citwf-4) was selected by the Director's Fortnight at the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival") and won the Grand Prize at the [Taormina Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taormina_Film_Festival "Taormina Film Festival"). All of his subsequent films have also won major awards at film festivals all over the world.

Dehlavi has worked on various projects for the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"), [Channel Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_Four "Channel Four"), and French television, including _Qâf – The Sacred Mountain_, which won awards at five environmental film festivals. He worked on _Passover_, a [passion play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passion_play "Passion play") shot in [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba,_Andalusia "Córdoba, Andalusia") and made in collaboration with the celebrated flamenco guitarist [Paco Peña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paco_Pe%C3%B1a "Paco Peña"). Dehlavi has also worked in the Radio & Visual Services Division at the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") and as an associate professor in the School of Arts, Humanities & Social Sciences at [Habib University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habib_University "Habib University") in [Karachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karachi "Karachi").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-Habib_University-3)

In August 2018, the [BFI Southbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Film_Institute "British Film Institute") presented a retrospective of his work entitled _Between the Sacred and the Profane: The Cinema of Jamil Dehlavi_, which was described as "a rare opportunity to examine the contribution of one of the most intriguing and least understood figures of cinema."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2) With screenings of several films held over the weekend of 10–12 August, the event also featured a conversation with Dehlavi.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-7)

## Awards and filmography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jamil_Dehlavi&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Awards and filmography")]

*   1973: _The Guitarist_ (starring Jamil Dehlavi & Ellen Pauwels)

Gold Medal – [Atlanta Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Film_Festival "Atlanta Film Festival")
*   1976: _Towers of Silence_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-citwf-4) (starring Judy Van Hook & Jamil Dehlavi)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2)

Grand Prize - Festival of the Americas
*   1980: _[The Blood of Hussain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Blood\_of\_Hussain "The Blood of Hussain")_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-citwf-4) (starring Salman Peerzada, [Kika Markham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kika_Markham "Kika Markham"), Durriya Kazi & Jamil Dehlavi)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-BFI-1)

*   1984: _Qâf – The Sacred Mountain_ (short documentary film, also known as _Qâf_)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2)

Best Environmental Film – Jackson Hole Mountain Film Festival Special Jury Award – [Telluride Mountain Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telluride_Mountainfilm "Telluride Mountainfilm")Silver Gentian Best Mountain Film – Trento Mountain Film Festival Diable d'Or – Les Diablerets, [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland")Best Environmental Documentary – Worldfest Houston
*   1986: _Born of Fire_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-citwf-4) (starring [Peter Firth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Firth "Peter Firth")&[Suzan Crowley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzan_Crowley "Suzan Crowley"))[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-BFI-1)

| Occupation | Scholar |
| Website | [Official website](http://www.american.edu/sis/faculty/akbar.cfm) |

**Akbar Salahuddin Ahmed** (born 15 January 1943) is a [Pakistani-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistani_Americans "Pakistani Americans") academic, author, poet, playwright, filmmaker and former diplomat.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Nader362-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-AhmedForstxiixiii-3) He currently is a professor of International Relations and holds the Ibn Khaldun Chair of Islamic Studies at the [American University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_University "American University"), School of International Service in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Nader362-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-AhmedForstxiixiii-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Watson219-4) Akbar Ahmed served as the Pakistan High Commissioner to the UK and Ireland. He currently is a Global Fellow at the Woodrow Wilson Center.

Immediately prior, he taught at Princeton University and served as a visiting professor at the [Institute for Advanced Study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_Advanced_Study "Institute for Advanced Study") in [Princeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton,_New_Jersey "Princeton, New Jersey").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Nader362-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-AhmedForstxiixiii-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Bennett31-5) He also taught at Harvard University and was a visiting scholar at the Department of Anthropology.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Bennett31-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-AhmedHart331-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Peabody3-7) Ahmed was the First Chair of Middle East and Islamic Studies at the US Naval Academy, [Annapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapolis "Annapolis"), and a Nonresident Senior Fellow at the [Brookings Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookings_Institution "Brookings Institution").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Nader362-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Bennett31-5) In 2004 Ahmed was named [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia "District of Columbia") Professor of the Year by the [Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Foundation_for_the_Advancement_of_Teaching "Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching") and the [Council for Advancement and Support of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_for_Advancement_and_Support_of_Education "Council for Advancement and Support of Education").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-AhmedForstxiixiii-3) A former Pakistani High Commissioner to the UK and Ireland, Ahmed was a member of the [Civil Service of Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Service_of_Pakistan "Civil Service of Pakistan") and served as Political Agent in [South Waziristan Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Waziristan_Agency "South Waziristan Agency") and Commissioner in [Balochistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balochistan "Balochistan").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Nader362-2)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Ahmede133-8)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Bennett31-5) He also served as the Iqbal Fellow (Chair of Pakistan Studies) at the [University of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Nader362-2)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Ahmede133-8)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Bennett31-5) An [anthropologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropologist "Anthropologist") and scholar of Islam, he completed his MA at Cambridge University and received his PhD from the [School of Oriental and African Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_Oriental_and_African_Studies "School of Oriental and African Studies") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Nader362-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Bennett31-5) He has been called "the world's leading authority on contemporary Islam" by the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Ahmede133-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-11)

Ahmed received the [Tamgha-i-Imtiaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamgha-i-Imtiaz "Tamgha-i-Imtiaz") (Medal of Excellence) and [Sitara-i-Imtiaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitara-i-Imtiaz "Sitara-i-Imtiaz") (Star of Excellence) from the Pakistani government for academic distinction and the [Sir Percy Sykes Memorial Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Percy_Sykes_Memorial_Medal "Sir Percy Sykes Memorial Medal") by the [Royal Society for Asian Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_for_Asian_Affairs "Royal Society for Asian Affairs") in London.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-AhmedForstxiixiii-3)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-WignarajaHussain359-12) He was also awarded the inaugural [Purpose Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purpose_Prize "Purpose Prize") in 2006 alongside [Judea Pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judea_Pearl "Judea Pearl")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-Ahmede133-8) and is frequently named in the annual book, _The Muslim 500: The World's 500 Most Influential Muslims,_[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_S._Ahmed#cite_note-13) and was named a 2015 Global Thought Leader by _The World Post_ and the [Gottlieb Duttweiler Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottlieb_Duttweiler_Institute "Gottlieb Duttweiler Institute").

**Donald E. Stewart** (24 January 1930–28 April 1999) was an American [screenwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenwriter "Screenwriter"), best known for his screenplay for _[Missing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missing\_(1982\_film) "Missing (1982 film)")_, which won the [Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay"), the [Writers Guild of America Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America_Award "Writers Guild of America Award"), the [London Film Critics' Circle award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Film_Critics'_Circle "London Film Critics' Circle"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_E._Stewart#cite_note-1) a Christopher Award, (www.christophers.org) and the [BAFTA Award for Best Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Screenplay "BAFTA Award for Best Screenplay"), all shared with the film's director, [Costa-Gavras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa-Gavras "Costa-Gavras").

## Life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Donald_E._Stewart&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

Born in [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit"), [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan"), he had an early passion for cars.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_E._Stewart#cite_note-Obituary-2) He began his writing career as a journalist for [The Detroit Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Times "Detroit Times").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_E._Stewart#cite_note-Obituary-2) In his 20s, he founded and co-published _Competition Press_, a weekly magazine devoted to car-racing that eventually became _[Autoweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoweek "Autoweek")_; he also briefly edited _Motor Life_ magazine.

In 1960 he left reporting and moved to New York for the advertising industry, becoming copywriter and creative executive for a series of agencies such as J. Walter Thompson, Young & Rubicam and BBDO. Not surprisingly, he specialized in advertising copy for the motor trade, an area of booming competition in the car-obsessed economy of 1960s America. He became creative director of the Fletcher-Richards Agency and an expert on all things automotive.

He moved to [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles") in his 40s to try his hand at screenwriting. His first film was [Roger Corman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Corman "Roger Corman")'s _[Jackson County Jail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson\_County\_Jail\_(film) "Jackson County Jail (film)")_.

In his Oscar acceptance speech for _Missing_, Stewart thanked not only the film's director ("my co-writer and friend") but also [Charles Horman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Horman "Charles Horman"), the American journalist whose disappearance was the centerpiece of the film.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_E._Stewart#cite_note-3) When interviewed about what impact the foreign policy issues raised by _Missing_ had on audiences, Stewart commented: "Movies have a tendency to really heat up the emotions."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_E._Stewart#cite_note-4) The screenplay for _Missing_ is used in film schools for instruction in structure and development.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_E._Stewart#cite_note-Obituary-2)

He wrote or co-wrote the screenplays for the [Tom Clancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Clancy "Tom Clancy") trilogy of [Jack Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ryan_(character) "Jack Ryan (character)") films: _[The Hunt for Red October](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hunt\_for\_Red\_October\_(film) "The Hunt for Red October (film)")_, _[Patriot Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot\_Games\_(film) "Patriot Games (film)")_, and _[Clear and Present Danger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clear\_and\_Present\_Danger\_(film) "Clear and Present Danger (film)")_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_E._Stewart#cite_note-5)

Stewart died in his apartment at the Sierra Towers in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") of [cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer "Cancer") in 1999 at age 69. He had three children, Scott Stewart (now deceased), Sarah Cassleman, and Peter Stewart. He was separated from his fifth wife at the time of his death.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_E._Stewart#cite_note-6)

His last film before his death was _Dead Silence_, a [TV-movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_film "Television film") starring [James Garner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Garner "James Garner"). _[Hostiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hostiles\_(film) "Hostiles (film)")_, released in December 2017, was based on a manuscript written by Stewart in the 1980s and brought to life by director and co-writer [Scott Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Cooper_(director) "Scott Cooper (director)").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American screenwriter, film director and film producer

**W. Peter Iliff** (November 19, 1957) is an American screenwriter, film director, and film producer. He is known for writing the screenplay of the 1991 film [Point Break](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Break "Point Break").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._Peter_Iliff#cite_note-1) He also wrote the screenplay of the 2000 film [Under Suspicion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Suspicion_(2000_film) "Under Suspicion (2000 film)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._Peter_Iliff#cite_note-2) Other films for which he wrote the screenplay include [Patriot Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot_Games_(film) "Patriot Games (film)") (1992), [Varsity Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varsity_Blues_(film) "Varsity Blues (film)") (1999) and [The Enforcer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Enforcer_(2022_film) "The Enforcer (2022 film)") (2022).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._Peter_Iliff#cite_note-3)

He attended the [University of California, Santa Barbara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Santa_Barbara "University of California, Santa Barbara").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._Peter_Iliff#cite_note-iliff-4) Iliff is married to Ruthanne[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._Peter_Iliff#cite_note-5) and they have two children, Dane and Bella.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._Peter_Iliff#cite_note-iliff-4)

# Joseph Losey's rebirth in Britain

This article is more than 17 years old

Joseph Losey was a wreck when he fled America for Britain. But the snobbery and injustice he found here inspired The Servant and other angry, masterful movies

[David Thomson](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/davidthomson)

Sun 21 Jun 2009 17.00 EDT

[Share](mailto:?subject=Joseph%20Losey's%20rebirth%20in%20Britain%20|%20David%20Thomson&body=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2009/jun/21/joseph-losey-the-servant-bfi?CMP=share_btn_url)

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

J oseph Losey would have been 100 this year, and it is worth paying attention to the anniversary. As a director, he was variable in achievement yet steadfast in ambition. He wanted to be as good as anyone, in a way that matched his tall, rangy, handsome self, his Ivy League education, his midwestern voice; he was thoroughly and idealistically American. In the 1930s, he became a dedicated ­communist, ready to remake the world, which meant that his astonishing early career – The Boy with Green Hair, The Lawless, The Prowler, M, The Big Night – came to an end: Losey was obliged to come to England. And, in his own brusque way, Losey changed England and its attitude to the movies.

He came, in 1952, because of the common language – and because ­England housed other victims of the McCarthyite purges (screenwriter Carl Foreman met him at Heathrow). He might not have come had he known he was in for 10 lean years. He fell apart. He was subject to anxiety attacks and quickly decided that he had a bad heart. He could be neurotic, self-­pitying and self-dramatising, and all those things struck home. He ­directed a ­couple of plays in London, and did some television ­directing, for which he was paid the equivalent of $100 a week under the table and received no credit. In time, he got a work permit.

Losey began to marvel at 1950s Britain, where class, education, accent, money (or the suggestion of it) could let toffs, gents and frauds get away with murder. This was a time of fresh, often sour, voices nagging away at snobbery, unfairness and privilege; it was the moment of John Osborne, John Arden, working-class actors, the poetry of Philip Larkin, the critical writings of Kenneth Tynan, Al Alvarez and John Berger. "Angry young men" were at large, and Losey was a truculent, uneasy American ready to join the club.

Gradually, he seems to have been tempted by this new subject matter. He found challenging company. When he made The Sleeping Tiger – a lurid melodrama about a psychiatrist who takes a hoodlum into his house – he had the wit to cast Dirk Bogarde as the hoodlum. Bogarde was then becoming a matinee idol, but he always nursed deeper and darker ambitions. Just as important was a meeting with Richard MacDonald, a designer from Bristol who was barred from the movies through a lack of union credentials, and worked clandestinely at first for Losey. The director continued to fight the system, struggling to find potential in a series of mediocre scripts. But the improvement was clear: in Time Without Pity (1957), The Gypsy and the Gentleman (1957) and Blind Date (1959). None of these films is perfect, but you can see Losey emerging as an English director, digging into the ­national character.

In 1962 he took a plunge into Europe, to make Eve with Jeanne Moreau and Stanley Baker. In hindsight, I think it's fair to say the film revealed a lot of ­Losey's pretensions. But the disastrous experience of Eve (the film ran into censorship troubles) led directly to what remains Losey's key English work.

That film is The Servant, an inspired elevation of trashy material through the screenplay by Harold Pinter (the decisive friendship in Losey's career); it was a chance to take on the key relationship in a decaying society, that of servant and master.Set almost entirely in one Chelsea house, The Servant ­relied upon a series of related sets built by MacDonald, and the camera team of Douglas Slocombe and Chic Waterson. Jazz musician John Dankworth did the score. This film was a vindication of the team Losey had been building, and the pay-off in his friendship with Bogarde. This was the film (along with Victim) that changed the British public's ­expectation of Bogarde.

In one of those rare juxtapositions of life and justice, The Servant was an artistic and a ­commercial success; and although it played poorly in America, it was at least acknowledged as a Losey film. In Britain, it opened up the possibility of modest budgets and searing social ­impact: it now stands at the head of lines of work by [John Schlesinger](https://www.theguardian.com/film/john-schlesinger), Lindsay Anderson, John Boorman, Stephen Frears and so on. The subversive energy of The Servant left a deep mark on film and television for years.

Of course Losey's English period was not over. But in time, Losey the European figure came to dominate the Brit. He had plans to go back to America, but they never came to fruition. Instead, he made a lot of films in Europe with international stars. A few were ­exceptional – above all Mr Klein, with Alain Delon – but others seemed like prestige ventures: The Romantic ­Englishwoman, The Assassination of Trotsky. The films of those last years now seem less impressive, less urgent than The Prowler or The Servant.

When Losey died in 1984, it was in Britain. He had stayed a London ­resident, when he wasn't off on the continent setting up big pictures. It may be that success undermined him more than failure. It's not the rarest thing that an artist is at his best when he believes he's a wreck. But for at least 15 years, Losey in England was just what we needed

A season of **Joseph Losey**'s films is at BFI, London SE1, until 30 July. Box office: 020-7928 3232.

_**A Bridge Too Far**_ is a 1977 war film that tells the story of [Operation Market Garden](https://kids.kiddle.co/Operation_Market_Garden "Operation Market Garden"). This was a big [Allied](https://kids.kiddle.co/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") plan during [World War II](https://kids.kiddle.co/World_War_II "World War II") in the [Netherlands](https://kids.kiddle.co/Netherlands "Netherlands"). The film shows how this important military operation did not go as planned.

The movie is based on a true story from a [non-fiction](https://kids.kiddle.co/Non-fiction "Non-fiction")[book](https://kids.kiddle.co/A_Bridge_Too_Far_(book) "A Bridge Too Far (book)") by [Cornelius Ryan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cornelius_Ryan "Cornelius Ryan"). It was directed by [Richard Attenborough](https://kids.kiddle.co/Richard_Attenborough "Richard Attenborough") and written by [William Goldman](https://kids.kiddle.co/William_Goldman "William Goldman"). The film features many famous actors like [Sean Connery](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sean_Connery "Sean Connery"), [Michael Caine](https://kids.kiddle.co/Michael_Caine "Michael Caine"), [Anthony Hopkins](https://kids.kiddle.co/Anthony_Hopkins "Anthony Hopkins"), and [Robert Redford](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_Redford "Robert Redford").

_A Bridge Too Far_ was made by companies in the [United Kingdom](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") and the [United States](https://kids.kiddle.co/United_States "United States"). Many scenes were filmed in the real places where the events happened in the Netherlands. Even though some critics didn't love the movie, it won several awards. For example, it won four [BAFTA Awards](https://kids.kiddle.co/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts "British Academy of Film and Television Arts"), including one for [Edward Fox](https://kids.kiddle.co/Edward_Fox_(actor) "Edward Fox (actor)") as Best Supporting Actor.

## The Story of Operation Market Garden

The film's story is about [Operation Market Garden](https://kids.kiddle.co/Operation_Market_Garden "Operation Market Garden"), a daring plan by the Allies. The goal was to fly 35,000 soldiers from England into the [Netherlands](https://kids.kiddle.co/Netherlands "Netherlands"). They would land behind enemy lines. Two American paratrooper groups were supposed to capture roads and bridges near [Nijmegen](https://kids.kiddle.co/Nijmegen "Nijmegen"). A British group, led by Major-General Roy Urquhart, aimed to secure the bridge at [Arnhem](https://kids.kiddle.co/Arnhem "Arnhem"). Polish paratroopers were also part of this plan.

### The Plan's Challenges

The main idea was for XXX Armoured Corps to quickly drive up the roads. They would use the bridges captured by the paratroopers and reach Arnhem in just two days. However, there were problems from the start. The British landing zone was far from the Arnhem bridge. This meant their portable radios wouldn't work.

Also, photos showed German tanks near Arnhem. But General Frederick Browning didn't believe these reports. He also ignored warnings from the [Dutch resistance](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dutch_resistance "Dutch resistance"). He thought the mission would succeed no matter what.

### The Battle for the Bridges

The Arnhem bridge was very important. It was the last way for German forces to escape the Netherlands. It also offered a direct route into Germany for the Allies. But the road to it was narrow, making it hard for vehicles to pass.

When the paratroopers landed, they surprised the Germans. But the bridge at Son was blown up by the Germans before the Allies could secure it. The British group also faced issues. Many of their jeeps were destroyed or didn't arrive. Their radios also failed.

Meanwhile, the XXX Corps moved slowly. German forces fought back, and the narrow roads caused delays. They even had to build a new [Bailey bridge](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bailey_bridge "Bailey bridge") at Son. They were then stopped at Nijmegen. American soldiers had to make a very risky river crossing in daylight to capture the Nijmegen bridge. This caused more delays.

### The Retreat from Arnhem

The Germans surrounded the British paratroopers at Arnhem. Polish troops, led by General Stanisław Sosabowski, finally arrived. But they were too late to help the British. After days of heavy fighting against German [SS](https://kids.kiddle.co/SS "SS") and [panzer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Panzer "Panzer") tanks, the British were outnumbered. They were either captured or forced to retreat to Oosterbeek.

Major-General Urquhart was ordered to pull his troops back. Other Allied commanders blamed the many problems for their failure to provide support. Urquhart escaped with less than a fifth of his original 10,000 soldiers. Those too injured to leave stayed behind to cover the retreat.

Back in Oosterbeek, a Dutch woman named Kate ter Horst left her home. It had been used as a hospital by the British. She passed through her yard, which had become a graveyard for fallen soldiers. Wounded British troops sang "[Abide with Me](https://kids.kiddle.co/Abide_with_Me "Abide with Me")" as they waited to be captured.

## Main Characters

The film features many actors playing real-life soldiers and civilians. Here are some of the key characters:

### British Soldiers

*   [Dirk Bogarde](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dirk_Bogarde "Dirk Bogarde") as Lieutenant-General Frederick Browning: A high-ranking British general.
*   [Edward Fox](https://kids.kiddle.co/Edward_Fox_(actor) "Edward Fox (actor)") as Lieutenant-General [Brian Horrocks](https://kids.kiddle.co/Brian_Horrocks "Brian Horrocks"): Commander of the XXX Corps.
*   [Sean Connery](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sean_Connery "Sean Connery") as Major-General Roy Urquhart: Commander of the British 1st Airborne Division at Arnhem.
*   [Michael Caine](https://kids.kiddle.co/Michael_Caine "Michael Caine") as Lieutenant-Colonel Joe Vandeleur: A British tank commander.
*   [Anthony Hopkins](https://kids.kiddle.co/Anthony_Hopkins "Anthony Hopkins") as Lieutenant-Colonel John Frost: Commander of the British paratroopers at the Arnhem bridge.

### American Soldiers

*   [Ryan O'Neal](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ryan_O%27Neal "Ryan O'Neal") as Brigadier General James Gavin: Commander of the US 82nd Airborne Division.
*   [Robert Redford](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_Redford "Robert Redford") as Major Julian Cook: Led a dangerous river crossing to capture the Nijmegen bridge.
*   [James Caan](https://kids.kiddle.co/James_Caan "James Caan") as Staff Sergeant Eddie Dohun: A brave American soldier.

### Other Allies

*   [Gene Hackman](https://kids.kiddle.co/Gene_Hackman "Gene Hackman") as Major General Stanisław Sosabowski: Commander of the Polish paratroopers.
*   Peter Faber as Captain Arie Bestebreurtje: A Dutch liaison officer.

### German Commanders

*   [Hardy Krüger](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hardy_Kr%C3%BCger "Hardy Krüger") as Generalmajor der Waffen-SS Karl Ludwig: A German tank division commander.
*   [Maximilian Schell](https://kids.kiddle.co/Maximilian_Schell "Maximilian Schell") as General der Waffen-SS Wilhelm Bittrich: A German corps commander.

### Dutch Civilians

*   [Laurence Olivier](https://kids.kiddle.co/Laurence_Olivier "Laurence Olivier") as Dr. Jan Spaander: A Dutch doctor.
*   [Liv Ullmann](https://kids.kiddle.co/Liv_Ullmann "Liv Ullmann") as Kate ter Horst: A Dutch woman who helped wounded British soldiers.

## Making the Movie

Making _A Bridge Too Far_ was a huge project. It involved many planes, vehicles, and actors.

### Filming the Air Drops

In September 1976, they filmed the air drops. About 1,000 men were dropped from [Dakota](https://kids.kiddle.co/Douglas_C-47_Skytrain "Douglas C-47 Skytrain") aircraft. The film company bought or borrowed eleven Dakotas for these scenes. One Dakota was even used as a camera plane. It had cameras mounted in several places to capture the action.

They also built ten fake Horsa gliders. These gliders were used for scenes where troops were taking off. A windstorm damaged most of them, but they were quickly fixed.

### Vehicles and Locations

For the ground scenes, they found many real World War II tanks, jeeps, and trucks. These vehicles came from military units in countries like Greece and Turkey.

The scenes around the Arnhem bridge were filmed in [Deventer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Deventer "Deventer"). This city had a similar bridge over the IJssel River. The original Arnhem bridge had too much modern development around it to be used for a 1940s setting. Some scenes were also shot in [Zutphen](https://kids.kiddle.co/Zutphen "Zutphen") and at Twickenham Studios.

### Movie Costs

To save money, all the famous actors agreed to be paid the same amount each week: $250,000. This was a lot of money back then!

One part of the filming was called the "Million-Dollar Hour." This was the American assault on the Nijmegen Bridge. The crew only had one hour on October 3, 1976, to film this scene because of heavy traffic. If they didn't finish, it would have cost over a million dollars to reschedule.

The movie did well in Europe but not as well in North America.

## Promoting the Film

To help promote the movie, the scriptwriter [William Goldman](https://kids.kiddle.co/William_Goldman "William Goldman") wrote a book called _Story of A Bridge Too Far_. It came out in 1977 and included essays, photos from the film, and thoughts from the actors and the real people they played.

# Luchino Visconti facts for kids

[Kids Encyclopedia Facts](https://kids.kiddle.co/)

For the Milanese ruler, see Luchino Visconti (died 1349).

| Quick facts for kids Luchino Visconti |
| --- |
| [![Image 3: Luchino Visconti 1972b.jpg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/c/c1/Luchino_Visconti_1972b.jpg/300px-Luchino_Visconti_1972b.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Luchino_Visconti_1972b.jpg) Visconti in 1972 |
| Born | Luchino Visconti di Modrone (1906-11-02)2 November 1906 [Milan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Milan "Milan"), [Kingdom of Italy](https://kids.kiddle.co/Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy") |
| Died | 17 March 1976(1976-03-17) (aged 69) [Rome](https://kids.kiddle.co/Rome "Rome"), [Italy](https://kids.kiddle.co/Italy "Italy") |
| Occupation | * [Film director](https://kids.kiddle.co/Movie_director "Movie director") * [screenwriter](https://kids.kiddle.co/Screenwriter "Screenwriter") * theater director * opera director |
| Notable work | * * _Ossessione_ (1943) * _Senso_ (1954) * _Rocco and His Brothers_ (1960) * _The Leopard_ (1963) * _The Damned_ (1969) * _Death in Venice_ (1971) * _Ludwig_ (1972) |
| Title | [Conte](https://kids.kiddle.co/Count "Count") di Lonate Pozzolo |
| Relatives | Eriprando Visconti (nephew) |
| Family | Visconti di Modrone |
| Honours | [![Image 4: Ordine Civile di Savoia BAR.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/a/a0/Ordine_Civile_di_Savoia_BAR.svg/35px-Ordine_Civile_di_Savoia_BAR.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Ordine_Civile_di_Savoia_BAR.svg) Civil Order of Savoy |

Luchino Visconti di Modrone (born November 2, 1906 – died March 17, 1976) was a famous Italian [film director](https://kids.kiddle.co/Movie_director "Movie director"), stage director, and [screenwriter](https://kids.kiddle.co/Screenwriter "Screenwriter"). He was a very important person in Italian art and culture during the mid-1900s.

Visconti was one of the creators of a film style called [cinematic neorealism](https://kids.kiddle.co/Italian_neorealism "Italian neorealism"). This style focused on showing real-life stories. Later, he started making grand, beautiful movies that explored ideas like beauty, change, and European history. Many of his films looked at how noble and wealthy families changed over time.

He won many awards, including the [Palme d'Or](https://kids.kiddle.co/Palme_d%27Or "Palme d'Or") and the [Golden Lion](https://kids.kiddle.co/Golden_Lion "Golden Lion"). His movies are still seen as very important and have influenced many filmmakers who came after him.

Born into a noble family in [Milan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Milan "Milan"), Visconti loved art from a young age. He started his career helping director [Jean Renoir](https://kids.kiddle.co/Jean_Renoir "Jean Renoir"). His first movie, _Ossessione_ (1943), was about working-class people facing tough challenges. The [Fascist](https://kids.kiddle.co/Fascist_Italy "Fascist Italy") government didn't like it, but today it's seen as a groundbreaking film in Italian cinema.

Some of his most famous films include _Senso_ (1954) and _The Leopard_ (1963), which were historical dramas based on famous Italian books. He also made the intense drama _Rocco and His Brothers_ (1960) and his "German Trilogy": _The Damned_ (1969), _Death in Venice_ (1971), and _Ludwig_ (1973). Besides films, he was also a talented director for plays and operas in Italy and other countries.

## Early Life and Artistic Beginnings

[![Image 5: COA Visconti di Modrone di Milano](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/5/5d/COA_Visconti_di_Modrone_di_Milano.jpg/120px-COA_Visconti_di_Modrone_di_Milano.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:COA_Visconti_di_Modrone_di_Milano.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:COA_Visconti_di_Modrone_di_Milano.jpg "Enlarge")

 Family arms

Luchino Visconti was born into a well-known noble family in [Milan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Milan "Milan"). He was one of seven children. His father was Giuseppe Visconti di Modrone, a Duke and Count. His mother, Carla Erba, came from a wealthy family that owned a pharmaceutical company. Luchino was known as Count Luchino Visconti di Modrone. His family was a branch of the Visconti of Milan, who ruled Milan from 1277 to 1447.

He grew up in his family's grand home, the _Palazzo Visconti di Modrone_ in Milan. He also spent time at their country estate, _Grazzano Visconti Castle_. When his parents separated in the early 1920s, he moved with his mother to her house in Milan and her summer home, Villa Erba, on Lake Como. He later inherited his father's villa in Rome, where he lived for many years.

*   [![Image 6: 8955 - Milano - Palazzo Visconti di Grazzano (sec. XVIII) - Foto Giovanni Dall'Orto 22-Apr-2007](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/a/a9/8955_-_Milano_-_Palazzo_Visconti_di_Grazzano_%28sec._XVIII%29_-_Foto_Giovanni_Dall%27Orto_22-Apr-2007.jpg/264px-8955_-_Milano_-_Palazzo_Visconti_di_Grazzano_%28sec._XVIII%29_-_Foto_Giovanni_Dall%27Orto_22-Apr-2007.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:8955_-_Milano_-_Palazzo_Visconti_di_Grazzano_(sec._XVIII)_-_Foto_Giovanni_Dall%27Orto_22-Apr-2007.jpg)  Palazzo Visconti di Modrone in Milan  
*   [![Image 7: Grazzano Visconti - panoramio - Gregorini Demetrio (1)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/4/40/Grazzano_Visconti_-_panoramio_-_Gregorini_Demetrio_%281%29.jpg/150px-Grazzano_Visconti_-_panoramio_-_Gregorini_Demetrio_%281%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Grazzano_Visconti_-_panoramio_-_Gregorini_Demetrio_(1).jpg)  Grazzano Visconti Castle  
*   [![Image 8: Villa Erba - dal lago](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/2/24/Villa_Erba_-_dal_lago.jpg/335px-Villa_Erba_-_dal_lago.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Villa_Erba_-_dal_lago.jpg)  Villa Erba on Lake Como  

From a young age, Luchino was surrounded by art, music, and theater. His family's Milan palace had its own small private theater where the children performed. They also had a special box at the famous [La Scala](https://kids.kiddle.co/La_Scala "La Scala") opera house. Luchino learned to play the cello and met famous artists like composer [Giacomo Puccini](https://kids.kiddle.co/Giacomo_Puccini "Giacomo Puccini") and conductor [Arturo Toscanini](https://kids.kiddle.co/Arturo_Toscanini "Arturo Toscanini"). He loved reading, especially the book _[In Search of Lost Time](https://kids.kiddle.co/In\_Search\_of\_Lost\_Time "In Search of Lost Time")_ by Proust, which he hoped to turn into a film one day. Before becoming a filmmaker, he was very keen on training racehorses.

## Fighting for Freedom: Wartime Activities

During [World War II](https://kids.kiddle.co/World_War_II "World War II"), Visconti joined the Italian Communist Party. He believed this group was the best way to fight against the [Fascist](https://kids.kiddle.co/Italian_fascism "Italian fascism") government led by [Benito Mussolini](https://kids.kiddle.co/Benito_Mussolini "Benito Mussolini"). At first, he had been impressed by the look of the Fascist parades, but he soon grew to hate Mussolini's rule. He felt that the wealthy people had betrayed their country by supporting the harsh government.

After the king left Italy in 1943 and the Germans took control, Visconti began working with the [Italian resistance](https://kids.kiddle.co/Italian_resistance_movement "Italian resistance movement"). He bravely helped communist fighters, even though it was very dangerous. His home in Rome became a secret meeting place for artists who opposed the government.

He even went into hiding in the mountains, using a fake name. Visconti helped English and American prisoners of war who had escaped. He also gave shelter to resistance fighters in his Rome house, with help from actress María Denis.

In April 1944, after the Germans occupied Rome, Visconti was arrested. He was held by a cruel anti-resistance leader and sentenced to be executed. Luckily, María Denis stepped in at the last moment and saved his life. After the war, Visconti gave evidence against his captor, who was later punished.

## Filmmaking Career

[![Image 9: Luchino Visconti 5](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/6/69/Luchino_Visconti_5.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Luchino_Visconti_5.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Luchino_Visconti_5.jpg "Enlarge")

 Luchino Visconti

### Early Films and Neorealism

Visconti started his film career working on the sets of [Jean Renoir](https://kids.kiddle.co/Jean_Renoir "Jean Renoir")'s movie _Partie de campagne_ (1936). He got this job thanks to their shared friend, [Coco Chanel](https://kids.kiddle.co/Coco_Chanel "Coco Chanel"). After a short trip to Hollywood in the United States, he returned to Italy to assist Renoir again on _Tosca_ (1941).

With other writers from a Milanese film magazine, Visconti wrote the script for his first movie as a director: _Ossessione_ (_Obsession_, 1943). This film was one of the very first [neorealist](https://kids.kiddle.co/Italian_neorealism "Italian neorealism") movies. It was an unofficial adaptation of the book _The Postman Always Rings Twice_.

When _Ossessione_ first showed at a film festival, Mussolini's son, Vittorio, who was in charge of cinema, was very angry. He reportedly walked out, saying, "This is not Italy!" The Fascist government then tried to stop the film from being shown. It wasn't publicly seen in Rome until May 1945, after the war.

In 1948, Visconti wrote and directed _La terra trema_ (_The Earth Trembles_). This movie was based on a novel and continued his neorealist style.

### Moving Beyond Neorealism

Visconti kept making films in the 1950s, but he started to move away from strict neorealism. His 1954 film, _Senso_, was shot in color. It was set in Venice in 1866, when the city was under Austrian control. In this movie, Visconti mixed real-life details with romantic feelings, which was a new direction for him.

He returned to neorealism one more time with _Rocco e i suoi fratelli_ (_Rocco and His Brothers_, 1960). This powerful story was about a family from Southern Italy who moved to Milan hoping to find a better life. In 1961, he was part of the jury at the 2nd Moscow International Film Festival.

### Later, More Personal Films

Throughout the 1960s, Visconti's films became more personal and grand. _Il Gattopardo_ (_The Leopard_, 1963) was based on a famous book about the decline of a noble Sicilian family during the [Risorgimento](https://kids.kiddle.co/Italian_unification "Italian unification") (the time when Italy became a united country). The film shows how times were changing through its characters. The old prince, played by [Burt Lancaster](https://kids.kiddle.co/Burt_Lancaster "Burt Lancaster"), is kind but traditional. A new, clever businessman from the village, played by Paolo Stoppa, seems humble but is actually very cunning. The story shows the tension as the old ways fade and a new Italy rises. The American version of this film had important scenes cut, which Visconti did not approve of.

In 1969, Visconti's film _The Damned_ earned him a nomination for an [Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay](https://kids.kiddle.co/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay"). This well-known film is about a wealthy German industrial family that falls apart as the [Nazis](https://kids.kiddle.co/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") gain power in the 1930s. The film's rich beauty and focus on decline are typical of Visconti's style. This style is also very clear in his movie _Death in Venice_ (1971), which was based on a famous book by [Thomas Mann](https://kids.kiddle.co/Thomas_Mann "Thomas Mann").

## Theatre and Opera Direction

Visconti was also a highly respected director for plays and [operas](https://kids.kiddle.co/Opera "Opera"). From 1946 to 1960, he directed many performances for the Rina Morelli-Paolo Stoppa Company, often working with actor [Vittorio Gassman](https://kids.kiddle.co/Vittorio_Gassman "Vittorio Gassman"). He also directed many famous opera productions.

His love for opera is clear in his 1954 film _Senso_, which starts with scenes from an opera filmed at the [Teatro La Fenice](https://kids.kiddle.co/La_Fenice "La Fenice") in Venice. His opera career began in December 1954 when he directed _[La vestale](https://kids.kiddle.co/La\_vestale\_(Spontini) "La vestale (Spontini)")_ at Milan's [Teatro alla Scala](https://kids.kiddle.co/La_Scala "La Scala"). He also directed a very famous revival of _[La traviata](https://kids.kiddle.co/La\_traviata "La traviata")_ at La Scala in 1955, starring the legendary singer [Maria Callas](https://kids.kiddle.co/Maria_Callas "Maria Callas"). Another famous production was _[Anna Bolena](https://kids.kiddle.co/Anna\_Bolena "Anna Bolena")_ (also at La Scala) in 1957, also with Callas.

In 1958, he directed a significant production of Verdi's _[Don Carlos](https://kids.kiddle.co/Don\_Carlos "Don Carlos")_ at the [Royal Opera House](https://kids.kiddle.co/Royal_Opera_House "Royal Opera House") in London. He also directed _[Macbeth](https://kids.kiddle.co/Macbeth\_(opera) "Macbeth (opera)")_ in Spoleto in 1958 and a famous black-and-white _[Il trovatore](https://kids.kiddle.co/Il\_trovatore "Il trovatore")_ at the Royal Opera House in 1964. In 1966, Visconti's beautiful production of _[Falstaff](https://kids.kiddle.co/Falstaff\_(opera) "Falstaff (opera)")_ for the Vienna State Opera, conducted by [Leonard Bernstein](https://kids.kiddle.co/Leonard_Bernstein "Leonard Bernstein"), was highly praised. However, his simple 1969 production of _[Simon Boccanegra](https://kids.kiddle.co/Simon\_Boccanegra "Simon Boccanegra")_ with unusual costumes caused some debate.

## Filmmaking Style and Ideas

After [World War II](https://kids.kiddle.co/World_War_II "World War II"), Visconti became one of the key figures in the [Italian neorealist film](https://kids.kiddle.co/Italian_neorealism "Italian neorealism") movement. This movement focused on showing the difficult economic and social conditions of the time, and how they affected ordinary people. Even though Visconti came from a wealthy, educated noble family and never lacked money, his films often showed this tension between different social classes. He once said he felt like he belonged to an older world, from the 1800s.

In his film _The Leopard_, he explored the decline of an old social order and the arrival of "modern times." He didn't see his grand, historical scenes as an escape into imaginary worlds. Instead, he saw them as a way to understand important historical changes that would only become clear later. He looked for great books that showed the differences between generations and their ways of seeing the world. He believed this was part of being realistic in art. When some people called his work "decadent," he referred to [Thomas Mann](https://kids.kiddle.co/Thomas_Mann "Thomas Mann"), another artist who created art in a similar way.

## Later Life and Passing

# John Cairncross facts for kids

[Kids Encyclopedia Facts](https://kids.kiddle.co/)

| Quick facts for kids John Cairncross |
| --- |
| [![Image 3: John Cairncross.jpg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/7/79/John_Cairncross.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:John_Cairncross.jpg) |
| Allegiance | [Soviet Union](https://kids.kiddle.co/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") |
| Service | Foreign Office The Government Code and Cypher School, Bletchley Park |
| Codename(s) | Liszt |
| * * * |
| Born | (1913-07-25)25 July 1913 [Lesmahagow](https://kids.kiddle.co/Lesmahagow "Lesmahagow"), [Lanarkshire](https://kids.kiddle.co/Lanarkshire "Lanarkshire"), Scotland |
| Died | 8 October 1995(1995-10-08) (aged 82) [Herefordshire](https://kids.kiddle.co/Herefordshire "Herefordshire"), England |
| Spouse | * Gabriella Oppenheim * Gayle Brinkerhoff |
| Alma mater | [University of Glasgow](https://kids.kiddle.co/University_of_Glasgow "University of Glasgow") [The Sorbonne](https://kids.kiddle.co/University_of_Paris "University of Paris") [Trinity College, Cambridge](https://kids.kiddle.co/Trinity_College,_Cambridge "Trinity College, Cambridge") |

**John Cairncross** (born July 25, 1913 – died October 8, 1995) was a British government worker. He became a [spy](https://kids.kiddle.co/Espionage "Espionage") for the [Soviet Union](https://kids.kiddle.co/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") during [World War II](https://kids.kiddle.co/World_War_II "World War II"). He secretly shared important information with the Soviets. This information helped them win major battles against Germany.

Cairncross was thought to be the fifth member of a famous spy group called the [Cambridge Five](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cambridge_Five "Cambridge Five"). He also worked as a translator and writer. He secretly admitted to being a spy in 1964. Later, in 1979, he spoke to journalists about it. He was not charged with any crime for his spying.

His role as the "fifth man" was confirmed in 1990 by a former Soviet spy, Oleg Gordievsky. Another former Soviet agent, Yuri Modin, also confirmed this in his 1994 book.

## Contents

*   [Early Life and School](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross#Early_Life_and_School)
*   [Starting His Career](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross#Starting_His_Career)
*   [World War II Spy Work](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross#World_War_II_Spy_Work)
    *   [Secret Messages from Bletchley Park](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross#Secret_Messages_from_Bletchley_Park)
        *   [Helping at the Battle of Kursk](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross#Helping_at_the_Battle_of_Kursk)
        *   [Information on Yugoslav Partisans](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross#Information_on_Yugoslav_Partisans)

*   [Working as a Spy](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross#Working_as_a_Spy)
*   [Later Life](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross#Later_Life)
*   [In Books and Movies](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross#In_Books_and_Movies)
*   [Awards](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross#Awards)

## Early Life and School

John Cairncross was born in [Lesmahagow](https://kids.kiddle.co/Lesmahagow "Lesmahagow"), Scotland. He was the youngest of eight children. His mother was a teacher and his father managed a hardware store.

Three of his brothers became university professors. One of them was the famous economist [Sir Alexander Kirkland Cairncross](https://kids.kiddle.co/Alexander_Cairncross_(economist) "Alexander Cairncross (economist)"). John grew up in Lesmahagow, a small town near [Lanark](https://kids.kiddle.co/Lanark "Lanark").

He went to Lesmahagow Higher Grade School, where he won a top student award in 1928. He then studied at Hamilton Academy, the [University of Glasgow](https://kids.kiddle.co/University_of_Glasgow "University of Glasgow"), the [Sorbonne](https://kids.kiddle.co/University_of_Paris "University of Paris") in Paris, and [Trinity College, Cambridge](https://kids.kiddle.co/Trinity_College,_Cambridge "Trinity College, Cambridge"). At Cambridge, he studied French and German.

## Starting His Career

After finishing university, John Cairncross took a difficult government exam. He came in first place for both the "home civil service" (working in Britain) and the "foreign office and diplomatic service" (working abroad). This was a big achievement.

He first worked in the [British Foreign Office](https://kids.kiddle.co/Foreign,_Commonwealth_and_Development_Office "Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office"), which deals with other countries. Then he moved to the Treasury, which handles money matters. Later, he worked for [Lord Hankey](https://kids.kiddle.co/Maurice_Hankey,_1st_Baron_Hankey "Maurice Hankey, 1st Baron Hankey") in the Cabinet Office.

It is thought that Cairncross joined the Communist Party while at Cambridge. However, his brother Alec, who was also at Cambridge, did not notice any political activity from John. Alec remembered John as a "prickly young man" who could be difficult.

Around 1936, while working for the Foreign Service, he was recruited to spy for the Soviets. A man named James Klugmann from the Communist Party of Great Britain recruited him.

## World War II Spy Work

During World War II, John Cairncross worked at [Bletchley Park](https://kids.kiddle.co/GCHQ "GCHQ"). This was a secret place where British experts broke German codes. He worked in "Hut 3," which dealt with ULTRA codes. This meant he had access to secret messages from the German military.

In June 1943, he left Bletchley Park to work for [MI6](https://kids.kiddle.co/MI6 "MI6"), Britain's foreign intelligence service.

### Secret Messages from Bletchley Park

Cairncross secretly passed decoded German documents to the [Soviet Union](https://kids.kiddle.co/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). The Russians gave him the codename _Liszt_ because he loved music. They had told him to get a job at Bletchley Park, which they called _Kurort_.

From 1942, the German High Command used a special machine called _Tunny_ to talk to their army groups. Cairncross would sneak _Tunny_ decryptions out of Bletchley Park. He would hide them in his trousers and then move them to his bag at the train station. He would then meet his Soviet contact in London.

The Soviets were very interested in these messages. They wanted to know about German plans and movements. Cairncross's actions showed the Soviets that the British were able to break German codes.

It was helpful for the Soviets to know German plans, but the British didn't want them to know _how_ they got the information. This was because the Soviet Union's security was not very good. At first, the Soviets thought the information was a trick because it was so good. But they used it and found it to be true.

#### Helping at the Battle of Kursk

One of the most important things Cairncross did was provide information about "Operation Citadel." This was the German plan for a huge attack that led to the [Battle of Kursk](https://kids.kiddle.co/Battle_of_Kursk "Battle of Kursk"). The Battle of Kursk was a major turning point in World War II. After losing this battle, the German army began to retreat.

The _Tunny_ decryptions gave the British early warnings about Operation Citadel. Cairncross provided these raw, secret messages directly to the Soviets. This helped the Soviets prepare for the German attack.

#### Information on Yugoslav Partisans

Axis forces (Germany and its allies) in [Yugoslavia](https://kids.kiddle.co/Yugoslavia "Yugoslavia") used radio to communicate a lot. Bletchley Park intercepted and decoded these messages. They also decoded messages between Yugoslav fighters (called partisans) and the Soviet Union. Cairncross had access to these secret messages. He likely passed information about Yugoslavia to the Soviets as well.

## Working as a Spy

Between 1941 and 1945, Cairncross gave the Soviets 5,832 documents. This number comes from Russian records. In 1944, he joined MI6, the British foreign intelligence service. He worked in the counter-intelligence section. He helped create a list of the German SS forces. Cairncross later said he didn't know that his boss, [Kim Philby](https://kids.kiddle.co/Kim_Philby "Kim Philby"), was also a Soviet spy.

In October 1944, he wrote to his Soviet contacts. He said he was happy his help was useful and proud to have contributed to the Soviet victory. In March 1945, he was offered a yearly payment of £1,000, but he turned it down.

A Russian spy controller, Yuri Modin, claimed Cairncross gave him details about nuclear weapons. These weapons were supposedly going to be placed with [NATO](https://kids.kiddle.co/NATO "NATO") in West Germany. However, there were no such plans at that time. This information might have been a trick to mislead the Soviets.

In 1951, British counterintelligence questioned Cairncross. They asked about his connection to another spy, Donald Maclean, and the Communist Party. Cairncross had been taught by the Soviets how to act during questioning. He told the interrogator that he didn't hide his party membership. He also said he only greeted Maclean at work and didn't keep in touch with him after university.

Cairncross admitted to some wrongdoing in 1951. This happened after MI5 found papers with his handwriting in another spy's apartment. The official report said there wasn't enough proof to charge him with spying at that time.

Evidence from Soviet records shows that Cairncross gave early information about Britain's plans to develop [atomic weapons](https://kids.kiddle.co/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon"). In 1940, he worked for [Maurice Hankey](https://kids.kiddle.co/Maurice_Hankey,_1st_Baron_Hankey "Maurice Hankey, 1st Baron Hankey"), who was on committees discussing atomic weapons. While he didn't give technical details, he let the Soviets know Britain was thinking about making atomic bombs. He was never charged, which led some to believe the government tried to hide his role.

The identity of the "fifth man" in the Cambridge Five was a secret for a long time. It wasn't until 1990 that Oleg Gordievsky, a KGB spy who switched sides, publicly confirmed it was Cairncross. Cairncross worked mostly on his own. He didn't come from the same wealthy background as the other four spies. He knew some of them but claimed he didn't know they were also spying for Russia.

Cairncross left his government job in 1952 and lost his pension. In 1964, he admitted to an investigator named Arthur Martin that he had spied for the Soviets.

In December 1979, a journalist named Barrie Penrose approached Cairncross. Cairncross confessed to him, and the news became widely known. This made many people believe he was the "fifth man," which was later confirmed in 1989.

Cairncross didn't see himself as part of the Cambridge Five. He believed the information he sent to Moscow didn't harm Britain. He felt he was helping an ally (the Soviet Union) who was being denied information by a "right-wing group." Some historians agree that his most important spy work ended with World War II. Unlike the other Cambridge spies, who were from wealthy families, Cairncross was from a working-class background.

## Later Life

After the war, Cairncross worked for the Treasury. He said he stopped working for the Soviet intelligence agency (MGB, later KGB) at this time. However, later KGB reports said he continued to work for them.

After his first confession in 1952, Cairncross lost his government job. He had no money and no work. With some help from his former Soviet contact, he moved to the United States. There, he taught at universities in [Chicago](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chicago "Chicago") and [Cleveland](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cleveland "Cleveland"), Ohio. Cairncross was an expert on French writers. He translated many works by famous 17th-century French poets and playwrights. He also wrote three of his own books.

His teaching career ended after more investigations by MI5. In 1964, Cairncross fully confessed to investigator Arthur Martin. Even though he confessed, he was never charged with spying. His confession was made in the US and couldn't be used in a British court. MI5 asked him to return to Britain to confess again, but he refused.

In 1967, Cairncross moved to [Rome](https://kids.kiddle.co/Rome "Rome"), Italy. He worked as a translator for the United Nations [Food and Agriculture Organization](https://kids.kiddle.co/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization "Food and Agriculture Organization"). He also did work for banks. In 1970, he moved to [France](https://kids.kiddle.co/France "France").

In December 1979, his secret became public. A former government worker hinted to a journalist that there was another spy in the Foreign Office. The journalist figured out it was Cairncross and confronted him.

Cairncross's confession became front-page news. In 1981, Prime Minister [Margaret Thatcher](https://kids.kiddle.co/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher") told the British Parliament that Cairncross was a Soviet agent. She said he was living in England and writing his memoirs. His role as the "fifth man" was confirmed in 1990.

Cairncross retired to the south of France. In 1995, he returned to Britain and married Gayle Brinkerhoff. This was one month after his first wife, Gabriella Oppenheim, died. Later that year, he died at age 82 after having a stroke.

Unlike many other spies, Cairncross was never put in jail for spying. He was once jailed in Rome for issues involving money, but not for being a spy.

Cairncross's autobiography, _The Enigma Spy_, was published in 1997. In the book, he denied being the "fifth man" and even said such a person didn't exist. Many critics felt the book was his last attempt to clear his name.

## In Books and Movies

John Cairncross has been shown in several TV shows and movies:

*   In the 2003 BBC TV series _Cambridge Spies_, he is shown as not wanting to give Bletchley Park information to the Russians. He was worried German spies had gotten into the Red Army.
*   He appears in the comic book _India Dreams_.
*   He is shown as the fifth of the Cambridge Five in [Frederick Forsyth](https://kids.kiddle.co/Frederick_Forsyth "Frederick Forsyth")'s novel _The Deceiver_.
*   In the 2014 film _The Imitation Game_, Cairncross is played by [Allen Leech](https://kids.kiddle.co/Allen_Leech "Allen Leech"). He is shown as a codebreaker at Bletchley Park. The movie suggests he was an unknowing double agent used by MI6 to pass information to the Soviets. However, historians and Cairncross's own book confirm he spied for the Soviets because of his own beliefs. MI6 didn't find out until much later.

## Awards

*   Order of the Red Banner: This award was given to him for successfully getting information about German plans and operations during World War II.

**Phillip Roger Noyce**[AO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Officer of the Order of Australia") (born 29 April 1950) is an Australian film and television director. Since 1977, he has directed over 19 feature films in various genres, including historical drama (_[Newsfront](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsfront "Newsfront")_, _[Rabbit-Proof Fence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbit-Proof\_Fence "Rabbit-Proof Fence")_, _[The Quiet American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Quiet\_American\_(2002\_film) "The Quiet American (2002 film)")_); thrillers (_[Dead Calm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_Calm\_(film) "Dead Calm (film)")_, _[Sliver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sliver\_(film) "Sliver (film)")_, _[The Bone Collector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bone\_Collector "The Bone Collector")_); and action films (_[Blind Fury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind\_Fury "Blind Fury")_, _[The Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Saint\_(1997\_film) "The Saint (1997 film)")_, _[Salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt\_(2010\_film) "Salt (2010 film)")_). He has also directed the [Jack Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ryan_(character) "Jack Ryan (character)") adaptations _[Patriot Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot\_Games\_(film) "Patriot Games (film)")_ (1992) and _[Clear and Present Danger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clear\_and\_Present\_Danger\_(film) "Clear and Present Danger (film)")_ (1994), as well as the [2014 adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Giver_(film) "The Giver (film)") of [Lois Lowry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lois_Lowry "Lois Lowry")'s _[The Giver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Giver "The Giver")_.

Noyce has worked at various times with such actors as [Val Kilmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Kilmer "Val Kilmer"), [Harrison Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrison_Ford "Harrison Ford"), [Denzel Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denzel_Washington "Denzel Washington"), [Michael Caine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Caine "Michael Caine"), [Angelina Jolie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angelina_Jolie "Angelina Jolie"), [Nicole Kidman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicole_Kidman "Nicole Kidman"), [Meryl Streep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meryl_Streep "Meryl Streep"), [Rutger Hauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutger_Hauer "Rutger Hauer") and three films with [Thora Birch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thora_Birch "Thora Birch") over 25 years. He has also directed, written and executive-produced television programmes in both Australia and North America, including _[The Cowra Breakout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cowra\_Breakout\_(miniseries) "The Cowra Breakout (miniseries)")_, _[Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam\_(miniseries) "Vietnam (miniseries)")_, _[Revenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenge\_(TV\_series) "Revenge (TV series)")_, _[Roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots\_(2016\_miniseries) "Roots (2016 miniseries)")_, and [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix")'s _[What/If](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What/If "What/If")._

Noyce's work has won him several accolades, including [AACTA Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AACTA_Awards "AACTA Awards") for Best Film, Best Director and a special [Longford Lyell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AACTA_Longford_Lyell_Award "AACTA Longford Lyell Award") lifetime achievement award.

**Margaret Hilda Thatcher** (born Margaret Roberts; 13 October 1925 – 8 April 2013) was a British politician. She served as the [Prime Minister of the United Kingdom](https://kids.kiddle.co/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") from 1979 to 1990. She was also the Leader of the Conservative Party from 1975 to 1990.

Margaret Thatcher was the first female British prime minister. She was also the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century. As prime minister, she introduced new economic policies. These policies became known as Thatcherism. A Soviet journalist gave her the nickname "**Iron Lady**". This name stuck because of her strong and determined leadership style.

Thatcher studied chemistry at [Somerville College, Oxford](https://kids.kiddle.co/Somerville_College,_Oxford "Somerville College, Oxford"). She worked briefly as a research chemist before becoming a [barrister](https://kids.kiddle.co/Lawyer "Lawyer") (a type of lawyer). In 1959, she was elected as a [Member of Parliament](https://kids.kiddle.co/Member_of_Parliament "Member of Parliament") for [Finchley](https://kids.kiddle.co/Finchley_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Finchley (UK Parliament constituency)"). She later became the [Secretary of State for Education and Science](https://kids.kiddle.co/Secretary_of_State_for_Education "Secretary of State for Education") in 1970. In 1975, she became the [Leader of the Opposition](https://kids.kiddle.co/Leader_of_the_Opposition_(United_Kingdom) "Leader of the Opposition (United Kingdom)"). She was the first woman to lead a major political party in the United Kingdom.

After winning the 1979 general election, Thatcher became prime minister. She introduced economic policies to reduce high inflation and improve Britain's economy. Her ideas focused on reducing government control (deregulation), selling off state-owned companies (privatisation), and limiting the power of trade unions.

Her popularity dropped at first due to a recession and rising unemployment. However, Britain's victory in the 1982 [Falklands War](https://kids.kiddle.co/Falklands_War "Falklands War") and an improving economy brought back public support. This led to her re-election in 1983. She won a third term in 1987. But a new local tax, the "poll tax," became very unpopular. Her views on the [European Economic Community](https://kids.kiddle.co/European_Economic_Community "European Economic Community") also caused disagreements within her government. She resigned in 1990 after a challenge to her leadership. [John Major](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Major "John Major") became the new prime minister.

After leaving Parliament in 1992, she became Baroness Thatcher, a [life peer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Life_peer "Life peer") in the [House of Lords](https://kids.kiddle.co/House_of_Lords "House of Lords"). She died from a stroke in 2013 at the age of 87. Margaret Thatcher is seen as a very important figure in British politics. Her time as prime minister changed Britain's economic and political direction.

## Early Life and Education

Birthplace in Grantham

[![Image 5: The corner of a terraced suburban street. The lower storey is a corner shop, now advertising as a chiropractic clinic. The building is two storeys high, with some parts three storeys high. It was formerly Alfred Roberts' shop.](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/a/ae/Maison_natale_de_Margaret_Thatcher%2C_Grantham.JPG/306px-Maison_natale_de_Margaret_Thatcher%2C_Grantham.JPG)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Maison_natale_de_Margaret_Thatcher,_Grantham.JPG)

2009 photograph of her father's former shop

[![Image 6: photograph of a plaque reading "Birth place of the Rt.Hon. Margaret Thatcher, M.P. First woman prime minister of Great Britain and Northern Ireland"](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/4/4c/Plaque%2C_maison_natale_de_Margaret_Thatcher.JPG/258px-Plaque%2C_maison_natale_de_Margaret_Thatcher.JPG)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Plaque,_maison_natale_de_Margaret_Thatcher.JPG)

Commemorative plaque

Margaret and her elder sister were raised in the bottom of two flats on North Parade.

### Childhood and School Days (1925–1943)

Margaret Hilda Roberts was born on 13 October 1925 in [Grantham](https://kids.kiddle.co/Grantham "Grantham"), England. Her parents were Alfred Roberts and Beatrice Ethel Stephenson. Her father owned a shop and was also a local politician. He raised Margaret and her older sister Muriel as strict Methodists.

Margaret grew up helping in her father's grocery shop. In 1938, before World War II, her family briefly gave shelter to a Jewish teenage girl. This girl had escaped from Nazi Germany. Margaret and her sister saved their pocket money to help pay for the girl's journey.

Margaret attended Huntingtower Road Primary School. She then won a scholarship to Kesteven and Grantham Girls' School. Her school reports showed she worked hard and always improved. She was the head girl in her final year. During World War II, she volunteered as a fire watcher.

In 1943, Margaret was accepted to study chemistry at [Somerville College, Oxford](https://kids.kiddle.co/Somerville_College,_Oxford "Somerville College, Oxford"). This was a women's college. She started her studies there in October 1943.

### University Life at Oxford (1943–1947)

[![Image 7: Somerville College](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/8f/Somerville_College.jpg/230px-Somerville_College.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Somerville_College.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Somerville_College.jpg "Enlarge")

 Roberts studied chemistry at [Somerville College](https://kids.kiddle.co/Somerville_College,_Oxford "Somerville College, Oxford") (_pictured_) in 1943–1947

Margaret Roberts graduated from Oxford in 1947 with a degree in chemistry. She focused on [X-ray crystallography](https://kids.kiddle.co/X-ray_crystallography "X-ray crystallography"). She also earned a Master of Arts degree in 1950. Even though she studied chemistry, she was already thinking about a career in law and politics. She was very proud to be the first prime minister with a science degree.

While at Oxford, Margaret was known for being serious and focused. She became President of the Oxford University Conservative Association in 1946. She was influenced by political books that argued against too much government control.

### Starting Her Career (1947–1951)

After university, Margaret worked as a research chemist for a company called BX Plastics. In 1948, she applied for a job at ICI but was not hired. She then worked for J. Lyons and Co., helping to develop ingredients for ice cream.

She joined the local Conservative Association. In 1948, she attended a party conference. She was chosen as a Conservative candidate for Dartford in 1950. At a dinner, she met [Denis Thatcher](https://kids.kiddle.co/Denis_Thatcher "Denis Thatcher"), a successful businessman. They married in December 1951. Denis supported her studies to become a lawyer. She qualified as a barrister in 1953. Later that year, their twins, [Carol](https://kids.kiddle.co/Carol_Thatcher "Carol Thatcher") and Mark, were born.

## Early Political Journey

### Becoming a Member of Parliament (1959–1970)

In the 1950 and 1951 general elections, Margaret Thatcher ran for the Conservative Party in Dartford. She lost both times but showed great determination. She was the youngest and only female Conservative candidate at the time.

After taking a break for her young children, Thatcher was selected as the candidate for [Finchley](https://kids.kiddle.co/Finchley_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Finchley (UK Parliament constituency)") in 1958. She was elected as a Member of Parliament (MP) for Finchley in the 1959 election. Her first speech in Parliament was about making local council meetings open to the public. This idea became law.

In 1961, she was promoted to a junior government role as Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry for Pensions. She was the youngest woman to hold such a position. After the Conservatives lost the 1964 election, she became a spokeswoman on housing. She supported the policy of allowing people to buy their [council houses](https://kids.kiddle.co/Council_house "Council house"). In 1966, she moved to the Shadow Treasury team. She argued against government controls on prices and incomes.

In 1967, she visited the United States to meet political figures and learn about economic issues. After this trip, she was appointed to the Shadow Cabinet. She became the spokeswoman for fuel and power, and later for transport and education.

### Education Secretary (1970–1974)
