# Guy Burgess facts for kids

[Kids Encyclopedia Facts](https://kids.kiddle.co/)

| Quick facts for kids Guy Burgess |
| --- |
| [![Image 3: Guy Burgess.jpg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/d/d0/Guy_Burgess.jpg/300px-Guy_Burgess.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Guy_Burgess.jpg) Photo portrait, before 1951 |
| Born | (1911-04-16)16 April 1911 [Devonport, Devon](https://kids.kiddle.co/Devonport,_Plymouth "Devonport, Plymouth"), England |
| Died | 30 August 1963(1963-08-30) (aged 52) Moscow, [Soviet Union](https://kids.kiddle.co/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") |
| Other names | Codenames "Mädchen", "Hicks" |
| Known for | Member of "Cambridge Five" spy ring; defected to Soviet Union 1951 |

**Guy Francis de Moncy Burgess** (born April 16, 1911 – died August 30, 1963) was a British diplomat and a secret agent for the [Soviet Union](https://kids.kiddle.co/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). He was part of a group known as the [Cambridge Five](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cambridge_Five "Cambridge Five") spy ring. This group worked secretly from the mid-1930s until the early years of the [Cold War](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cold_War "Cold War").

In 1951, Burgess moved to the Soviet Union with another spy, Donald Maclean. This event caused big problems for the intelligence sharing between Britain and the United States. It also created a lot of trouble and low morale within Britain's foreign and diplomatic services for a long time.

Guy Burgess came from a middle-class family. He went to famous schools like [Eton College](https://kids.kiddle.co/Eton_College "Eton College") and [Trinity College, Cambridge](https://kids.kiddle.co/Trinity_College,_Cambridge "Trinity College, Cambridge"). At Cambridge, he became interested in left-wing politics and joined the British [Communist Party](https://kids.kiddle.co/Communist_Party_of_Great_Britain "Communist Party of Great Britain"). In 1935, Soviet intelligence recruited him. This happened because [Harold "Kim" Philby](https://kids.kiddle.co/Kim_Philby "Kim Philby"), who later became a double-agent, suggested him.

After leaving Cambridge, Burgess worked for the [BBC](https://kids.kiddle.co/BBC "BBC") as a producer. For a short time, he also worked as a full-time intelligence officer for [MI6](https://kids.kiddle.co/MI6 "MI6"). Then, in 1944, he joined the [Foreign Office](https://kids.kiddle.co/Foreign_Office "Foreign Office").

At the Foreign Office, Burgess worked as a private secretary for [Hector McNeil](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hector_McNeil "Hector McNeil"). McNeil was the deputy to [Ernest Bevin](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ernest_Bevin "Ernest Bevin"), who was the Foreign Secretary. This job gave Burgess access to many secret documents about Britain's foreign policy after 1945. It is thought that he gave thousands of these documents to his Soviet contacts. In 1950, he became the second secretary at the British Embassy in Washington. He was sent home from this job because of repeated problems with his conduct. Even though he was not suspected of being a spy at this time, Burgess went with Maclean when Maclean had to flee to Moscow in May 1951 because he was about to be caught.

No one in the West knew where Burgess was until 1956. Then, he appeared with Maclean at a short press conference in Moscow. He said his reason for leaving was to help improve relations between the Soviet Union and the West. He never left the Soviet Union. Friends and journalists from Britain often visited him. Most of them said he lived a lonely life. He never regretted his actions and did not believe his activities were treason. He had enough money and things he needed, but his health got worse due to his habits. He died in 1963.

Experts find it hard to know how much damage Burgess's spying caused. However, they believe that the problems he caused in relations between Britain and America were perhaps more helpful to the Soviets than any secret information he provided. Guy Burgess's life has often been used in books and plays. Famous examples include the 1981 play _Another Country_ by Julian Mitchell and its 1984 film version.

Burgess also told the Soviets about the [Information Research Department](https://kids.kiddle.co/Information_Research_Department "Information Research Department") (IRD). This was a secret part of the [Foreign Office](https://kids.kiddle.co/Foreign,_Commonwealth_and_Development_Office "Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office"). It dealt with Cold War and pro-colonial propaganda. However, Burgess was quickly fired from the IRD for breaking rules.

## Life Story

### Early Years and School

[![Image 4: MK17840 Eton College](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/1/1c/MK17840_Eton_College.jpg/230px-MK17840_Eton_College.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:MK17840_Eton_College.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:MK17840_Eton_College.jpg "Enlarge")

 Eton College, which Burgess attended in 1924 and between 1927 and 1930

The Burgess family's history in England goes back to 1592. That's when Abraham de Bourgeous de Chantilly came to Britain. He was a refugee from religious troubles in France. The family settled in [Kent](https://kids.kiddle.co/Kent "Kent") and became wealthy, mostly as bankers. Later, some family members joined the military. Guy Burgess's grandfather, Henry Miles Burgess, was an officer in the Royal Artillery. He served mostly in the [Middle East](https://kids.kiddle.co/Middle_East "Middle East").

His youngest son, Malcolm Kingsford de Moncy Burgess, was born in [Aden](https://kids.kiddle.co/Aden "Aden") in 1881. Malcolm had a regular career in the Royal Navy. He eventually became a [commander](https://kids.kiddle.co/Commander_(Royal_Navy) "Commander (Royal Navy)"). In 1907, he married Evelyn Gillman, whose father was a rich banker from [Portsmouth](https://kids.kiddle.co/Portsmouth "Portsmouth"). The couple lived in [Devonport](https://kids.kiddle.co/Devonport,_Plymouth "Devonport, Plymouth"). Their first son, Guy Francis de Moncy, was born there on April 16, 1911. His brother, Nigel, was born two years later.

The Gillman family's wealth made sure Guy's home life was comfortable. Guy probably had a governess for his first schooling. At age nine, he became a [boarder](https://kids.kiddle.co/Boarding_school "Boarding school") at Lockers Park School. This was a private preparatory school near [Hemel Hempstead](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hemel_Hempstead "Hemel Hempstead"). He did well there, getting good grades and playing for the school's football team. He finished the Lockers curriculum a year early. He was too young to go straight to the Royal Naval College at [Dartmouth](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dartmouth,_Devon "Dartmouth, Devon"). Instead, he spent a year at [Eton College](https://kids.kiddle.co/Eton_College "Eton College") starting in January 1924.

After his father retired from the navy, the family moved to West Meon in [Hampshire](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hampshire "Hampshire"). On September 15, 1924, Malcolm died suddenly from a heart attack. Despite this sad event, Guy's education continued as planned. In January 1925, he started at Dartmouth. At Dartmouth, there were strict rules and a strong focus on order. Burgess did well in this environment, both in his studies and in sports. The college thought he would make an "excellent officer." However, an eye test in 1927 showed a problem. This meant he could not have a career in the navy's main officer branch. Burgess was not interested in other navy jobs, so he left Dartmouth in July 1927 and went back to Eton.

Burgess's second time at Eton, from 1927 to 1930, was mostly good. He did well in his studies and made many friends. He started to build a network of contacts that would be helpful later in his life. People remembered Burgess as lively and a bit unusual because of his left-wing political ideas. In January 1930, he won a history scholarship to [Trinity College, Cambridge](https://kids.kiddle.co/Trinity_College,_Cambridge "Trinity College, Cambridge"). He finished school with more awards in history and drawing. He always remembered Eton fondly. His biographers said he was never embarrassed about being educated in such a privileged school.

### Time at Cambridge University

#### Student Life

[![Image 5: Trinity College - Great Court 02](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/9/94/Trinity_College_-_Great_Court_02.jpg/450px-Trinity_College_-_Great_Court_02.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Trinity_College_-_Great_Court_02.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Trinity_College_-_Great_Court_02.jpg "Enlarge")

 Great Court, Trinity College, Cambridge

Burgess arrived at Cambridge in October 1930. He quickly got involved in many student activities. Not everyone liked him; some found him self-centered and unreliable. But others thought he was funny and good company. After one term, he joined the Trinity Historical Society. This group was for the brightest students in history. Here, he met [Harold ("Kim") Philby](https://kids.kiddle.co/Kim_Philby "Kim Philby") and Jim Lees. Lees was a former miner studying on a scholarship. Burgess found his working-class views interesting.

In June 1931, Burgess designed the [stage sets](https://kids.kiddle.co/Set_construction "Set construction") for a student play. It was [Bernard Shaw](https://kids.kiddle.co/George_Bernard_Shaw "George Bernard Shaw")'s _Captain Brassbound's Conversion_, with [Michael Redgrave](https://kids.kiddle.co/Michael_Redgrave "Michael Redgrave") as the main actor. Redgrave thought Burgess was "one of the bright stars of the university scene." He had a reputation for being able to do anything.

In 1931, Burgess met [Anthony Blunt](https://kids.kiddle.co/Anthony_Blunt "Anthony Blunt"), who was four years older and a postgraduate student at Trinity. They shared interests in art and became friends. Blunt was a member of an intellectual group called the "Apostles". In 1932, he helped Burgess get elected to this group. This gave Burgess many more chances to meet important people. Being an Apostle was for life, so he met many leading thinkers of the time. These included [G. M. Trevelyan](https://kids.kiddle.co/G._M._Trevelyan "G. M. Trevelyan"), a history professor, the writer [E. M. Forster](https://kids.kiddle.co/E._M._Forster "E. M. Forster"), and the economist [John Maynard Keynes](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Maynard_Keynes "John Maynard Keynes").

In the early 1930s, the world's political situation was very unstable. In Britain, the [financial crisis of 1931](https://kids.kiddle.co/Great_Depression_in_the_United_Kingdom#National_Government "Great Depression in the United Kingdom") showed that capitalism had problems. In Germany, the rise of [Nazism](https://kids.kiddle.co/Nazism "Nazism") caused growing worry. These events made people in Cambridge and elsewhere more radical. Burgess's interest in [Marxism](https://kids.kiddle.co/Marxism "Marxism") grew deeper. He had learned about it from friends like Lees. He also heard the historian [Maurice Dobb](https://kids.kiddle.co/Maurice_Dobb "Maurice Dobb") talk about "Communism: a Political and Historical Theory." Another influence was David Guest, who led the Cambridge University Socialist Society (CUSS). Under Guest's influence, Burgess began studying the works of [Marx](https://kids.kiddle.co/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx") and [Lenin](https://kids.kiddle.co/Vladimir_Lenin "Vladimir Lenin").

In 1932, Burgess earned first-class honours in the first part of his history degree. He was expected to get similar honors the next year. But political activities took up too much of his time. By his final exams in 1933, he was not ready. He fell ill during the exams and could not finish them. The examiners gave him an _aegrotat_. This is an unclassified degree given to students who deserve honors but cannot finish their exams due to illness.

#### Postgraduate Studies and Political Action

[![Image 6: Cambridge War Memorial](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/e/ed/Cambridge_War_Memorial.jpg/230px-Cambridge_War_Memorial.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Cambridge_War_Memorial.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Cambridge_War_Memorial.jpg "Enlarge")

 Cambridge War Memorial, focus of demonstrations in November 1933

Even with his disappointing degree, Burgess returned to Cambridge in October 1933. He became a postgraduate student and teaching assistant. His research topic was "Bourgeois Revolution in Seventeenth-Century England." But he spent most of his time on political activism. That winter, he officially joined the British [Communist Party](https://kids.kiddle.co/Communist_Party_of_Great_Britain "Communist Party of Great Britain"). He became part of its group within CUSS.

On November 11, 1933, he joined a large protest against the city's [Armistice Day](https://kids.kiddle.co/Armistice_Day "Armistice Day") celebrations. The protesters wanted to lay a wreath with a peace message at the [Cambridge War Memorial](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cambridge_War_Memorial "Cambridge War Memorial"). They succeeded, even with attacks and counter-protests. These included "a hail of pro-war eggs and tomatoes." Next to Burgess was Donald Maclean. Maclean was a language student and an active CUSS member. In February 1934, Burgess, Maclean, and other CUSS members welcomed groups from Tyneside and Tees-side. These groups were part of the National Hunger March as they passed through Cambridge on their way to London.

When not in Cambridge, Burgess often visited [Oxford](https://kids.kiddle.co/Oxford "Oxford") to meet like-minded people. He became friends with Goronwy Rees, a young Fellow at [All Souls College](https://kids.kiddle.co/All_Souls_College,_Oxford "All Souls College, Oxford"). Rees had planned to visit the [Soviet Union](https://kids.kiddle.co/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") in the summer of 1934 but couldn't go. Burgess took his place. During this trip in June–July 1934, Burgess met some important people. He might have met [Nikolai Bukharin](https://kids.kiddle.co/Nikolai_Bukharin "Nikolai Bukharin"), a former secretary of the Comintern. When he returned, Burgess didn't have much to say. He only mentioned the "appalling" housing but praised the country for having no unemployment.

#### Becoming a Soviet Agent

When Burgess came back to Cambridge in October 1934, his chances of becoming a college fellow and having an academic career were fading. He stopped his research because he found out that a new book by Basil Willey covered the same topic. He started a new study on the [Indian Rebellion of 1857](https://kids.kiddle.co/Indian_Rebellion_of_1857 "Indian Rebellion of 1857"). However, he spent most of his time on politics.

[![Image 7: Guy Burgess 1935](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/a/a9/Guy_Burgess_1935.jpg/230px-Guy_Burgess_1935.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Guy_Burgess_1935.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Guy_Burgess_1935.jpg "Enlarge")

 Burgess in 1935

In early 1934, Arnold Deutsch, a long-time Soviet secret agent, arrived in London. He pretended to be doing research at [University College, London](https://kids.kiddle.co/University_College_London "University College London"). Known as "Otto," his job was to recruit the smartest students from Britain's best universities. These students might later hold important positions in British institutions. In June 1934, he recruited Philby. Philby had caught the Soviets' attention earlier that year in Vienna. Philby recommended several of his Cambridge friends to Deutsch. These included Maclean, who was already working in the [Foreign Office](https://kids.kiddle.co/Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Office "Foreign and Commonwealth Office"). He also recommended Burgess, though he had some doubts because Burgess was sometimes unpredictable.

Deutsch thought Burgess was worth the risk. He described him as "an extremely well-educated fellow, with valuable social connections, and the inclinations of an adventurer." Burgess was given the codename "Mädchen," meaning "Girl." Later, it was changed to "Hicks." Burgess then convinced Blunt that working for the Soviets was the best way to fight [fascism](https://kids.kiddle.co/Fascism "Fascism"). A few years later, another Apostle, [John Cairncross](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Cairncross "John Cairncross"), was recruited by Burgess and Blunt. This completed the spy ring often called the "[Cambridge Five](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cambridge_Five "Cambridge Five")".

Finally, realizing he had no future at Cambridge, Burgess left in April 1935. The Soviet intelligence services wanted Burgess to join British intelligence. To do this, he needed to publicly show that he was no longer a communist. So, he resigned from the Communist Party. He publicly said he was no longer a communist, which surprised his former friends. He then looked for a job. He applied for positions with the Conservative Research Department and Conservative Central Office but was not successful. He also tried to get a teaching job at Eton but was rejected.

In late 1935, Burgess took a temporary job. He became a personal assistant to [John Macnamara](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Macnamara "John Macnamara"). Macnamara was a recently elected [Conservative](https://kids.kiddle.co/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)")[Member of Parliament](https://kids.kiddle.co/Member_of_Parliament#United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Northern_Ireland "Member of Parliament") (MP). Macnamara was on the right side of his party. He and Burgess joined the Anglo-German Fellowship. This group promoted friendship with [Nazi Germany](https://kids.kiddle.co/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany"). This allowed Burgess to hide his political past very well. It also helped him gather important information about Germany's foreign policy plans. Within the Fellowship, Burgess would say that fascism was "the wave of the future." But in other places, like with the Apostles, he was more careful. His work with Macnamara involved several trips to Germany.

In the autumn of 1936, Burgess met Jack Hewit in a bar in [The Strand](https://kids.kiddle.co/Strand,_London "Strand, London"). Hewit was nineteen and wanted to be a dancer in London. Hewit

**Sir David Lean** (25 March 1908–16 April 1991) was an English filmmaker and editor, widely considered one of the most important figures of [British cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_Kingdom "Cinema of the United Kingdom"). # After Gremlins and The Goonies, what other 80s films need a remake?

This article is more than 12 years old

With The Goonies, Gremlins and Karate Kid all set to return to cinemas, what other 80s hits are crying out for a modern reboot?

Ben Travis

Tue 8 Apr 2014 07.38 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Apr 2014 07.46 EDT

[Share](mailto:?subject=After%20Gremlins%20and%20The%20Goonies,%20what%20other%2080s%20films%20need%20a%20remake?&body=https://www.theguardian.com/film/filmblog/2014/apr/08/after-gremlins-and-the-goonies-what-other-80s-films-would-you-like-to-see-remade?CMP=share_btn_url)

[174 174](http://www.theguardian.com/film/filmblog/2014/apr/08/after-gremlins-and-the-goonies-what-other-80s-films-would-you-like-to-see-remade#comments)

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

Children of the 80s, get ready: your youth is about to come crashing back into cinemas, older, greyer, and probably a little softer around the middle than you remember. Within the space of 48 hours, three franchise revivals have been mooted that might send misty-eyed nostalgics to despair.

First up, Richard Donner [appears to be on board](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2014/apr/07/goonies-sequel-richard-donner-feldman-brolin-astin-cohen) for a sequel to his 1985 Spielberg-produced pirate classic The Goonies. Bringing back the key players of the original may prove challenging – Josh Brolin, Sean Astin and Corey Feldman were all involved first time around – and though the prospect of a reunion might raise a nostalgic smile, the question remains: what are they going to do this time around? Are the cast going to be believably geared up for another adventure 30 years on? While The Goonies may have flashy ‘80s trappings, famous child stars and a Cyndi Lauper song, at its heart is an old fashioned story of treasure maps, grouchy baddies and pirate ships – is an audience raised on Michael Bay interested in this sort of goofy fun anymore?

![Image 3: Jeff Cohen, Anne Ramsey, Jonathan Ke Quan, Corey Feldman and Sean Astin in The Goonies](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/static/sys-images/Guardian/Pix/pictures/2014/4/8/1396956892965/3d7a6718-f78f-4aa3-8caa-a0eb1c673f36-2060x1236.jpeg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)[View image in fullscreen](http://www.theguardian.com/film/filmblog/2014/apr/08/after-gremlins-and-the-goonies-what-other-80s-films-would-you-like-to-see-remade#img-2)

Jeff Cohen, Anne Ramsey, Jonathan Ke Quan, Corey Feldman and Sean Astin in The Goonies Photograph: Allstar/WARNER BROS/Sportsphoto Ltd. Photograph: Allstar/WARNER BROS/Sportsphoto Ltd./Allstar

It’s not just The Goonies who will be making a comeback soon. Gremlins, another Spielberg-produced classic that’s far darker than you might remember, is apparently being [fast-tracked for a reboot,](http://www.digitalspy.co.uk/movies/news/a562768/gremlins-reboot-movie-fast-tracked-at-warner-bros.html) begging further questions: can we get away with kids putting gremlins in blenders in 2014? And will the wonderful puppetry make a comeback, or will the mogwai be revived in soulless CGI?

The Karate Kid is also set to crane-kick its way back to the cinema, with [a sequel to the 2010 remake](http://www.bleedingcool.com/2014/04/07/its-jackie-chans-60th-birthday-so-a-sequel-to-the-karate-kid-gets-announced%E2%80%8F/) starring Jaden Smith and Jackie Chan. That reboot wasn’t quite the travesty that fans of the original feared it would be, effectively filling a gap in the market for simple, well-constructed storytelling for a young audience. Though it won’t have replaced the original in the hearts of 40-somethings, it nevertheless proved the nuts-and-bolts mechanics and plot beats of The Karate Kid are indestructible - though where a sequel chooses to go remains to be seen.

There’s a chance that this could all prove worthwhile. Since Spielberg left his classic suburban adventure stories behind him in the early ‘90s, no-one ever really stood up to take his mantle. The Transformers generation could perhaps do with a bit of The Goonies, Gremlins and Karate Kid spirit, as JJ Abrams’ Super 8 proved.

Some ‘80s revisits might work well – the [long-gestating Beetlejuice sequel](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2014/feb/17/michael-keaton-beetlejuice-sequel-burton) could provide a return to form for Tim Burton, who has lately found himself stuck in a genre-muddled rut. However, lines must be drawn – should a remake of Stand By Me ever rear its ugly head, all involved should take a long hard look at themselves.

If the Goonies ‘R’ good enough for a cinematic return, who else would you like to see back on the big screen? Should Back To The Future come back in the future? Do we need to find out what Elliott got up to after E.T. phoned home? Let us know which films you think might work in the comments.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Pakistani actor (1943–2023)

This article is about the television actor. For other uses, see [Shakeel (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel_(disambiguation) "Shakeel (disambiguation)").

**Yousuf Kamal** ([Urdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urdu_language "Urdu language"): یوسف کمال; 29 May 1943 – 29 June 2023), known professionally as **Shakeel Yousuf** ([Urdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urdu_language "Urdu language"): شکیل یوسف), was a Pakistani actor best known for his roles in the PTV drama series _[Uncle Urfi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle\_Urfi "Uncle Urfi")_ (1972), as Taimoor Ahmad in _[Ankahi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankahi "Ankahi")_ (1982) and as Mehboob Ahmed in PTV's _[Aangan Terha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aangan\_Terha "Aangan Terha")_ (1984).

Due to his blue eyes and looks he was compared to Hollywood actor [Tony Curtis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Curtis "Tony Curtis").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-:0-2)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shakeel&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Shakeel was born Yusuf Kamal in [Bhopal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhopal "Bhopal"), [British India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_India "British India") in 1943.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-Tribune-3) His family later migrated to [Karachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karachi "Karachi"), Pakistan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-:0-2)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-360degrees-1)

His father was from [Lucknow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucknow "Lucknow"), where Shakeel spent his initial years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-4) He received his primary education from an English-medium school in Lucknow and in a French missionary school in India, the [La Martiniere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Martini%C3%A8re_College,_Lucknow "La Martinière College, Lucknow").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-360degrees-1) Following the [1947 partition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India "Partition of India"), his family moved to [Karachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karachi "Karachi"), Pakistan in 1952, settling down in [Nazimabad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazimabad "Nazimabad"), where Shakeel continued his education.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-:0-2)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shakeel&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Radio and cinema

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shakeel&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Radio and cinema")]

Shakeel began his career in Karachi, where he was introduced to broadcasting through a school programme on [Radio Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Pakistan "Radio Pakistan") and later to theatre by a college teacher. He initially appeared in films during the 1960s under the name Yousuf Kamal, later adopting the screen name Shakeel, though he achieved limited success in cinema; his first movie was _Honehar_ (1966) as the second male lead, co-starring [Waheed Murad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waheed_Murad "Waheed Murad")_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite\_note-Tribune-3)_ His career gained momentum with the expansion of television broadcasting from Karachi following the establishment of [Pakistan Television Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Television_Corporation "Pakistan Television Corporation") (PTV) in 1968.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-:0-2)

### Television

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shakeel&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Television")]

#### 1970s-1980s:leading roles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shakeel&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1970s-1980s:leading roles")]

He rose to prominence in the early 1970s with the Eid television play _Happy Eid Mubarak_ (1970), written by [Haseena Moin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haseena_Moin "Haseena Moin"), marking both his breakthrough role and the beginning of a long association with the writer. His pairing with _Neelofer Aleem_ was widely appreciated and led to the popular PTV serial _[Shehzori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shehzori "Shehzori")_ (1972). During this period, Shakeel established himself as a leading romantic actor in television dramas, including _[Zair Zabar Paish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zair,\_Zabar,\_Pesh "Zair, Zabar, Pesh")_ (1974) and _[Parchhaiyaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parchhaiyan\_(film) "Parchhaiyan (film)")_ (1976), the latter being the first colour serial aired on PTV.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-:0-2)

In the late 1970s and 1980s, Shakeel expanded into leading roles, continuing to appear in major productions. His notable performances include _[Uncle Urfi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle\_Urfi "Uncle Urfi")_ (1975), _[Ankahi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankahi "Ankahi")_ (1982), where he played Taimur, and _[Aangan Terha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aangan\_Terha "Aangan Terha")_ (1984), written by [Anwar Maqsood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anwar_Maqsood "Anwar Maqsood"). He also worked extensively in dramas by _[Fatima Surayya Bajia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatima\_Surayya\_Bajia "Fatima Surayya Bajia")_, including _[Uroosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aroosa "Aroosa")_ (1994), _Shaheen_ (1986), and the science-fiction series _Tick Tick Company_ (1979).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-:0-2)

#### 1990s and later career: character roles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shakeel&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1990s and later career: character roles")]

In the 1990s, Shakeel took on more complex roles, most notably portraying a bureaucrat in _[Chand Girhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chand\_Grehan "Chand Grehan")_ (1992), written by [Asghar Nadeem Syed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asghar_Nadeem_Syed "Asghar Nadeem Syed"). He also appeared in theatre productions and remained selective in his television work. In cinema, he portrayed [Nawabzada Liaquat Ali Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaquat_Ali_Khan "Liaquat Ali Khan") in the biographical film [_Jinnah_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinnah_(1998_film) "Jinnah (1998 film)") (1998), directed by [Jamil Dehlavi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi "Jamil Dehlavi").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-:0-2)

In December 2012, Shakeel performed a 35-minute one-man stage show in Karachi, in which he addressed themes of war, poverty, and social decline. During the performance, he expressed the view that prolonged conflict leads to hunger and economic hardship, and reflected on an earlier period characterized by greater social cohesion, honesty, and mutual concern.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakeel#cite_note-Tribune-3) Numerous celebrities including [Fatima Surayya Bajia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatima_Surayya_Bajia "Fatima Surayya Bajia"),

**Joseph Walton Losey III** (born January 14, 1909 – died June 22, 1984) was an American director for both theatre and films. He also worked as a producer and screenwriter. Born in Wisconsin, he studied in Germany with a famous writer named [Bertolt Brecht](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bertolt_Brecht "Bertolt Brecht").

Later, he returned to the United States. In the 1950s, he was put on the [Hollywood blacklist](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hollywood_blacklist "Hollywood blacklist"). This meant he was not allowed to work in Hollywood because of his political views. So, he moved to Europe, mostly to the United Kingdom, where he made the rest of his movies. Some of his most successful films were _The Servant_ (1963) and _The Go-Between_ (1971). These were written by [Harold Pinter](https://kids.kiddle.co/Harold_Pinter "Harold Pinter").

Losey's 1976 film _Monsieur Klein_ won the [César Awards](https://kids.kiddle.co/C%C3%A9sar_Awards "César Awards") for Best Film and Best Director. He was nominated many times for important awards like the [Palme d'Or](https://kids.kiddle.co/Palme_d%27Or "Palme d'Or") (which he won once) and the [Golden Lion](https://kids.kiddle.co/Golden_Lion "Golden Lion"). He was also nominated twice for a [BAFTA](https://kids.kiddle.co/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts "British Academy of Film and Television Arts") award.

## Joseph Losey's Early Life and Career

[![Image 4: LoseyArch](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/9/9d/LoseyArch.JPG/300px-LoseyArch.JPG)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:LoseyArch.JPG)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:LoseyArch.JPG "Enlarge")

 Losey Memorial Arch (1901) was built to honor Losey's grandfather, a well-known lawyer in La Crosse, Wisconsin.

Joseph Walton Losey III was born on January 14, 1909, in [La Crosse, Wisconsin](https://kids.kiddle.co/La_Crosse,_Wisconsin "La Crosse, Wisconsin"). He went to high school there with another famous director, [Nicholas Ray](https://kids.kiddle.co/Nicholas_Ray "Nicholas Ray"). Losey later attended [Dartmouth College](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College") and [Harvard University](https://kids.kiddle.co/Harvard_University "Harvard University"). He started studying medicine but ended up focusing on drama.

Losey became an important person in New York City's political theatre scene. In 1933, he directed a play called _Little Old Boy_. He also directed _Jayhawker_, a play written by [Sinclair Lewis](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sinclair_Lewis "Sinclair Lewis"). A newspaper review said that the play was very wordy, and Losey's directing didn't always make the story clear.

In 1935, he visited the [Soviet Union](https://kids.kiddle.co/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") for several months to learn about Russian theatre. In Moscow, he took a film class taught by [Sergei Eisenstein](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sergei_Eisenstein "Sergei Eisenstein"). He also met [Bertolt Brecht](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bertolt_Brecht "Bertolt Brecht") and composer [Hanns Eisler](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hanns_Eisler "Hanns Eisler") there.

In 1936, he directed _Triple-A Plowed Under_ on [Broadway](https://kids.kiddle.co/Broadway "Broadway"). This play was part of the [Works Progress Administration](https://kids.kiddle.co/Works_Progress_Administration "Works Progress Administration")'s [Federal Theatre Project](https://kids.kiddle.co/Federal_Theatre_Project "Federal Theatre Project"). He then directed another show called _Injunction Granted_.

Losey served in the [U.S. military](https://kids.kiddle.co/Military_of_the_United_States "Military of the United States") during [World War II](https://kids.kiddle.co/World_War_II "World War II"). He was discharged in 1945. From 1946 to 1947, Losey worked with Bertolt Brecht, who was living in Los Angeles. They prepared for a play called _Galileo_ (_Life of Galileo_). Losey and Brecht directed it together, with [Charles Laughton](https://kids.kiddle.co/Charles_Laughton "Charles Laughton") playing the main role. The play opened in July 1947 in Beverly Hills.

In October 1947, Losey went with Brecht to Washington D.C. for Brecht's appearance before the [House Un-American Activities Committee](https://kids.kiddle.co/House_Un-American_Activities_Committee "House Un-American Activities Committee") (HUAC). Brecht left the U.S. the next day. Losey then directed _Galileo_ again in New York City. Many years later, when Losey was living in England, he directed a film version of Brecht's play _Galileo_ (1975).

Losey's first feature film was _[The Boy with Green Hair](https://kids.kiddle.co/The\_Boy\_with\_Green\_Hair "The Boy with Green Hair")_ (1947). It starred a young [Dean Stockwell](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dean_Stockwell "Dean Stockwell") as Peter, a war orphan whose hair mysteriously turns green. This makes him an outcast.

Later, Losey was hired to direct a new version of the classic film _M_ (1931). His new version, _M_, was released in 1951 and was set in Los Angeles.

## Facing Challenges: Politics and Moving to Europe

During the 1930s and 1940s, Losey knew many people who had left-wing political ideas. Some were communists or people who would become communists. He worked with [Bertolt Brecht](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bertolt_Brecht "Bertolt Brecht") and [Hanns Eisler](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hanns_Eisler "Hanns Eisler"), both of whom were investigated by HUAC. Losey had even written a letter to help Eisler get a visa to live in the U.S.

Losey had also worked on the [Federal Theatre Project](https://kids.kiddle.co/Federal_Theatre_Project "Federal Theatre Project"), which HUAC often investigated. One of the plays he directed, _Triple-A Plowed Under_, was called communist propaganda. Many of his Hollywood co-workers, like [Dalton Trumbo](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dalton_Trumbo "Dalton Trumbo"), were also targets of HUAC.

In 1946, Losey joined the [Communist Party USA](https://kids.kiddle.co/Communist_Party_USA "Communist Party USA").

Losey had a long-term contract with [Dore Schary](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dore_Schary "Dore Schary") at RKO Pictures. But when [Howard Hughes](https://kids.kiddle.co/Howard_Hughes "Howard Hughes") bought RKO in 1948, he started removing people with left-wing views. Hughes stopped giving Losey work but still kept him under contract. In 1949, Schary helped Losey get out of his contract. Losey then started working on films independently.

In 1951, Losey's name was mentioned by two people testifying before HUAC. His lawyer suggested he make a deal to testify in secret. Instead, Losey stopped working on his film _The Big Night_ and left for Europe. His ex-wife also left the country. HUAC tried for weeks to make them appear, but they couldn't.

After working in Italy for over a year, Losey returned to the U.S. briefly in October 1952. He then went back to Rome and finally settled in London on January 4, 1953.

## Career in Europe

Losey made his new home in Britain and started directing different kinds of films. His first British film was _The Sleeping Tiger_ (1954), a crime thriller. He used a fake name, Victor Hanbury, for this film. This was because the movie's stars, [Alexis Smith](https://kids.kiddle.co/Alexis_Smith "Alexis Smith") and Alexander Knox, were worried they would be blacklisted in Hollywood if people knew they worked with Losey. _The Intimate Stranger_ (1956) also used a fake name. His films ranged from a historical drama called _The Gypsy and the Gentleman_ (1958) to a gangster film, _The Criminal_ (1960).

Losey was supposed to direct _X the Unknown_ (1956). But after a few days, the main actor, [Dean Jagger](https://kids.kiddle.co/Dean_Jagger "Dean Jagger"), refused to work with someone thought to be a Communist. So, Losey was removed from the project. Another story says he was replaced because he was sick. Losey later directed _The Damned_ (1963), a science fiction film.

In the 1960s, Losey began working with playwright [Harold Pinter](https://kids.kiddle.co/Harold_Pinter "Harold Pinter"). They became good friends, and Pinter started a successful career writing screenplays. Losey directed three famous films based on Pinter's scripts: _The Servant_ (1963), _Accident_ (1967), and _The Go-Between_ (1971).

*   _The Servant_ won three [British Academy Film Awards](https://kids.kiddle.co/British_Academy_Film_Awards "British Academy Film Awards").
*   _Accident_ won a special award at the 1967 [Cannes Film Festival](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival").
*   _The Go-Between_ won the top award, the [Golden Palm Award](https://kids.kiddle.co/Palme_d%27Or "Palme d'Or"), at the 1971 [Cannes Film Festival](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival"). It also won four prizes at the 1972 [BAFTA](https://kids.kiddle.co/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts "British Academy of Film and Television Arts") awards.

In _The Servant_, a house helper slowly takes control of his rich boss's life. In _The Go-Between_, a young boy becomes a secret messenger for a love affair between a farmer and a rich girl.

Losey's films often looked very real, but _The Servant_ mixed different styles. _Accident_ and _The Go-Between_ used special camera work, editing, and music to create unique ways of telling stories. Pinter's scripts had short, mysterious conversations. Losey often used busy and detailed scenes to show what was happening without words.

In 1966, Losey directed _Modesty Blaise_, a spy-comedy film. It was based on a popular comic strip.

Losey also directed [Robert Shaw](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_Shaw_(actor) "Robert Shaw (actor)") and [Malcolm McDowell](https://kids.kiddle.co/Malcolm_McDowell "Malcolm McDowell") in _Figures in a Landscape_ (1970). This action film was shot in Spain.

Losey worked with Pinter again on a script for a film based on _[A la recherche du temps perdu](https://kids.kiddle.co/In\_Search\_of\_Lost\_Time "In Search of Lost Time")_ by [Marcel Proust](https://kids.kiddle.co/Marcel_Proust "Marcel Proust"). However, Losey died before they could get enough money to make the film.

In 1975, Losey finally made a film version of Brecht's play _Galileo_, called _Life of Galileo_, starring [Chaim Topol](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chaim_Topol "Chaim Topol"). This film was made in the UK.

Losey's film _Monsieur Klein_ (1976) showed a day in France when Jewish people were arrested during World War II. He said he used different "visual categories" for filming: unreal, real, and abstract. This film helped show the story of the Vel' d'Hiv Roundup of French Jews in July 1942.

In 1979, Losey filmed [Mozart](https://kids.kiddle.co/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart")'s opera _[Don Giovanni](https://kids.kiddle.co/Don\_Giovanni "Don Giovanni")_ in Italy. This film was nominated for several [César Awards](https://kids.kiddle.co/C%C3%A9sar_Awards "César Awards") in 1980, including Best Director.

## Personal Life

In 1964, Losey said he would love to work in America again if the right project came along. He told an interviewer before he died that he wasn't bitter about being blacklisted. He said, "Without it I would have three Cadillacs, two swimming pools and millions of dollars, and I'd be dead. It was terrifying, it was disgusting, but you can get trapped by money and complacency. A good shaking up never did anyone any harm."

His old college, Dartmouth, gave Losey an honorary degree in 1973. The University of Wisconsin–Madison did the same in 1983.

Losey was married four times. He had two sons. His son Gavrik Losey (born 1938) helped with some of his father's films. Gavrik's two sons, Marek Losey and Luke Losey, are also film directors. His other son, Joshua Losey (born 1957), became an actor.

On September 29, 1970, Losey married Patricia Mohan. Patricia Losey later helped adapt the opera script for Losey's _Don Giovanni_ and a play for his last film, _Steaming_.

Joseph Losey died at his home in London on June 22, 1984. He passed away four weeks after finishing his last film.

In the 1991 film _Guilty by Suspicion_, a character named "Joe Lesser," played by [Martin Scorsese](https://kids.kiddle.co/Martin_Scorsese "Martin Scorsese"), leaves Hollywood for England to avoid investigations. This character is based on Joseph Losey's experiences.

# Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy

[Zoe Williams](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/zoewilliams)

He won a Bafta while only a teen, and now he’s the lead in a creepy sitcom adapted by Alan Partridge’s writers. Ahead of The Reluctant Vampire, he talks mates, mums who write him letters – and his love of David Brent

![Image 3: Zoe Williams](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/uploads/2017/10/09/Zoe-Williams,-L.png?width=75&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)

Fri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT

Share

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

O nly when absolutely badgered will [Lenny Rush](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/ng-interactive/2025/dec/14/im-having-so-much-fun-lenny-rush-on-fame-father-christmas-and-why-essex-needs-to-watch-out) admit that the title role of The Reluctant Vampire, Val, was written for him: “Shane Allen, the executive producer, loved the books when he was young, and he was the exec on [Am I Being Unreasonable?](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2022/sep/23/am-i-being-unreasonable-review-daisy-may-cooper-is-absurdly-brilliant). So yes, the scripts were written with me in mind. I’m so happy they were so good. I’d have felt awful if they said ‘We’ve written this for you’ and …” he trails off, pulling a face of exquisite pained courtesy.

Rush likens the show to The Naked Gun and Airplane!, and it has the writing team behind Alan Partridge, so can conjure awkwardness out of thin air. But it also taps into a comic tradition that goes even further back: a delight in the ridiculous, people talking to bats and gargoyles, invisible women interjecting by surprise, a surrealism whose comedy comes from the audacity of acting it with such commitment. “In my opinion,” says Rush, “sometimes things are labelled as a family show but they’re aimed at kids. I really do get the feeling that The Reluctant Vampire is for everyone.”

The Reluctant Vampire was written in the 80s by Eric Morecambe, in a surprising digression into children’s fiction from the comedy giant. It’s about the young scion of a bloodsucking household who doesn’t have any skills: his teeth aren’t pointy, he hates the taste of blood, and it transpires that he’s not a vampire at all but a rogue human. In the hands of [Neil and Rob Gibbons](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2016/feb/16/back-of-the-net-25-years-of-alan-partridge-steve-coogan), it’s like watching the essence of British comic sensibility – slapstick shot through with genuine pathos.

![Image 4: Rush with Sian Clifford as Valeeta, Gabriel Nagy as Vernon and Tom Davis as Victor in The Reluctant Vampire.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ef4206e5b974c04ac0cde6a87e22a68643831fd0/638_66_3463_2770/master/3463.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)[View image in fullscreen](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2026/oct/02/the-reluctant-vampire-bbc-lenny-rush-eric-morecambe-vampire-comedy#img-2)

Rush with Sian Clifford as Valeeta, Gabriel Nagy as Vernon and Tom Davis as Victor in The Reluctant Vampire. Photograph: James Pardon/BBC/Buffola Pictures

“You’ve got [Tom Davis](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2020/jan/07/tom-davis-king-gary-murder-in-successville) playing a vampire, this big character, with these big movements and this big voice, that can’t not attract a younger audience,” says Rush, “but the lines are genuinely funny.”The show opens with Davis in full vampire regalia, ready to strike an elderly victim in her bed, only for Rush to derail it all by rushing in saying he needs a wee.

Still only 17, Rush has been a fixture on TV for many years, starting aged seven in CBeebies documentary series Our Family. Then, aged eight in [Apple Tree House](https://www.theguardian.com/media/2017/may/14/new-cbeebies-drama-for-pre-schoolers-set-on-inner-city-council-estate)on CBeebies he played Eli, a young rascal on an estate of well-intentioned young rascals. If you have children this age, you’ll feel like you’ve known him for ever, and if you are watching the [latest season of Slow Horses](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2026/sep/16/slow-horses-season-six-review-gary-oldman-spy-thriller-apple-tv), you’ll know him as the foul-mouthed, ancient-beyond-his-years kid whose steel trap of a mind effortlessly vanquishes the spies.

But his breakthrough role was in Am I Being Unreasonable?, for which he won a Bafta at 14 for best male performance in a comedy – and he was nominated again for the same award this year. That role, Ollie, along with his magisterial Bafta acceptance speech, sealed his reputation as a guy who has hacked your mainframe, and could effortlessly make you laugh at any time.

![Image 5: Rush with Christopher Chung in Slow Horses.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e67c5c1ba3bda82f9a5662421d918ba1a17e1a0b/257_77_5917_4734/master/5917.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)[View image in fullscreen](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2026/oct/02/the-reluctant-vampire-bbc-lenny-rush-eric-morecambe-vampire-comedy#img-3)

Rush with Christopher Chung in Slow Horses. Photograph: Jack English/Apple

You can see in Rush’s performance as Val how much he’s gorged on Mr Bean, Alan Partridge, Monty Python. “I probably watched some things I shouldn’t have when I was younger,” he says. Never mind the age-appropriateness, how he found the time is anyone’s guess, since he has spent so long watching the British version of The Office that he knows it episode by episode, and has been working – as well as going to school – since he was seven. David Brent has always been his inspiration, and he delivers the kindest reading of that character I’ve ever heard. “You think: ‘What an idiot.’ Then you think: ‘What a not very nice man.’ Then you get to the end of series two, and there’s a really big element of pity. The _**James Bond**_ series is about a super cool fictional [British secret agent](https://kids.kiddle.co/Secret_Intelligence_Service "Secret Intelligence Service") named James Bond. He was created in 1953 by writer [Ian Fleming](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ian_Fleming "Ian Fleming"). Fleming wrote twelve novels and two short story collections about Bond. After Fleming passed away in 1964, many other authors continued writing official Bond stories. The latest novel, _On His Majesty's Secret Service_ by Charlie Higson, was published in May 2023. There are also books about a young James Bond and stories from the perspective of Moneypenny, a character from the series.

James Bond is also known by his code number, **007** (which sounds like "double-oh-seven"). His adventures have been turned into TV shows, radio plays, comic strips, video games, and movies. The _James Bond_ series is one of the most successful entertainment franchises ever. The movies are one of the longest-running film series and have earned over US$7.04 billion worldwide. The first movie, _Dr. No_, came out in 1962 and starred [Sean Connery](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sean_Connery "Sean Connery") as Bond. As of 2021, there have been twenty-five films in the main Eon Productions series. The most recent Bond film, _No Time to Die_ (2021), featured [Daniel Craig](https://kids.kiddle.co/Daniel_Craig "Daniel Craig") as Bond for the fifth time. He was the sixth actor to play Bond in the main film series. There were also two other Bond movies not made by Eon Productions: _Casino Royale_ (a funny movie from 1967) and _Never Say Never Again_ (a 1983 remake of an earlier film).

The Bond films are famous for many things, like their exciting soundtracks. Several theme songs have won [Academy Awards](https://kids.kiddle.co/Academy_Award "Academy Award")! Other important parts of the films include Bond's amazing cars, his special guns, and the cool gadgets he gets from Q Branch. The films also feature Bond interacting with various women, often called "[Bond girls](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bond_girl "Bond girl")."

## Discovering James Bond's World

### How James Bond Was Created

#### Ian Fleming's Inspiration

[Ian Fleming](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ian_Fleming "Ian Fleming") created James Bond as the main character for his books. Bond is an intelligence officer for the Secret Intelligence Service, also known as [MI6](https://kids.kiddle.co/MI6 "MI6"). He is known by his code number, 007. Fleming based Bond on many real people he met during his time in the [Naval Intelligence Division](https://kids.kiddle.co/Naval_Intelligence_Division_(United_Kingdom) "Naval Intelligence Division (United Kingdom)") during World War II. He said Bond was a mix of all the secret agents and commandos he knew.

Fleming gave Bond some of his own habits and tastes. This included his golf handicap, his love for scrambled eggs, and his favorite toiletries. Bond's passion for golf and gambling also came from Fleming's own life. Fleming used his experiences in espionage and other parts of his life to inspire his writing. He even used names of friends and relatives in his books.

#### The Name Behind the Agent

The name James Bond came from an American [ornithologist](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ornithologist "Ornithologist") (a bird expert) named [James Bond](https://kids.kiddle.co/James_Bond_(ornithologist) "James Bond (ornithologist)"). This expert wrote a famous guide called _Birds of the West Indies_. Fleming, who loved birdwatching, had a copy of this guide. He later explained that he wanted a simple, strong, and unromantic name for his hero. He thought "James Bond" was perfect because it sounded ordinary, making the extraordinary things that happened to him stand out even more.

In the later novel, _You Only Live Twice_, Fleming gave Bond a family background. He said Bond's parents were Andrew Bond from [Glencoe](https://kids.kiddle.co/Glencoe,_Highland "Glencoe, Highland"), [Scotland](https://kids.kiddle.co/Scotland "Scotland"), and Monique Delacroix from [Vaud](https://kids.kiddle.co/Vaud "Vaud"), Switzerland.

### James Bond Books and Stories

#### Ian Fleming's Original Novels

While working in Naval Intelligence, Ian Fleming decided he wanted to be a writer. He started writing his first James Bond novel, _Casino Royale_, on February 17, 1952. He wrote all his Bond novels at his Goldeneye estate in Oracabessa, Jamaica, every January and February. He began _Casino Royale_ just before his wedding, using the writing as a distraction.

[![Image 4: GoldeneyeEstate](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/e/e0/GoldeneyeEstate.jpg/300px-GoldeneyeEstate.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:GoldeneyeEstate.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:GoldeneyeEstate.jpg "Enlarge")

 Goldeneye, in Jamaica, where Fleming wrote all the Bond novels

After finishing _Casino Royale_, Fleming showed it to his friend William Plomer, who liked it. The book was published in 1953. Between 1953 and 1966, twelve novels and two short story collections were published. The last two books, _The Man with the Golden Gun_ and _Octopussy and The Living Daylights_, were published after Fleming's death.

*   1953 _Casino Royale_
*   1954 _Live and Let Die_
*   1955 _Moonraker_
*   1956 _Diamonds Are Forever_
*   1957 _From Russia, with Love_
*   1958 _Dr. No_
*   1959 _Goldfinger_
*   1960 _For Your Eyes Only_ (short stories)
*   1961 _Thunderball_
*   1962 _The Spy Who Loved Me_
*   1963 _On Her Majesty's Secret Service_
*   1964 _You Only Live Twice_
*   1965 _The Man with the Golden Gun_
*   1966 _Octopussy and The Living Daylights_ (short stories)

#### New Adventures by Other Authors

After Fleming's death, other authors continued the James Bond series. [Kingsley Amis](https://kids.kiddle.co/Kingsley_Amis "Kingsley Amis") wrote _Colonel Sun_ in 1968. Later, [John Gardner](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Gardner_(British_writer) "John Gardner (British writer)") took over in 1981 with _Licence Renewed_. Gardner wrote sixteen Bond books, including novelizations of two films. He updated Bond's world to the 1980s.

In 1996, American author Raymond Benson became the next Bond writer. He wrote six novels, three film novelizations, and three short stories before moving on in 2002.

After a break, [Sebastian Faulks](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sebastian_Faulks "Sebastian Faulks") wrote _Devil May Care_ in 2008. This book celebrated Fleming's 100th birthday. Then, Jeffery Deaver wrote _Carte Blanche_ in 2011, which imagined Bond as a modern agent. [William Boyd](https://kids.kiddle.co/William_Boyd_(writer) "William Boyd (writer)")'s _Solo_ came out in 2013. [Anthony Horowitz](https://kids.kiddle.co/Anthony_Horowitz "Anthony Horowitz") later wrote three Bond novels, _Trigger Mortis_ (2015), _Forever and a Day_ (2018), and _With a Mind to Kill_ (2022), using some of Fleming's unreleased material. Charlie Higson's first adult Bond novel, _On His Majesty's Secret Service_, was published in May 2023.

#### Young Bond's Early Years

The _Young Bond_ series tells stories about James Bond when he was a teenager. Charlie Higson started this series, publishing five novels and one short story between 2005 and 2009. The first book, _SilverFin_, was also made into a graphic novel. In 2013, [Stephen Cole](https://kids.kiddle.co/Stephen_Cole_(writer) "Stephen Cole (writer)") continued the series.

*   2005 _SilverFin_
*   2006 _Blood Fever_
*   2007 _Double or Die_
*   2007 _Hurricane Gold_
*   2008 _By Royal Command_&_SilverFin_ (graphic novel)
*   2009 "A Hard Man to Kill" (short story)

#### Moneypenny's Secret Diaries

_The Moneypenny Diaries_ is a series of three novels about the life of Miss Moneypenny, who is M's personal secretary. These books were written by Samantha Weinberg under the name Kate Westbrook. The first book, _Guardian Angel_, was released in 2005. The second, _Secret Servant_, came out in 2006, and the third, _Final Fling_, was released in 2008.

*   2005 _The Moneypenny Diaries: Guardian Angel_
*   2006 _Secret Servant: The Moneypenny Diaries_
*   2008 _The Moneypenny Diaries: Final Fling_

### James Bond on Screen and Sound

#### TV Shows and Radio Dramas

In 1954, [CBS](https://kids.kiddle.co/CBS "CBS") adapted Fleming's novel _Casino Royale_ into a one-hour TV show. It was part of the _Climax!_ series and starred [Barry Nelson](https://kids.kiddle.co/Barry_Nelson_(actor) "Barry Nelson (actor)") as James Bond. Later, in 1991, an animated series called _[James Bond Jr.](https://kids.kiddle.co/James\_Bond\_Jr. "James Bond Jr.")_ was made, featuring Bond's nephew. In 2022, a [reality competition show](https://kids.kiddle.co/Reality_television "Reality television") called _007: Road to a Million_ was released on [Amazon Prime Video](https://kids.kiddle.co/Amazon_Prime_Video "Amazon Prime Video").

In 1958, the novel _Moonraker_ was adapted for radio in [South Africa](https://kids.kiddle.co/South_Africa "South Africa"), with [Bob Holness](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bob_Holness "Bob Holness") as Bond's voice. The [BBC](https://kids.kiddle.co/BBC "BBC") has also adapted several Fleming novels for radio. These include _You Only Live Twice_ (1990), _Dr. No_ (2008), _Goldfinger_ (2010), _From Russia, with Love_ (2012), and _On Her Majesty's Secret Service_ (2014). Toby Stephens, who played a villain in a Bond film, often played Bond in these radio dramas.

#### Comic Book Adventures

In 1957, the _[Daily Express](https://kids.kiddle.co/Daily\_Express "Daily Express")_ newspaper asked Ian Fleming to turn his stories into comic strips. Fleming agreed, and the first strip, _Casino Royale_, was published from July to December 1958. John McLusky was the artist, and he gave Bond a more masculine look than Fleming's original idea.

[![Image 5: McLusky007](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/a/ac/McLusky007.jpg/230px-McLusky007.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:McLusky007.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:McLusky007.jpg "Enlarge")

 John McLusky's rendition of James Bond

Most of the Bond novels and short stories have been adapted into comic strips. Later, new original stories were created for the _Daily Express_ and _[Sunday Express](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sunday\_Express "Sunday Express")_ until 1977. Many comic book adaptations of the James Bond films have also been published over the years by companies like [Marvel Comics](https://kids.kiddle.co/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics"), Eclipse Comics, Dark Horse Comics, and Dynamite Entertainment.

#### The Famous James Bond Movies

##### Eon Productions' Main Film Series

[![Image 6: 007 logo](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/1/19/007_logo.svg/300px-007_logo.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:007_logo.svg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:007_logo.svg "Enlarge")

 Franchise logo, 1995–present

Eon Productions, founded by Harry Saltzman and Albert R. "Cubby" Broccoli, released the first James Bond movie, _Dr. No_, in 1962. [Sean Connery](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sean_Connery "Sean Connery") starred as 007. Connery played Bond in five more films before [George Lazenby](https://kids.kiddle.co/George_Lazenby "George Lazenby") took over for _On Her Majesty's Secret Service_ (1969). Lazenby only played Bond once, and Connery returned for _[Diamonds Are Forever](https://kids.kiddle.co/Diamonds\_Are\_Forever\_(film) "Diamonds Are Forever (film)")_.

[Roger Moore](https://kids.kiddle.co/Roger_Moore "Roger Moore") became Bond in _Live and Let Die_ (1973) and played the role seven times over twelve years. He was followed by [Timothy Dalton](https://kids.kiddle.co/Timothy_Dalton "Timothy Dalton") for two films. After a break, [Pierce Brosnan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Pierce_Brosnan "Pierce Brosnan") was cast as Bond in _GoldenEye_ (1995) and starred in four films. In 2006, [Daniel Craig](https://kids.kiddle.co/Daniel_Craig "Daniel Craig") took on the role for _Casino Royale_, which restarted the series. Craig appeared in five films, with his last being _No Time to Die_ (2021). The main film series has earned over $7 billion, making it one of the highest-grossing film series.

In March 2022, [Amazon](https://kids.kiddle.co/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)") bought [Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer") (MGM), which included the distribution rights to the James Bond movies. After creating Amazon MGM Studios, the company became involved in planning the next Bond film. By February 2025, the studio acquired creative control of the franchise from the long-time producers Barbara

## M ind-blowing F acts

[![Image 5: Pillars of creation 2014 HST WFC3-UVIS full-res denoised](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/6/68/Pillars_of_creation_2014_HST_WFC3-UVIS_full-res_denoised.jpg/300px-Pillars_of_creation_2014_HST_WFC3-UVIS_full-res_denoised.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Pillars_of_creation_2014_HST_WFC3-UVIS_full-res_denoised.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Pillars_of_creation_2014_HST_WFC3-UVIS_full-res_denoised.jpg "Enlarge")

 The Pillars of Creation in the [Eagle Nebula](https://kids.kiddle.co/Eagle_Nebula "Eagle Nebula"), one of the most famous space photographs in history taken by the Hubble Space Telescope.

**When the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") first opened its robotic eyes in 1990, scientists were shocked to see that every picture came out blurry.**

What had gone wrong? Hubble's giant main mirror had been polished into the wrong shape by a mistake smaller than 1/50th the thickness of a human hair! That tiny error was too small to see, but it was big enough to keep light from focusing correctly.

 Thankfully, astronomers and engineers did not give up. In December 1993, a brave crew of astronauts flew into space aboard the [Space Shuttle Endeavour](https://kids.kiddle.co/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") on a daring repair mission. During five intense spacewalks, they installed a special tool called COSTAR, which stands for Corrective Optics Space Telescope Axial Replacement. COSTAR worked like a pair of high-tech eyeglasses for Hubble, fixing its blurry vision. When Hubble looked back at the stars, everything was perfectly clear!

British film director and producer (born 1944)

| Jamil Dehlavi |
| --- |

| Education | [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") ([BA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts")) [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") ([MFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Fine_Arts "Master of Fine Arts")) |
| Occupations | Film director and producer |
| Notable work | _[The Blood of Hussain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Blood\_of\_Hussain "The Blood of Hussain")_ (1980); _Born of Fire_ (1987) _[Immaculate Conception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate\_Conception\_(film) "Immaculate Conception (film)")_ (1992); _[Jinnah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinnah\_(film) "Jinnah (film)")_ (1998); _[Infinite Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite\_Justice\_(film) "Infinite Justice (film)")_ (2006); _[Godforsaken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godforsaken "Godforsaken")_ (2010) |
| Website | [www.dehlavifilms.com](http://www.dehlavifilms.com/) |

**Jamil Dehlavi** ([Urdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urdu_language "Urdu language"): جمیل دہلوی) (born 1944) is a London-based independent film director and producer of [Pakistani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan")-[French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") origin.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-BFI-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-Habib_University-3)

Since he became a filmmaker in the 1970s, his work has been widely screened internationally, notable films including _[Jinnah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinnah\_(film) "Jinnah (film)")_ (1998),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-citwf-4) about the partition of India and the birth of Pakistan, which won the Grand Prize at the [Festival of the Dhow Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_the_Dhow_Countries "Festival of the Dhow Countries"), Best International Film at the World Film Awards in Indonesia, the Gold Award at Worldfest Flagstaff, Best Foreign Film at [Worldfest Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WorldFest-Houston_International_Film_Festival "WorldFest-Houston International Film Festival"), and was nominated for a Golden Pyramid at the [Cairo International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo_International_Film_Festival "Cairo International Film Festival").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TNI-5)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jamil_Dehlavi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Born in [Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolkata "Kolkata"), [West Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bengal "West Bengal"), to a [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people") mother and an [Pathan-Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathans_in_India "Pathans in India") father who was a diplomat and subsequently travelled extensively between Asia and Europe, Dehlavi is fluent in five languages (English, French, Italian, Spanish and Urdu).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-6)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TNI-5) He studied at [Karachi Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karachi_Grammar_School "Karachi Grammar School"), then at international schools in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") and [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), before going to [Rugby School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_School "Rugby School") and [Oxford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University "Oxford University").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2) He graduated with a BA degree in Politics and French Literature and an MA (Hons) in Jurisprudence. He was subsequently called to the Bar at [Lincoln's Inn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln's_Inn "Lincoln's Inn") but never practised, preferring instead to go into the world of cinema.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-BFI-1) Dehlavi studied film directing at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), where he was awarded an MFA degree.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-Habib_University-3)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jamil_Dehlavi&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

While studying in New York, Dehlavi trained as an actor with [Stella Adler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stella_Adler "Stella Adler") and made his first feature film, _Towers of Silence_, which he wrote, produced and directed. It won the Grand Prize at the Festival of the Americas. His next film, _[The Blood of Hussain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Blood\_of\_Hussain "The Blood of Hussain")_ (1980),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-citwf-4) was selected by the Director's Fortnight at the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival") and won the Grand Prize at the [Taormina Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taormina_Film_Festival "Taormina Film Festival"). All of his subsequent films have also won major awards at film festivals all over the world.

Dehlavi has worked on various projects for the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"), [Channel Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_Four "Channel Four"), and French television, including _Qâf – The Sacred Mountain_, which won awards at five environmental film festivals. He worked on _Passover_, a [passion play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passion_play "Passion play") shot in [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba,_Andalusia "Córdoba, Andalusia") and made in collaboration with the celebrated flamenco guitarist [Paco Peña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paco_Pe%C3%B1a "Paco Peña"). Dehlavi has also worked in the Radio & Visual Services Division at the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") and as an associate professor in the School of Arts, Humanities & Social Sciences at [Habib University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habib_University "Habib University") in [Karachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karachi "Karachi").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-Habib_University-3)

In August 2018, the [BFI Southbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Film_Institute "British Film Institute") presented a retrospective of his work entitled _Between the Sacred and the Profane: The Cinema of Jamil Dehlavi_, which was described as "a rare opportunity to examine the contribution of one of the most intriguing and least understood figures of cinema."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-TheNational-2) With screenings of several films held over the weekend of 10–12 August, the event also featured a conversation with Dehlavi.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamil_Dehlavi#cite_note-7)
