# Trivia

## The Merchant of Venice

Edit

[Cate Blanchett](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000949/?ref_=tttrv_tr) was set to play Portia, but had to drop out at the last minute after discovering she was pregnant.

Helpful•43 1

[Dustin Hoffman](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000163/?ref_=tttrv_tr) was interested in playing Shylock; however, when he contacted director [Michael Radford](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0705535/?ref_=tttrv_tr) about it, [Al Pacino](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000199/?ref_=tttrv_tr) had already been cast. In fact, in 1989, Hoffman had starred as Shylock in both the London and subsequent Broadway productions of "Merchant" directed by Sir [Peter Hall](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0355991/?ref_=tttrv_tr).

Helpful•37 1

[Ricky Gervais](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0315041/?ref_=tttrv_tr) turned down the role of Launcelot Gobbo, a role which went to his [The Office (2001)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0290978/?ref_=tttrv_tr) co-star [Mackenzie Crook](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0188871/?ref_=tttrv_tr).

Helpful•25 1

Shylock's "Hath not a Jew eyes?" speech is quoted in [Schindler's List (1993)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0108052/?ref_=tttrv_tr) by [Joseph Fiennes](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001212/?ref_=tttrv_tr)'s brother, [Ralph Fiennes](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000146/?ref_=tttrv_tr).

Helpful•45 5

[Peter O'Toole](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000564/?ref_=tttrv_tr) almost got a version up and running in 1970, but a change of management at MGM led to it being cancelled. This is actually the first non-TV, feature film adaptation of "The Merchant of Venice" that was produced for a theatrical release.

**John Francis Lane** (1 December 1928 – 15 January 2018)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Lane#cite_note-2) was an English journalist, critic and actor. He was known for being a small-part actor in many [Italian films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_Italy "Cinema of Italy"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Lane#cite_note-3) and as a contributor to _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ writing obituaries for Italian cultural figures.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Lane#cite_note-Mayes-1)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Francis_Lane&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Lane was born in [Tankerton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tankerton "Tankerton"), a suburb of [Whitstable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitstable "Whitstable") in [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent"), to a middle-class family in 1928. He became a boarder at the [Royal Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Grammar_School_Worcester "Royal Grammar School Worcester") in [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_England "Worcester, England"), and towards the end of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") attended [Dulwich College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulwich_College "Dulwich College") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Lane#cite_note-Timesobit-4) He then had a spell as a stage manager in London's [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_of_London "West End of London").

Lane first visited Italy in 1949, following a German boyfriend from Paris, where he was then studying at the [Sorbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris"). After learning Italian at the [University of Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Florence "University of Florence"), he had settled in Rome by 1951, finding Italy more tolerant of his homosexuality than the Britain of the time.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Lane#cite_note-Mayes-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Lane#cite_note-Timesobit-4) Learning Italian in Florence, he became entranced by the country after seeing [Franco Zeffirelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco_Zeffirelli "Franco Zeffirelli")'s production of _[Troilus and Cressida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troilus\_and\_Cressida "Troilus and Cressida")_. Zeffirelli later became one of his boyfriends.

He was made a [Cavaliere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavaliere "Cavaliere") in the 1975 Italian Order of Merit.

In retirement Lane lived in the town of [Rende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rende "Rende") in the region of [Calabria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabria "Calabria"). He wrote frequently on Italian life for _[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Economist "The Economist")_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Lane#cite_note-Mayes-1) His memoir, _To Each His Own Dolce Vita_, was published in 2013.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Lane#cite_note-Timesobit-4)

Lane died in January 2018 in [Cosenza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosenza "Cosenza") in southern Italy.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Lane#cite_note-5) Knowledge he had died was delayed and only emerged following the end of Zeffirelli's life.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Lane#cite_note-Timesobit-4)

**Ray McAnally** (30 March 1926 – 15 June 1989) was an Irish actor. He was the recipient of three [BAFTA Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Awards "BAFTA Awards") in the late 1980s: two [BAFTA Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Film_Awards "BAFTA Film Awards") for [Best Supporting Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Supporting_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role") (for [_The Mission_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mission_(1986_film) "The Mission (1986 film)") in 1986 and [_My Left Foot_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Left_Foot_(film) "My Left Foot (film)") in 1989), and a [BAFTA Television Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Television_Award "BAFTA Television Award") for [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_Television_Award_for_Best_Actor "British Academy Television Award for Best Actor") for _[A Very British Coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Very\_British\_Coup\_(mini-series) "A Very British Coup (mini-series)")_ in 1989. In 2020, he was ranked at number 34 on _[The Irish Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Irish\_Times "The Irish Times")_'s list of Ireland's greatest film actors.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_McAnally#cite_note-1)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ray_McAnally&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Ray McAnally was born in [Buncrana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buncrana "Buncrana"), a seaside town located on the [Inishowen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inishowen "Inishowen") peninsula of [County Donegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Donegal "County Donegal"), Ireland and raised in the nearby town of [Moville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moville "Moville") from the age of three. The son of a bank manager, he was educated at [St Eunan's College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Eunan's_College "St Eunan's College") in Letterkenny where he wrote, produced and staged a musical called _Madame Screwball_ at the age of 16. He entered [Maynooth College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maynooth_College "Maynooth College") at the age of 18 but left after a short time having decided that the priesthood was not his vocation. He joined the [Abbey Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey_Theatre "Abbey Theatre") in 1947 where he met and married actress [Ronnie Masterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Masterson "Ronnie Masterson").

## Acting career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ray_McAnally&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Acting career")]

McAnally and Masterson later formed Old Quay Productions and presented an assortment of classic plays in the 1960s and 1970s. He made his West End theatre debut in 1962 with _A Nice Bunch of Cheap Flowers_ and gave a well-received performance as George in _[Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who's\_Afraid\_of\_Virginia\_Woolf%3F "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?")_, opposite [Constance Cummings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constance_Cummings "Constance Cummings"), at the [Piccadilly Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piccadilly_Theatre "Piccadilly Theatre").

On television he was a familiar face, often in glossy thriller series like _[The Avengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Avengers\_(TV\_series) "The Avengers (TV series)")_, _[Man in a Suitcase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man\_in\_a\_Suitcase "Man in a Suitcase")_ and _[Strange Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange\_Report "Strange Report")_. In 1968 he took the title role in _[Spindoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spindoe "Spindoe")_, a series charting the return to power of an English gangster, Alec Spindoe, after a five-year prison term. This was a spin-off from another series, _[The Fellows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Man\_In\_Room\_17/The\_Fellows\_(Late\_of\_Room\_17) "The Man In Room 17/The Fellows (Late of Room 17)")_ (1967) in which McAnally appeared as the Spindoe character in several episodes. He could render English accents very convincingly.

In 1976 McAnally appeared in the [Granada Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_Television "Granada Television") daytime series _[Crown Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown\_Court\_(TV\_series) "Crown Court (TV series)")_. He played the character of Robert Scard, a [confidence trickster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_trick "Confidence trick") found guilty of [fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraud "Fraud").

In 1988, a century after the [Whitechapel Murders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitechapel_Murders "Whitechapel Murders"), he appeared in the television mini-series _[Jack the Ripper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack\_the\_Ripper\_(miniseries) "Jack the Ripper (miniseries)")_. McAnally played [William Gull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gull "William Gull"), a Physician-in-Ordinary to [Queen Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria "Queen Victoria"), who the program claimed was the killer.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_McAnally#cite_note-2)

**Sir John Vincent Hurt** (22 January 1940 – 25 January 2017) was an English actor. He was [knighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Bachelor "Knight Bachelor") in 2015 for his services to drama.

Michael James Radford (born 24 February 1946) is an English film director and screenwriter. He began his career as a documentary director and television comedy writer before transitioning into features in the early 1980s.

His best-known credits include the 1984 film adaptation of George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four starring John Hurt and Richard Burton (in his final role), the Shakespeare adaptation The Merchant of Venice, the true crime drama White Mischief, and the 1994 Italian-language comedy drama Il Postino: The Postman, for which he won the BAFTA Awards for Best Direction and Best Film Not in the English Language, and earned Academy Award nominations for Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay. ×

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

British journalist (born 1945)

For other people named James Fox, see [James Fox (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(disambiguation) "James Fox (disambiguation)").

**James Fox** (born 19 November 1945) is a British journalist best known for his book, _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(novel) "White Mischief (novel)"),_ and for co-authoring _Life,_ the best-selling memoir of [Rolling Stones'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stones "Rolling Stones") guitarist [Keith Richards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Richards "Keith Richards").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist)#cite_note-1)

## Life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Fox_(journalist)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

Fox was born in Washington, D.C., U.S. and worked as a journalist in Africa as well as reporting for London's _[Sunday Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Times "Sunday Times")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist)#cite_note-2) His first book, _White Mischief,_ is an account of the [Happy Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Valley_set "Happy Valley set") murder case in Kenya in 1941.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist)#cite_note-3) He researched the book with [Cyril Connolly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Connolly "Cyril Connolly") in 1969 and it was later adapted into a [film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film) "White Mischief (film)") by [Michael Radford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford "Michael Radford") in the 1980s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist)#cite_note-4) Fox also wrote _The [Langhorne Sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langhorne\_Sisters "Langhorne Sisters")_, also known as _Five Sisters: The Langhornes of Virginia_.

He married the fashion designer [Bella Freud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bella_Freud "Bella Freud") in 2001. They have a son, James "Jimmy" Lux Fox. The couple separated in 2017.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist)#cite_note-5)

He has a son, Thomas, from a previous marriage with Valérie Mariane Lalonde (née Lévy)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist)#cite_note-6)

Jonathan Gems (born 1952, London) is a British playwright and screenwriter mostly known for his work on Mars Attacks!, directed by Tim Burton. He also wrote the film's novelization.

The son of the playwright Pam Gems, Jonathan Gems wrote a number of plays for theatres on the London fringe before gradually turning to screenwriting. As well as Mars Attacks!, Gems did uncredited rewrite work on Batman. Gems has written a number of unproduced scripts for Burton, including a Beetlejuice sequel titled Beetlejuice Goes Hawaiian, an updating of Edgar Allan Poe's "The Fall of the House of Usher" set in Burbank, California, The Hawkline Monster, a cowboy/monster movie that was to star Clint Eastwood and Jack Nicholson and Go Baby Go, a beach movie in the style of Russ Meyer.

### [A review by CharlesTheBold](https://www.themoviedb.org/review/58ace0189251411fb0001bd1)

##### Written by [CharlesTheBold](https://www.themoviedb.org/u/CharlesTheBold/reviews) on February 22, 2017

Based on George Orwell's dystopian novel from the 1940s, the movie was produced in the very year that Orwell had set it, 1984.

**Michael James Radford** (born 24 February 1946) is an English film director and screenwriter.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT-1) He began his career as a documentary director and television comedy writer before transitioning into features in the early 1980s.

His best-known credits include the 1984 [film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film) "Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)") of [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell")'s _[Nineteen Eighty-Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four")_ starring [John Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hurt "John Hurt") and [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton") (in his final role), the [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") adaptation _[The Merchant of Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Merchant\_of\_Venice\_(2004\_film) "The Merchant of Venice (2004 film)")_, the [true crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/True_crime "True crime") drama _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_, and the 1994 Italian-language comedy drama _[Il Postino: The Postman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_Postino:\_The\_Postman "Il Postino: The Postman")_, for which he won the [BAFTA Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Awards "BAFTA Awards") for [Best Direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Direction "BAFTA Award for Best Direction") and [Best Film Not in the English Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Film_Not_in_the_English_Language "BAFTA Award for Best Film Not in the English Language"), and earned [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") nominations for [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") and [Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay").

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Radford&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Radford was born on 24 February 1946, in [New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi "New Delhi"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidencies_and_provinces_of_British_India "Presidencies and provinces of British India"), to a British father and an Austrian [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") mother. He was educated at [Bedford School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford_School "Bedford School") before attending [Worcester College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester_College,_Oxford "Worcester College, Oxford"). After teaching for a few years, he went to the [National Film and Television School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_and_Television_School "National Film and Television School"), becoming a student there in its inaugural year.

Between 1976 and 1982, Radford worked as a documentary film maker, mostly on projects for the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"), covering subjects such as Scottish islanders on the [Isle of Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Lewis "Isle of Lewis") in the [Outer Hebrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Hebrides "Outer Hebrides") who believe in the literal truth of the Bible: _The Last Stronghold of the Pure Gospel_; the soprano [Isobel Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isobel_Buchanan "Isobel Buchanan"): _La Belle Isobel_; the singer songwriter [Van Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison "Van Morrison"): _[Van Morrison in Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van\_Morrison\_in\_Ireland "Van Morrison in Ireland")_; and the self-explanatory _The Making of [The Pirates of Penzance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pirates\_of\_Penzance "The Pirates of Penzance")_. On the last two of these, Radford worked with the [cinematographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinematographer "Cinematographer")[Roger Deakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Deakins "Roger Deakins"), who would later shoot two of Radford's feature films; _[Nineteen Eighty-Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film) "Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)")_ and _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_. Another notable early work was _[Another Time, Another Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Another\_Time,\_Another\_Place\_(1983\_film) "Another Time, Another Place (1983 film)")_ (1983), a feature film set in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and centred on a love story between a local woman and an [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")[POW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war").

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Radford&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Radford came to international attention with _[Nineteen Eighty-Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film) "Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)")_, his adaptation of [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell")'s novel _[1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four")_, starring [John Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hurt "John Hurt") as Winston Smith, and in which [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton") gave his final film performance.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) The film was made in the time and place ([London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), April–June 1984) at which the book was set.

Radford's next film, released in 1987, was _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_, a period drama set in [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") during the 1940s.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) Radford again wrote the screenplay, an adaptation of the novel by [James Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist) "James Fox (journalist)") also called _White Mischief_.

Michael Radford is most widely known as the writer and director of the 1994 film _[Il Postino: The Postman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_Postino:\_The\_Postman "Il Postino: The Postman")_, which Radford adapted from the novel _[Ardiente Paciencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardiente\_paciencia "Ardiente paciencia")_ by [Antonio Skármeta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Sk%C3%A1rmeta "Antonio Skármeta").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT-1) The massive international success of the film (for many years it was the largest grossing non-English language film ever made) led to international acclaim for Radford and the star of the film [Massimo Troisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massimo_Troisi "Massimo Troisi"). Tragically, Troisi died, aged 41, the day after the filming of _Il Postino_ was completed. The film won many international film awards including the 'Best Film Not in the English Language' [BAFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts "British Academy of Film and Television Arts") for Radford, who was also nominated for the [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") and [Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Writing_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Writing Adapted Screenplay")[Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards").

In 2000, Radford's film _[Dancing at the Blue Iguana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing\_at\_the\_Blue\_Iguana "Dancing at the Blue Iguana")_ was released.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) In a departure from his more usual development technique, namely adapting novels, this film was largely improvised, although Radford shared the screenwriting credit with [David Linter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Linter?action=edit&redlink=1 "David Linter (page does not exist)").

In 2004, Radford directed _[The Merchant of Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Merchant\_of\_Venice\_(2004\_film) "The Merchant of Venice (2004 film)")_ (2004).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) He adapted the [William Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") play (see: [Shakespearean comedies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespearean_comedies "Shakespearean comedies")), and the film stars [Al Pacino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Pacino "Al Pacino") as [Shylock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shylock "Shylock") and [Jeremy Irons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Irons "Jeremy Irons") as [Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_(Merchant_of_Venice) "Antonio (Merchant of Venice)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) In 2007, he reunited [Demi Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demi_Moore "Demi Moore") and [Michael Caine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Caine "Michael Caine") (who had already been together in 1984 for _[Blame it on Rio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blame\_it\_on\_Rio "Blame it on Rio")_) in _[Flawless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flawless\_(2007\_film) "Flawless (2007 film)")_, a diamond heist story set in 1960.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-NYT2-2) His most recent film is _[Elsa & Fred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa\_&\_Fred\_(2014\_film) "Elsa & Fred (2014 film)")_ (2014), a romantic comedy starring [Shirley MacLaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_MacLaine "Shirley MacLaine") and [Christopher Plummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Plummer "Christopher Plummer").

Radford directed his first play in 2000, a [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_theatre "West End theatre") production of _[The Seven Year Itch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Seven\_Year\_Itch "The Seven Year Itch")_. This was an adaptation of [Billy Wilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Wilder "Billy Wilder")'s 1955 film starring [Marilyn Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Monroe "Marilyn Monroe").

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Radford&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Radford has a son, Felix (born 1991), from his first marriage to Iseult Teran. He also has a daughter, Amaryllis (born 2005), and a son, Linus (born 2010), with his current wife, Emma Tweed.

In addition to English (his first language), he speaks fluent Spanish, French, Italian, and some Mandarin.

In September 2013, he took part in the Clipper Round the World Sailing Race, in which he raced one of 12 identical 70-foot racing yachts from London to Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford#cite_note-3)

_**White Mischief**_ is a 1987 British [period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_drama "Historical drama")[crime drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_drama "Crime drama") film directed and co-written by [Michael Radford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford "Michael Radford"). It dramatises the events of the [Happy Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Valley_set "Happy Valley set") murder case in [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") in 1941, wherein Sir [Henry “Jock” Delves Broughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton "Jock Delves Broughton") was tried for the murder of [Josslyn Hay, 22nd Earl of Erroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josslyn_Hay,_22nd_Earl_of_Erroll "Josslyn Hay, 22nd Earl of Erroll"). The film stars [Greta Scacchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Scacchi "Greta Scacchi"), [Charles Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dance "Charles Dance"), [Joss Ackland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland "Joss Ackland"), [Sarah Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Miles "Sarah Miles"), [Geraldine Chaplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_Chaplin "Geraldine Chaplin"), [Ray McAnally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_McAnally "Ray McAnally"), [Murray Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murray_Head "Murray Head"), [John Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hurt "John Hurt"), and [Trevor Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Howard "Trevor Howard").

The screenplay is based on the non-fiction book _[White Mischief: The Murder of Lord Erroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(novel) "White Mischief (novel)")_ (1982), by [James Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist) "James Fox (journalist)"), which originated from a newspaper article published in 1969.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-whitemischief-6) Shooting took place on-location in Kenya and at [Shepperton Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepperton_Studios "Shepperton Studios").

At the [42nd British Academy Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_British_Academy_Film_Awards "42nd British Academy Film Awards"), the film was nominated for [Best Actor in a Supporting Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Supporting_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role") (for Joss Ackland) and [Best Costume Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Costume_Design "BAFTA Award for Best Costume Design").

The film came out around the same time as a BBC series set against the background of the same crime, _[The Happy Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Happy\_Valley "The Happy Valley")_ (1987).

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Throughout the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), aristocrats in the [Kenya Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Colony "Kenya Colony")'s Happy Valley region often led hedonistic lifestyles of indulgence in alcohol, drugs, and extramarital relationships. On 24 January 1941, Josslyn Hay, the philandering Earl of Erroll, was found dead in his car in a secluded area, with his reputation for adulterous relationships preceding him.

One such married woman is [Diana Delves Broughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_Caldwell "Diana Caldwell"), the beautiful wife of Sir John Henry Delves Broughton, known as "Jock", who is thirty years her senior, with whom she has a pre-nuptial understanding that, should either of them fall in love with someone else, the other party would not impede that romance.

Diana has indeed succumbed to the charms of the Earl of Erroll,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-jongh-7) whose other lovers include the drug-addicted American heiress [Alice de Janzé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_de_Janz%C3%A9 "Alice de Janzé") and the more reserved Nina Soames. The Earl is more serious about this affair than any of his earlier dalliances, and wants Diana to marry him. She is reluctant to leave what she thinks is the financial security of her marriage to formalise her relationship with Erroll (who has no funds or prospects), unaware that her husband is deep in debt. Privately humiliated but appearing to honour their agreement, Delves Broughton publicly toasts the couple's affair at the club in Nairobi, asking Erroll to bring Diana home at a specified time. Delves Broughton appears to be extremely intoxicated for the rest of the evening; once he is alone it is clear he was feigning drunkenness. After dropping off Diana, Erroll is shot dead in his car near the home of Delves Broughton, who is soon charged with the murder.

Diana is distraught over losing her lover, as is Alice, who openly masturbates next to his corpse at the mortuary. A local plantation owner, Gilbert Colvile, whose only friend is Delves Broughton, quietly offers Diana advice and solace and ultimately shocks her by proposing marriage.

Delves Broughton stands trial. There are no witnesses to the crime and the physical evidence that appears incriminating is also circumstantial. He obviously had the motive and means, but is found innocent, and the scandal comes to an end. De Janzé ultimately kills herself, and Diana discovers further evidence that implicates her husband in her lover's death. After killing their dog and then menacing her with a shotgun, Broughton shoots himself in front of her. The film ends with a fleeing, bloodstained Diana discovering the remaining Happy Valley set partying around de Janzé's grave.

## Original book

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Original book")]

In 1969, James Fox and [Cyril Connolly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Connolly "Cyril Connolly") began investigating the case for an article in _The Sunday Times_ called "Christmas at Karen." After Connolly died in 1974, Fox inherited his notes and theories, and returned to Kenya to undertake further research. The result was the book _White Mischief_, published in 1982.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-8)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-sight-3) The title came from _[Black Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Mischief "Black Mischief")_, [Evelyn Waugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_Waugh "Evelyn Waugh")'s satirical novel set in the mythical African kingdom of Azania. _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ called it "a fascinating book."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-9)_[The Boston Globe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boston\_Globe "The Boston Globe")_ said "had ‘White Mischief’ been a work of fiction it would have required the collaboration of [Agatha Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agatha_Christie "Agatha Christie") and [P. G. Wodehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._G._Wodehouse "P. G. Wodehouse")."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-10) While researching the book Fox also collected information about [Beryl Markham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryl_Markham "Beryl Markham"), which was turned into the film _[A Shadow on the Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryl\_Markham:\_A\_Shadow\_on\_the\_Sun "Beryl Markham: A Shadow on the Sun")_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-11)

## Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")]

The film rights to the book were optioned by [Michael White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_White_(producer) "Michael White (producer)"), a friend of Fox's, while the book was being written.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-12)

Director [Michael Radford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford "Michael Radford") collaborated with British playwright [Jonathan Gems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Gems "Jonathan Gems") on the script. Radford emphasized that "films of [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa") should be made by Africans" and described the project as "a film of melancholy about people who have everything and yet have nothing. It's about people who want to possess what they can't possess."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-csm-13)

Securing funding for the film posed a challenge. The financing was sourced from a chain of Canadian cinemas, [Cineplex Odeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cineplex_Odeon_Corporation "Cineplex Odeon Corporation"), plus [Goldcrest Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldcrest_Films "Goldcrest Films")[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-ink-14), BBC Television, [Nelson Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Entertainment "Nelson Entertainment") (headed by [Barry Spikings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Spikings "Barry Spikings"), which provided $2.5 million in exchange for North American video rights), with the remaining amount coming from [Columbia Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Pictures "Columbia Pictures"), then under [David Puttnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Puttnam "David Puttnam") as head of production.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-white-2)

[Richard Attenborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Attenborough "Richard Attenborough") was offered and turned down the lead role, because he wanted to focus on directing films.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-15)

## Shooting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Shooting")]

Filming took place from February to May 1987 at [Shepperton Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepperton_Studios "Shepperton Studios") and on location in Kenya.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-16)[Wrotham Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrotham_Park "Wrotham Park") was used as [Doddington Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doddington_Hall,_Cheshire "Doddington Hall, Cheshire"), the home of Delves Broughton.

## Historical accuracy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Historical accuracy")]

The real Alice De Janzé shot herself on 30 September 1941,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-17) while Jock Delves Broughton eventually returned to England and committed suicide by [morphine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphine "Morphine") overdose in the [Adelphi Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britannia_Adelphi_Hotel "Britannia Adelphi Hotel") in [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool") in December 1942, over a year later.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-18)

"There is a difference between fact and truth," said producer Simon Perry. "You can be truthful without being factual. It's inevitable there will be people who think Kenya was and still is a paradise of [remittance men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remittance_man "Remittance man") and black sheep of aristocratic families. Kenya was an exaggerated microcosm of society in Britain at that time, painted in primary colours with characters larger than life."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-csm-13)

Sir Jock Broughton's son, Sir Evelyn, complained that the film depicted his father as a murderer. He said his father was too drunk that night to have committed the crime and that Diana was more likely to have done it.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-19)

Diana Broughton died in 1987.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-20)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(film)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Box office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(film)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Box office")]

The film grossed £1,532,903 in the United Kingdom and $3.1 million in the United States and Canada.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-screen-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-mojo-5) It lost money during its theatrical release, however, [Jake Eberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_Eberts "Jake Eberts") reported that [Goldcrest Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldcrest_Films "Goldcrest Films") invested £1,300,000 in the film, and received £1,633,000, earning them a profit of £333,000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-screen-4)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-23)

### Critical

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(film)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Critical")]

_[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ wrote the film "displays high production values, impressive acting talent, and a strong — virtually factual — storyline. The money invested can be seen on the screen, and with an excellent lead performance (following his major role in ‘‘The Sicilian’’) Joss Ackland should finally receive the acting kudos he deserves. Pic should make a healthy b.o. impact worldwide."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-24)

Book author James Fox said he was "ambivalent" about the movie.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-jongh-7)

Radford said the reviews of the film " almost ruined my career. It stopped it in its tracks... I think it was difficult for critics because Britain is obsessed by class. It wasn’t done to make a film about upper-class people. I think people were expecting one of those James Ivory films or _A Passage to India_... It wasn’t meant to be like _Out of Africa_, the cinema of waxed furniture. I was trying to make something much more decadent."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-25)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(film)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Legacy")]

In 1996, [Mariette Bosch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariette_Bosch "Mariette Bosch") murdered Ria Wolmerans in [Botswana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botswana "Botswana"). Both women were white South Africans. The case was referred to as "Botswana's white mischief".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film)#cite_note-BarrowBBC-26)

Michael Radford was born on 24 February 1946 in New Delhi, British India [now India]. He is a director and writer, known for [The Postman (1994)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0110877/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [1984 (1984)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0087803/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [The Merchant of Venice (2004)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0379889/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He is married to [Emma Tweed](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1912817/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). They have two children. He was previously married to Iseult Teran.

"Another Time, Another Place" spielt in Schottland während des Zweiten Weltkriegs: Drei italienische Kriegsgefangene werden dort zur Arbeit auf eine raue, abgelegene Farm geschickt. Weder die schottische Bevölkerung, noch die Kriegsgefangenen sind damit glücklich. Nur die junge, in ihrer Ehe eher unglückliche Janie widmet sich den Italienern etwas mehr, insbesondere dem charmanten Luigi und zwischen den Beiden entwickelt sich eine heimliche Romanze. Ob diese Liebe ein gutes Ende nehmen kann, trotz der widrigen Umstände, könnt ihr in diesem Film sehen.

Michael Radford nimmt sich hier viel Zeit für seine Figuren, was mich zu Beginn ein wenig abgeschreckt hat, denn es dauerte mir zu lang bis die Geschichte an Fahrt aufnimmt. Aufmuntern konnten mich die wirklich schönen Bilder der schottischen Landschaft und die zweite Hälfte des Films, der zwar kein Gute-Laune-Film ist, aber auch aufgrund seiner Bilder eine traurig-schöne Geschichte erzählt, die man bei entsprechender Stimmung sich mal geben kann.

A beautifully unadorned portrait of infidelity as an act of illusory respite from tedium and loneliness. Finely crafted by Michael Radford with an eye to mood and character rather than incident or melodrama, the film is engaging and moving principally as a result of Phyllis Logan’s delicate portrayal. She deftly gives the material an emotional authenticity, captivating the viewer and carrying the quiet drama as a result.

Atmosphere is the most important element of this film. A sense of the monotony and boredom that Janie was faced with, and the vibrancy of Luigi in comparison. One of those films where the story seems to happen at the end rather than the whole way through, but such an interesting topic that I did not mind.

Quiet, slow and with some beautiful shots (Roger Deakins strikes again) Another Time, Another Place relies on the acting to elevate it. Phyllis Logan rightfully earned a BAFTA for this performance -the final scene in itself is worthy of that. I'm not even sure how I feel about the actual story/ conclusion, but it is something that I will not easily forget. Even just the look into rural Scottish life felt so fantastically authentic- and strikingly similar to the rural Ireland with which I am so familiar. Worth a watch.

Michael James Radford (born 24 February 1946) is an English film director and screenwriter. He began his career as a documentary director and television comedy writer before transitioning into features in the early 1980s.

His best-known credits include the 1984 film adaptation of George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four starring John Hurt and Richard Burton (in his final role), the Shakespeare adaptation The Merchant of Venice, the true crime drama White Mischief, and the 1994 Italian-language comedy drama Il Postino: The Postman, for which he won the BAFTA Awards for Best Direction and Best Film Not in the English Language, and earned Academy Award nominations for Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay. ×

# James Fox

*    Post author  By [Myles](link_10)
*    Post date [8 Feb 2020](https://sheffielder.net/2020/02/08/james-fox/)

![Image 1](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/72570192_137995967569603_2579481208207441920_n.jpg?w=468)

Imagine you are a famous actor, at the top of your game, and have just appeared in a movie with Mick Jagger. And then you give it all up and move to Sheffield to become a travelling salesman. This story has done the rounds since the 1970s and yes, it is all true.

William Fox, born London 1939, was the son of theatrical agent Robin Fox and actress Angela Worthington. He first appeared on film in 1960 in The Miniver Story but was working in a bank when director Tony Richardson offered him a minor role in The Loneliness of a Long-Distance Runner.

Under his stage name, James Fox, he went on to star in The Servant, King Rat, Thoroughly Modern Millie, Those Magnificent Men in their Flying Machines and The Chase. Handsome and appealing, Hollywood was calling, but there was a problem.

After playing alongside Mick Jagger in Performance in 1968 (not released until 1970 owing to its sexual content and graphic violence), James Fox was in a crisis.

“There were so many things that caused tension in me,” he said. “Working on Sundays, making love on screen and using bad language.”

The result of this self-torture was that Fox turned to religion. In 1970 he joined a Christian group called The Navigators, his involvement the subject of a BBC documentary, Escape to Fulfilment, in 1971.

“When it was over, I had to decide what to do in the longer term. I had met another Christian, Alan, from near Sheffield, that summer, and we immediately became friends. He was an administrative manager with British Steel at Stocksbridge. He invited me to come north to live with his family.

“I was told that I’d have to get a job, so I bought a copy of the Sheffield Morning Telegraph and sat down in Barker’s Pool to study it. Just about the only job I could see that I could do was as a salesman and there was a vacancy for a post with Phonatas, to get new clients for their office telephone sterilising service in the Sheffield and Rotherham area.

“On my first day at work, I went to London Road. My second stop was a car showroom. The manager interviewed me. ‘You’re James Fox, aren’t you? What on earth are you doing here?’ I told him I wanted him to sign up to have five phones cleaned weekly and that I’d come to live in Sheffield and was doing this as a job. I was given the contract by the incredulous manager.”

For the next eighteen months he toured every business district in Sheffield and Rotherham, the evenings spent making evangelism visits, attending meetings and Bible studies.

Attracted by the estate agency business, Fox moved to T. Saxton and Co, to become an assistant in its commercial property department. During the summer of 1972 he met Mary, a nurse, whom he married the following year and set up home at Oughtibridge.

“I went to the office each day by bus down London Road, which I had walked so many times as a salesman, and in the evening, I came home to my wonderful wife and her cooking.”

After he was offered a chance to join the staff of The Navigators, Fox and his wife finally left Sheffield and moved to Leeds in 1974.

By the early eighties, suitably refreshed, Fox decided to return to acting. The first role he was offered was playing opposite Meryl Street in The French Lieutenant’s Woman, a role he understandably turned down.

In the end, his comeback involved several dramas for the BBC before hitting the big screen again with Greystoke: The legend of Tarzan, Lord of the Apes, A Passage to India and Absolute Beginners.

Since then, Fox has enjoyed a second career on stage and screen, although often overshadowed by acting brother, Edward Fox.

James and Mary Fox have five children – Thomas, Robin, Laurence (DS James Hathaway in Lewis), Lydia and Jack, the youngest two also capable actors. He is, of course, also uncle to other acting offspring – Emilia and Freddie Fox.

The Sheffield connection may now be forgotten, but when James Fox appeared on Desert Island Discs, he chose Oft in the Stilly Night by the Bolsterstone Male Voice Choir, as one of his eight discs.

James Fox is a veteran British film star renowned for his appearances in such classics as "Passage to India" (directed by David Lean), "Remains of the Day" (with Sir Anthony Hopkins), "Performance" (with Sir Mick Jagger) and, more recently, "Sexy Beast" (with Ray Winstone & Sir Ben Kingsley). A patriarch of the famous Fox acting dynasty, James notable relations include his brother, Edward Fox, and his son, Laurence.

Seldom interviewed, James Fox offers rare insights into his life in film, his colourful time in 'Swinging London', recollections of famed figures such as director David Lean, his adult conversion to Christianity and his opinion of his son Laurence's foray into politics.

## [Wahlgren & Wistam En sångerska och en tv-personlighet slår sig ihop för att varje vecka fundera över små och stora saker i denna glamour/vardags-podd. Ex-män, barnuppfostran, kärlek och misslyckanden avhandlas med en stor portion humor. Livet blir inte alltid som man har tänkt sig. Kanske blir det roligare. I Bikten har man chansen att bli förlåten för sina synder. Pernilla och Sofia tar med glädje sig an lyssnarnas historier och kontrar även med sina egna synder och upplevelser. I veckans Aha får vi lära oss något nytt och i momentet Telefonboken går ingen säker. Det blir självklart även tips på enkla goda maträtter från Pernilla. Tveka inte att vara med och påverka vår podd. Nytt avsnitt varje fredag. ## [The night that Sheffield lost its paintings](link_8)

*    Post author  By [Myles](https://sheffielder.net/author/freshbreezes/)
*    Post date [27 Oct 2024](link_8)

![Image 1](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/wwiini-heinkel-he111.jpg?w=1024)

_Heinkel HE111 bombers in formation. The HE111 was the mainstay of the German Luftwaffe bomber force and bombed Sheffield in 1940._

It was a cold and clear Thursday night in December 1940. The skies were vibrating with the noise of German Luftwaffe Heinkel HE111 and Junkers 88 aircraft that had crossed over the sea from France. When they reached Sheffield, they dropped parachute bombs that descended at 40mph and exploded when they reached the level of the rooftops sending shockwaves over a wide area. They screeched as they fell, closely followed by thunderous explosions that could be heard right across the city. The streets were scenes of panic, fires raged, and the air was thick with smoke. Sheffield had experienced its first encounter with Hitler’s blitzkrieg, the psychological shock and resultant disorganisation through which the employment of surprise, speed, and firepower, was designed to weaken the city’s resolve.

One of the bombs dropped through the glass roof at the back of the Mappin Art Gallery, near Mushroom Lane. It obliterated three of the Mappin’s six galleries, and the shockwave caused major damage throughout the rest of the building, shattering almost every pane of glass, and destroying artefacts. The damage was inconceivable and when daylight came, only the facade, the front two galleries and the Graves Museum extension had survived; the rest of the building was deemed unsafe. Two days later, rain fell and added to the bleakness.

Afterwards, the remainder of the art collection was moved to two premises on the Duke of Devonshire’s estates in Derbyshire, outhouses of Edensor Vicarage and a pub in Pilsley. Meanwhile the shell of the two surviving Mappin galleries was used as a makeshift store, its gutted roof sheeted over.

A year later, the Illustrated London News reported that the Graves Art Gallery, above Sheffield’s Central Library, had opened an unusual exhibition. It consisted of pictures – paintings, watercolours and drawings – damaged in the air raid on Sheffield when they were hung at the Mappin Art Gallery. Some were in the condition in which they were found after the raid, some were restored completely and others only partly.

![Image 2](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/jchorsley_grandmothersbirthdaypresent_bna.jpg?w=580)

_Grandmother’s Birthday Present by John Calcott Horsley. Damage to this picture was extensive and the linen backing can be seen where the original canvas had been stripped. Believed to have been destroyed._ _Image: British Newspaper Archive_

Approximately 250 pictures were damaged by flying glass, bomb blast, or the rain which followed the raid before they could be collected and safely housed. The blast made crazy patterns on the varnish, flying glass caused cuts, some large, in the canvas, and the rain caused those pictures that had been re-lined to separate. But for all this it was hoped to restore between 80 and 90 percent of them.

A lot of the work in the Mappin Art Gallery had been bequeathed to the city by John Newton Mappin and later by Sir Frederick Mappin, and amongst the twenty-three works from the original collection which were totally destroyed were key works from like Dorothy Tennant’s The Emigrants and Darnby’s The Vale of Tempe; four of the most important donations made to the gallery, T.C. Gotch’s The Mother Enthroned, H.C. Selous’ The Crucifixion, Noel Paton’s Lux in Tenebris and G.F. Watt’s portrait of J.A. Roebuck; while some important works were so badly damaged that they weren’t repaired until the late 1980s, like Val Prinsemp’s To Versailles, and W.C. Horsley’s The French in Cairo. Among other damaged pictures were works by John Pettie, David Cox, John Phillip, Sir William Rothenstein, G.F. Watts, Dame Laura Knight, Wilson Steer, Orchardson, Sir John Gilbert, and Eric Gill. The total value of damage and loss was estimated at £6,300 by Professor John Wheatley, who had been appointed director of Sheffield Art Galleries in 1938.

![Image 3](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/garmfield_dogs_bna.jpg?w=723)

_Dogs by George Armfield. Showing the picture before restoration, covered with plaster and other debris. Shown at the Graves Art Gallery in 1941 and now believed to be lost. Image: British Newspaper Archive_

![Image 4](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/barnet_freedman_the_farmyard_bna.jpg?w=927)

_The Farmyard by Barnet Freedman. An example of an oil painting showing damage by blast and glass splinters. This painting was later restored and remains in the Sheffield collection. Image: British Newspaper Archive._

War damage payments for the actual works of art destroyed or damaged turned out to be low, reflecting the low value placed on Mappin’s collection.

At the time of the 1941 exhibition between 60 and 70 raid-damaged pictures had already been restored, but it was estimated that the work of restoration would take two or three years to complete. Wheatley explained that Sheffield was reaping the benefit of having appointed in peacetime a practical assistant on the staff.

That person was Harry Frank Constantine (1919-2014), painter, restorer and curator, who had studied at Sheffield and Southampton Colleges of Art and at the Courtauld Institute. He was assisted by his daughter and was only then finding damage that hadn’t been apparent immediately after the raid. Paint loosened by the blast was beginning to flake off, and the greatest difficulty was with the large cuts in canvases, that were carefully drawn together, given a new backing, the cuts filled in with a composition, and the surrounding paint carefully matched.

![Image 5](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/img_7662.jpg?w=600)

_Gallery One as it was from 1940 – 1962. Photograph taken in 1962_

Constantine took over as director of Sheffield City Art Galleries in 1964 when only the Graves Art Gallery was open. Sheffield had received a major war damage reparation payment, but the ruins of the Mappin Art Gallery hadn’t been touched after the war ended. In 1960, auditors had investigated why the sum for war damage reparation hadn’t been spent, and questions were being asked by the Mappin family. Sheffield Corporation deemed that the rebuilding of the Mappin Art Gallery was low on the list of rebuilding projects, but reconstruction was finally approved in February 1963 and the gallery fully reopened in June 1965.

The Mappin’s Victorian painting collection had been substantially reduced when the building was bombed, and Constantine spent the rest of his career spotting acquisitions in salerooms and in deserted corners of commercial galleries that others had missed. When he retired in 1982, he’d built a reputable collection for the city, curated numerous exhibitions and ensured that the city’s galleries were accessible to everyone.

![Image 6](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/img_7661.jpg?w=590)

_The Emigrants – 1886 – Dorothy Tennant (now destroyed)_

## [Endcliffe Hall – ‘The House Beautiful’ and its uncertain future](link_25)

*    Post author  By [Myles](https://sheffielder.net/author/freshbreezes/)
*    Post date [20 Oct 2024](link_25)

![Image 7](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/endcliffe_hall.jpg?w=820)

What is going to happen to Endcliffe Hall?

It was a headline that dominated local newspapers in 1913 when it was threatened with demolition. It might also apply to now, with the army planning to end its one hundred and ten year ownership of the large Victorian mansion.

In 1914, with Britain on the brink of war, Endcliffe Hall was bought by the Hallamshire Rifles (4th Yorks and Lancaster Regiment) and although the unit was disbanded in 1968 it remains the regimental Headquarters of Army Reserve Unit 212 (Yorkshire) Field Hospital.

A recent planning application asked for works to be removed ahead of the sale of the house and land. It is believed that the removal of a large painting called ‘Entering Fontenay’ and two glass fronted display cases, including the one for the Royal Army Medical Corps flag would require listed building consent, as part of the ballroom wall would need to be altered to take the items out safely.

![Image 8](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/onecms_a1041032-eec9-44ef-862f-48abf818f135.jpeg?w=640)

_Endcliffe Hall in modern times. Note that the French-style tower roof was removed in the twentieth century. Image: Sheffield Star_

What will happen to Endcliffe Hall when it is put on the market? This time around, demolition won’t be an option because it was Grade II* listed in 1973. I have an inkling that it might find a new life as a luxury hotel, although there might have to be extensions, thus increasing the number of rooms to make it viable.

Endcliffe Hall is referred to as Sheffield’s biggest mansion – ‘The House Beautiful’ as the Sheffield Daily Telegraph called it in 1893. It was built between 1863 and 1865 by Flockton and Gibbs for the industrialist John Brown for a reputed £100,000 (that is about £10.6m today).

John Brown was born in Favell’s Yard, Fargate, in 1816, a part of the town favoured by people in good position for residence. His father wanted to apprentice the fourteen year old to a linen draper, but John disagreed. “I want to be a merchant, because a merchant trades with the whole world.” He was apprenticed to Earl, Horton & Co, cutlery manufacturers, in Orchard Place, and eventually took over the business.

In 1844, Brown moved into steel production on Orchard Street and Furnival Street manufacturing railway springs and files. His invention of the conical spring buffer brought him incredible wealth and allowed him to open further factories on Holly Street, Hereford Street and Backfields. These were later consolidated into one site – Atlas Works – in Savile Street.

Adopting the Bessemer process, Brown was a pioneer of the armour making industry, deciding that hammered armour plating could be rolled instead, and would receive orders to protect about three quarters of the ships of the Royal Navy.

In 1856, Brown became a member of the Town Council, an alderman three years later, and Mayor in 1861 and 1862.

John Brown married his childhood sweetheart, Mary Schofield, and lived comfortably at Shirle Hill (now Nether Edge) but with immense wealth, wanted to build a magnificent mansion. In 1863, when the Endcliffe Hall estate went to auction, Brown bought it and demolished the old hall (the second to have stood on the site) and replaced it with a mansion in the Italian style, with free use of the French interpretation. The only relic to survive from the previous hall was a piece of quaint animal carving that was fixed over the fireplace of the principal kitchen.

In those days, the house stood in countryside. _“The air is pure, from the best source, the high moors. A lofty range of hills rising behind this south-eastern aspect, forming a grand and imposing background, sheltering it from northern winds. A view of Sylvan Scenery in the valley of the River Porter, and the wood-crowned heights of Brinkcliffe Edge. The eye is carried through the lovely Vale of Whiteley Wood, up to the Moorlands of Hallamshire. There is a plentiful supply of the purest water and building materials from the ground.”_

John Brown employed Flockton and Abbott to design and carry out the 36 room mansion almost regardless of cost, and those gentlemen succeeded in producing a building which, for perfect architecture, excellent workmanship, unique domestic arrangement, and appropriate accessories, could not be surpassed in the provinces.

Nearly 300 workmen had worked on it and the proportions of all the rooms were said to be magnificent, with a light and cheerful appearance, and a sense of perfect ventilation throughout. On completion, in 1865, the house was, on the invitation of the architects, opened over two days for inspection, and on each day crowds of leading gentry and merchants visited to see it for themselves.

![Image 9](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/uuu.jpg?w=640)

_Endcliffe Hall in all its former glory. Built between 1863 and 1865 by Flockton and Gibbs for the industrialist John Brown. Image: Picture Sheffield_

John Brown was knighted in 1867, and there is a saying that money cannot buy happiness. In hindsight, one wonders whether John Brown and his wife were truly happy at Endcliffe Hall. A year later, Brown denied that he had sold the estate, the rumour fuelled by their desire to spend the winter months in Torquay, and only returning to Sheffield in the spring. Sir John and Lady Mary both suffered ill-health, and it is only during research for this post that we can now speculate that his ailments were due to his mental health.

In 1871, the John Brown Co had set up its subsidiary —the Bilbao River and Cantabrian Railway Company Limited— and bought plots in Sestao (Bilbao), Spain, to construct blast furnaces and process iron ore from the nearby Galdames mines they owned, which was to be transported by a factory owned railway they started building that same year. The railway was finished in 1876, and blast furnaces were completed in 1873. The political climate —the third Carlist War [1873-76] and its aftermath— are one of the reasons which motivated the company to abandon the blast furnace project and sell the installations to the Duke of Mudela —Francisco de las Rivas— in July of 1879. The second and more important reason for selling its processing plant was the fact that ore deposits in Galdames were significantly less than prospected. It was lamentable that Sir John’s career should have been so clouded owing to heavy losses in the Bilbao project.

Lady Brown died from a painful disease in 1881, and Sir John gradually withdrew from public life, his health deteriorated, and he spent increasing amounts of time in southern England. He left Endcliffe Hall for the last time in 1892 and two years before his death in 1896 had been declared legally insane.

![Image 10](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/john_brown_006.jpg?w=557)

_Sir John Brown (1816-1896), KT, DL, Mayor of Sheffield (1861-1862)_

Rumours circulated as to the future of the estate. Some suggested that it would remain in local hands, others speculated that it was being split up for building plots, while a third rumour suggested that the Duke of Norfolk might buy the house. Certainly, an enquiry was made but never followed up.

The sale of Endcliffe Hall had been put in the hands of London-based Maple and Co, and in January 1893 it offered Sheffield Corporation the chance to buy it for £70,000. The amount of money involved and uncertainty as to what to do with it meant that the corporation politely declined. Neither had there been any other offers for the estate.

Maple and Co sent the entire contents of Endcliffe Hall to auction in April 1893. “The best of furniture, the richest of appointments, the costly statuary, bronzes, pictures – the art treasures collected through many years – are to be scattered far and wide,” the Sheffield Daily Telegraph reported. The contents raised between £9.000 and £10,000 and were believed to have been sold for about a third of their cost

“_In local eyes it was the embodiment, in stone and lime, of a career unique even among merchant princes and manufacturers. Next week the beautiful home will be desolate; its costly contents, collected from all quarters, dispersed under the hammer, and no doubt not a few Sheffield families will in days to come treasure in their lares and penates some relic of the most complete and perfect amongst the many pleasant dwelling-places reared by the Men of Mark in our midst. Surely the goodliest habitation within our borders, its masonry fair of face as the day one stone was laid upon another, will not come down in the cutting up of the gardens and grounds, the terraces and parks, to make way for rows of villas to be raised by the speculative builder.” – Sheffield Daily Telegraph, Sat 15 April 1893_

In July 1895, Endcliffe Hall and the estate went to auction at Nicholson, Greaves, Barber, and Hastings. I

## [The night that Sheffield lost its paintings](link_8)

*    Post author  By [Myles](https://sheffielder.net/author/freshbreezes/)
*    Post date [27 Oct 2024](link_8)

![Image 1](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/wwiini-heinkel-he111.jpg?w=1024)

_Heinkel HE111 bombers in formation. The HE111 was the mainstay of the German Luftwaffe bomber force and bombed Sheffield in 1940._

It was a cold and clear Thursday night in December 1940. The skies were vibrating with the noise of German Luftwaffe Heinkel HE111 and Junkers 88 aircraft that had crossed over the sea from France. When they reached Sheffield, they dropped parachute bombs that descended at 40mph and exploded when they reached the level of the rooftops sending shockwaves over a wide area. They screeched as they fell, closely followed by thunderous explosions that could be heard right across the city. The streets were scenes of panic, fires raged, and the air was thick with smoke. Sheffield had experienced its first encounter with Hitler’s blitzkrieg, the psychological shock and resultant disorganisation through which the employment of surprise, speed, and firepower, was designed to weaken the city’s resolve.

One of the bombs dropped through the glass roof at the back of the Mappin Art Gallery, near Mushroom Lane. It obliterated three of the Mappin’s six galleries, and the shockwave caused major damage throughout the rest of the building, shattering almost every pane of glass, and destroying artefacts. The damage was inconceivable and when daylight came, only the facade, the front two galleries and the Graves Museum extension had survived; the rest of the building was deemed unsafe. Two days later, rain fell and added to the bleakness.

Afterwards, the remainder of the art collection was moved to two premises on the Duke of Devonshire’s estates in Derbyshire, outhouses of Edensor Vicarage and a pub in Pilsley. Meanwhile the shell of the two surviving Mappin galleries was used as a makeshift store, its gutted roof sheeted over.

A year later, the Illustrated London News reported that the Graves Art Gallery, above Sheffield’s Central Library, had opened an unusual exhibition. It consisted of pictures – paintings, watercolours and drawings – damaged in the air raid on Sheffield when they were hung at the Mappin Art Gallery. Some were in the condition in which they were found after the raid, some were restored completely and others only partly.

![Image 2](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/jchorsley_grandmothersbirthdaypresent_bna.jpg?w=580)

_Grandmother’s Birthday Present by John Calcott Horsley. Damage to this picture was extensive and the linen backing can be seen where the original canvas had been stripped. Believed to have been destroyed._ _Image: British Newspaper Archive_

Approximately 250 pictures were damaged by flying glass, bomb blast, or the rain which followed the raid before they could be collected and safely housed. The blast made crazy patterns on the varnish, flying glass caused cuts, some large, in the canvas, and the rain caused those pictures that had been re-lined to separate. But for all this it was hoped to restore between 80 and 90 percent of them.

A lot of the work in the Mappin Art Gallery had been bequeathed to the city by John Newton Mappin and later by Sir Frederick Mappin, and amongst the twenty-three works from the original collection which were totally destroyed were key works from like Dorothy Tennant’s The Emigrants and Darnby’s The Vale of Tempe; four of the most important donations made to the gallery, T.C. Gotch’s The Mother Enthroned, H.C. Selous’ The Crucifixion, Noel Paton’s Lux in Tenebris and G.F. Watt’s portrait of J.A. Roebuck; while some important works were so badly damaged that they weren’t repaired until the late 1980s, like Val Prinsemp’s To Versailles, and W.C. Horsley’s The French in Cairo. Among other damaged pictures were works by John Pettie, David Cox, John Phillip, Sir William Rothenstein, G.F. Watts, Dame Laura Knight, Wilson Steer, Orchardson, Sir John Gilbert, and Eric Gill. The total value of damage and loss was estimated at £6,300 by Professor John Wheatley, who had been appointed director of Sheffield Art Galleries in 1938.

![Image 3](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/garmfield_dogs_bna.jpg?w=723)

_Dogs by George Armfield. Showing the picture before restoration, covered with plaster and other debris. Shown at the Graves Art Gallery in 1941 and now believed to be lost. Image: British Newspaper Archive_

![Image 4](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/barnet_freedman_the_farmyard_bna.jpg?w=927)

_The Farmyard by Barnet Freedman. An example of an oil painting showing damage by blast and glass splinters. This painting was later restored and remains in the Sheffield collection. Image: British Newspaper Archive._

War damage payments for the actual works of art destroyed or damaged turned out to be low, reflecting the low value placed on Mappin’s collection.

At the time of the 1941 exhibition between 60 and 70 raid-damaged pictures had already been restored, but it was estimated that the work of restoration would take two or three years to complete. Wheatley explained that Sheffield was reaping the benefit of having appointed in peacetime a practical assistant on the staff.

That person was Harry Frank Constantine (1919-2014), painter, restorer and curator, who had studied at Sheffield and Southampton Colleges of Art and at the Courtauld Institute. He was assisted by his daughter and was only then finding damage that hadn’t been apparent immediately after the raid. Paint loosened by the blast was beginning to flake off, and the greatest difficulty was with the large cuts in canvases, that were carefully drawn together, given a new backing, the cuts filled in with a composition, and the surrounding paint carefully matched.

![Image 5](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/img_7662.jpg?w=600)

_Gallery One as it was from 1940 – 1962. Photograph taken in 1962_

Constantine took over as director of Sheffield City Art Galleries in 1964 when only the Graves Art Gallery was open. Sheffield had received a major war damage reparation payment, but the ruins of the Mappin Art Gallery hadn’t been touched after the war ended. In 1960, auditors had investigated why the sum for war damage reparation hadn’t been spent, and questions were being asked by the Mappin family. Sheffield Corporation deemed that the rebuilding of the Mappin Art Gallery was low on the list of rebuilding projects, but reconstruction was finally approved in February 1963 and the gallery fully reopened in June 1965.

The Mappin’s Victorian painting collection had been substantially reduced when the building was bombed, and Constantine spent the rest of his career spotting acquisitions in salerooms and in deserted corners of commercial galleries that others had missed. When he retired in 1982, he’d built a reputable collection for the city, curated numerous exhibitions and ensured that the city’s galleries were accessible to everyone.

![Image 6](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/img_7661.jpg?w=590)

_The Emigrants – 1886 – Dorothy Tennant (now destroyed)_

**_Many thanks to Professor Michael Tooby and James Hamilton for invaluable information in collating this post._**
