![Image 3](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/wwiini-heinkel-he111.jpg?w=1024)

_Heinkel HE111 bombers in formation. The HE111 was the mainstay of the German Luftwaffe bomber force and bombed Sheffield in 1940._

It was a cold and clear Thursday night in December 1940. The skies were vibrating with the noise of German Luftwaffe Heinkel HE111 and Junkers 88 aircraft that had crossed over the sea from France. When they reached Sheffield, they dropped parachute bombs that descended at 40mph and exploded when they reached the level of the rooftops sending shockwaves over a wide area. They screeched as they fell, closely followed by thunderous explosions that could be heard right across the city. The streets were scenes of panic, fires raged, and the air was thick with smoke. Sheffield had experienced its first encounter with Hitler’s blitzkrieg, the psychological shock and resultant disorganisation through which the employment of surprise, speed, and firepower, was designed to weaken the city’s resolve.

One of the bombs dropped through the glass roof at the back of the Mappin Art Gallery, near Mushroom Lane. It obliterated three of the Mappin’s six galleries, and the shockwave caused major damage throughout the rest of the building, shattering almost every pane of glass, and destroying artefacts. The damage was inconceivable and when daylight came, only the facade, the front two galleries and the Graves Museum extension had survived; the rest of the building was deemed unsafe. Two days later, rain fell and added to the bleakness.

Afterwards, the remainder of the art collection was moved to two premises on the Duke of Devonshire’s estates in Derbyshire, outhouses of Edensor Vicarage and a pub in Pilsley. Meanwhile the shell of the two surviving Mappin galleries was used as a makeshift store, its gutted roof sheeted over.

A year later, the Illustrated London News reported that the Graves Art Gallery, above Sheffield’s Central Library, had opened an unusual exhibition. It consisted of pictures – paintings, watercolours and drawings – damaged in the air raid on Sheffield when they were hung at the Mappin Art Gallery. Some were in the condition in which they were found after the raid, some were restored completely and others only partly.

![Image 4](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/jchorsley_grandmothersbirthdaypresent_bna.jpg?w=580)

_Grandmother’s Birthday Present by John Calcott Horsley. Damage to this picture was extensive and the linen backing can be seen where the original canvas had been stripped. Believed to have been destroyed._ _Image: British Newspaper Archive_

The blast made crazy patterns on the varnish, flying glass caused cuts, some large, in the canvas, and the rain caused those pictures that had been re-lined to separate. But for all this it was hoped to restore between 80 and 90 percent of them.

A lot of the work in the Mappin Art Gallery had been bequeathed to the city by John Newton Mappin and later by Sir Frederick Mappin, and amongst the twenty-three works from the original collection which were totally destroyed were key works from like Dorothy Tennant’s The Emigrants and Darnby’s The Vale of Tempe; four of the most important donations made to the gallery, T.C. Gotch’s The Mother Enthroned, H.C. Selous’ The Crucifixion, Noel Paton’s Lux in Tenebris and G.F. Watt’s portrait of J.A. Roebuck; while some important works were so badly damaged that they weren’t repaired until the late 1980s, like Val Prinsemp’s To Versailles, and W.C. Horsley’s The French in Cairo. Among other damaged pictures were works by John Pettie, David Cox, John Phillip, Sir William Rothenstein, G.F. Watts, Dame Laura Knight, Wilson Steer, Orchardson, Sir John Gilbert, and Eric Gill. The total value of damage and loss was estimated at £6,300 by Professor John Wheatley, who had been appointed director of Sheffield Art Galleries in 1938.

_Dogs by George Armfield. Showing the picture before restoration, covered with plaster and other debris. Shown at the Graves Art Gallery in 1941 and now believed to be lost. Image: British Newspaper Archive_

![Image 6](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/barnet_freedman_the_farmyard_bna.jpg?w=927)

_The Farmyard by Barnet Freedman. An example of an oil painting showing damage by blast and glass splinters. This painting was later restored and remains in the Sheffield collection. Image: British Newspaper Archive._

James Fox is a veteran British film star renowned for his appearances in such classics as "Passage to India" (directed by David Lean), "Remains of the Day" (with Sir Anthony Hopkins), "Performance" (with Sir Mick Jagger) and, more recently, "Sexy Beast" (with Ray Winstone & Sir Ben Kingsley). A patriarch of the famous Fox acting dynasty, James notable relations include his brother, Edward Fox, and his son, Laurence.

Seldom interviewed, James Fox offers rare insights into his life in film, his colourful time in 'Swinging London', recollections of famed figures such as director David Lean, his adult conversion to Christianity and his opinion of his son Laurence's foray into politics.

# James Fox

*    Post author  By [Myles](https://sheffielder.net/author/freshbreezes/)
*    Post date [8 Feb 2020](https://sheffielder.net/2020/02/08/james-fox/)

![Image 1](https://sheffielder.net/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/72570192_137995967569603_2579481208207441920_n.jpg?w=468)

Imagine you are a famous actor, at the top of your game, and have just appeared in a movie with Mick Jagger. And then you give it all up and move to Sheffield to become a travelling salesman. This story has done the rounds since the 1970s and yes, it is all true.

William Fox, born London 1939, was the son of theatrical agent Robin Fox and actress Angela Worthington. He first appeared on film in 1960 in The Miniver Story but was working in a bank when director Tony Richardson offered him a minor role in The Loneliness of a Long-Distance Runner.

Under his stage name, James Fox, he went on to star in The Servant, King Rat, Thoroughly Modern Millie, Those Magnificent Men in their Flying Machines and The Chase. Handsome and appealing, Hollywood was calling, but there was a problem.

After playing alongside Mick Jagger in Performance in 1968 (not released until 1970 owing to its sexual content and graphic violence), James Fox was in a crisis.

“There were so many things that caused tension in me,” he said. “Working on Sundays, making love on screen and using bad language.”

The result of this self-torture was that Fox turned to religion. In 1970 he joined a Christian group called The Navigators, his involvement the subject of a BBC documentary, Escape to Fulfilment, in 1971.

“When it was over, I had to decide what to do in the longer term. I had met another Christian, Alan, from near Sheffield, that summer, and we immediately became friends. He was an administrative manager with British Steel at Stocksbridge. He invited me to come north to live with his family.

“I was told that I’d have to get a job, so I bought a copy of the Sheffield Morning Telegraph and sat down in Barker’s Pool to study it. Just about the only job I could see that I could do was as a salesman and there was a vacancy for a post with Phonatas, to get new clients for their office telephone sterilising service in the Sheffield and Rotherham area.

“On my first day at work, I went to London Road. My second stop was a car showroom. The manager interviewed me. ‘You’re James Fox, aren’t you? What on earth are you doing here?’ I told him I wanted him to sign up to have five phones cleaned weekly and that I’d come to live in Sheffield and was doing this as a job. I was given the contract by the incredulous manager.”

For the next eighteen months he toured every business district in Sheffield and Rotherham, the evenings spent making evangelism visits, attending meetings and Bible studies.

Attracted by the estate agency business, Fox moved to T. Saxton and Co, to become an assistant in its commercial property department. During the summer of 1972 he met Mary, a nurse, whom he married the following year and set up home at Oughtibridge.

“I went to the office each day by bus down London Road, which I had walked so many times as a salesman, and in the evening, I came home to my wonderful wife and her cooking.”

After he was offered a chance to join the staff of The Navigators, Fox and his wife finally left Sheffield and moved to Leeds in 1974.

By the early eighties, suitably refreshed, Fox decided to return to acting. The first role he was offered was playing opposite Meryl Street in The French Lieutenant’s Woman, a role he understandably turned down.

In the end, his comeback involved several dramas for the BBC before hitting the big screen again with Greystoke: The legend of Tarzan, Lord of the Apes, A Passage to India and Absolute Beginners.

Since then, Fox has enjoyed a second career on stage and screen, although often overshadowed by acting brother, Edward Fox.

James and Mary Fox have five children – Thomas, Robin, Laurence (DS James Hathaway in Lewis), Lydia and Jack, the youngest two also capable actors. He is, of course, also uncle to other acting offspring – Emilia and Freddie Fox.

The Sheffield connection may now be forgotten, but when James Fox appeared on Desert Island Discs, he chose Oft in the Stilly Night by the Bolsterstone Male Voice Choir, as one of his eight discs.

[![Image 63: #FilmHistory #ClassicNoir #BritishCinema #DirkBogarde #JeanKent Five Angles on Murder (1950) Where to watch: Usually available on rotating classic‑film services such as Prime Video (rental), Apple TV (rental), and Classix depending on region. Summary: A noir‑structured British mystery told through five conflicting witness accounts, the film follows the investigation into the murder of fortune‑teller Agnes “Astra” Smith. Each person who knew her—her sister, her lover, a troubled young man, a jealous wife, and a local boy—presents a drastically different version of her personality, shifting her from kind to cruel, glamorous to manipulative, victim to villain. The police must navigate these contradictory narratives to uncover who Agnes truly was and who had the strongest motive to kill her. The film’s Rashomon‑style structure makes every character unreliable, and the shifting tone—from melodrama to noir to domestic tension—creates a layered portrait of a woman seen only through the distortions of others. Fans of anthology‑style mysteries or multi‑perspective crime dramas often seek this film out, and it is frequently recommended alongside other British noir titles of the era such as Green for Danger and Cast a Dark Shadow. Release Date: 1950 (UK), U.S. release under the title Five Angles on Murder shortly after. --------------------------------------------------------------------- Full IMDb‑Verified Cast: Jean Kent — Astra / Agnes Dirk Bogarde — Bob Baker John McCallum — Inspector Susan Shaw — Catherine Taylor Hermione Baddeley — Mrs. Finch Charles Victor — Mr. Pollard Duncan Lamont — Wilson Susan Stephen — Norma Smith Lana Morris — Molly Peter Copley — Dr. Urquhart Anthony Dawson — The Stranger George Woodbridge — Police Sergeant Arthur Howard — Coroner Laurence Naismith — Superintendent Alfie Bass — Newsboy Michael Medwin — Young Man Jack Watling — Reporter Esma Cannon — Woman Witness And all remaining credited supporting players listed on IMDb. --------------------------------------------------------------------- 5 Fun Facts + 5 Behind‑the‑Scenes (combined into one continuous set): 1. The film’s multi‑perspective structure was unusual for British cinema at the time and drew comparisons to Rashomon, even though it was released the same year. 2. Jean Kent considered Astra one of her most complex roles because she had to play five different “versions” of the same woman depending on who was telling the story. 3. Dirk Bogarde was still early in his career, and this film helped solidify his rising status in British noir and crime dramas. 4. Director Anthony Asquith was known for elegant staging, and he intentionally altered lighting and camera angles for each witness segment to subtly shift the audience’s perception of Astra. 5. The U.S. title Five Angles on Murder was chosen to emphasize the film’s structure rather than its original fortune‑teller theme. 6. The production used a modest budget typical of Rank Organisation mid‑tier releases, relying heavily on performance and narrative rather than elaborate sets. 7. Many scenes were shot on controlled studio stages to allow lighting changes between perspectives without continuity issues. 8. Jean Kent’s wardrobe was intentionally inconsistent—each witness imagined her differently, so costuming varied from glamorous to plain. 9. The film’s nonlinear editing was considered innovative and required unusually close collaboration between Asquith and editor Gerald Turney‑Smith. 10. Some U.S. promotional materials marketed it as a more sensational thriller than it actually was, hoping to attract American noir audiences. --------------------------------------------------------------------- created by SunLightSunBright with Suspense Sound Lab’s Dark Suspense](https://p16-common-sign.tiktokcdn-us.com/tos-useast5-p-0068-tx/ooADAsa8fBqQfCpAtBDkVInqSPgREFFgAVOEgY~tplv-tiktokx-origin.image?dr=9636&x-expires=1791266400&x-signature=4G4h3vxvZthP0axBNy4JuAmBVR0%3D&t=4d5b0474&ps=13740610&shp=81f88b70&shcp=43f4a2f9&idc=useast8) [![Image 64: SunLightSunBright,sunlightsunbright4](https://p16-common-sign.tiktokcdn-us.com/tos-useast5-avt-0068-tx/a98348a34c20874bf386fa118a0eab59~tplv-tiktokx-cropcenter:100:100.jpeg?dr=9640&refresh_token=f6e6a22d&x-expires=1791266400&x-signature=Qo4EsjzL75lUYCPghogtErpxSb8%3D&t=4d5b0474&ps=13740610&shp=a5d48078&shcp=81f88b70&idc=useast8)](https://www.tiktok.com/@sunlightsunbright4?lang=en)#### [SunLightSunBright](https://www.tiktok.com/@sunlightsunbright4?lang=en "sunlightsunbright4")](https://www.tiktok.com/@sunlightsunbright4/video/7655628044148788493)

[it can’t be that hard, right? 😬](https://www.tiktok.com/@fromrusttoroadtrip/video/7658002007482977558 "it can’t be that hard, right? 😬 Turns out driving to India isn't exactly straightforward... Quite a few of you have been asking what route we're actually planing to take from Cornwall to India. The truth is... we're still working it out. Back in the 1970s you could simply drive the Hippie Trail through Iran and Afghanistan all the way to India. Today it's a very different story. So instead, we'll be setting off from Land's End in our home county of Cornwall, driving through Europe, Türkiye, the Caucasus and Central Asia, crossing Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan before eventually reaching Pakistan and (hopefully!) the other Land's End at the southern tip of India. If we're lucky maybe we'll even make it into Turkmenistan. We're building this 1988 Freight Rover Sherpa into a Land Rover-powered 4x4 expedition van because the journey isn't about getting from A to B. It's about the snowy mountain passes, endless Central Asian steppes, remote villages, roadside mechanics who help us keep going, chance encounters, cups of tea and of course the stories from the road. The journey starts here in Cornwall. India is the destination. But the adventure is everything in between. The full story behind the Sherpa Project and the journey from Kernow to India is waiting in the comments if you'd like to come along for the ride 👇 *Disclaimer: Iran is effectively out of bounds for British people and Afghanistan is kind of open but– let’s say– tricky. Maybe some day the world’s borders will be open again 💙#overlanding #roadtrip #cornwall #india #vanlife ")

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

1982 novel by James Fox

White Mischief [![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/16/White_Mischief_%28novel%29.jpg/250px-White_Mischief_%28novel%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:White_Mischief_(novel).jpg)

First edition
Author[James Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist) "James Fox (journalist)")
Language English
Publisher[Jonathan Cape](link_3) (UK)
Publication date 1982
Publication place United Kingdom
Media type Print (hardback & paperback)
Pages 299

_**White Mischief**_ is a non-fiction book by British journalist [James Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fox_(journalist) "James Fox (journalist)"), first published in hardback by [Jonathan Cape](link_3) in 1982 and in paperback in 1984 by [Penguin](link_4).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(novel)#cite_note-catalogue-1) The book is an account of the unsolved murder in 1941 of [Josslyn Hay, 22nd Earl of Erroll](link_6), a British expatriate in [Kenya](link_7). The title is a pun on the title of [Evelyn Waugh](link_8)'s novel _[Black Mischief](link_9)_ (1932). The book was adapted as a [film of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(film) "White Mischief (film)") in 1987.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(novel)#cite_note-imdb-2)

## Synopsis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(novel)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Synopsis")]

Part novel and part journalistic report, the book is divided into two distinct sections.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(novel)#cite_note-wordpress-3) Initially presented as a classic murder mystery, the first part of the story focuses on the dissolute lifestyles of the wealthy elite in colonial Kenya. Casual affairs, wife-swapping, habitual drunkenness and cocaine abuse were all common. The main protagonists are the victim, [Josslyn Hay](link_5), a handsome womanising aristocrat; his beautiful married lover Lady [Diana Broughton](link_10); and Diana’s much older husband Sir Delves Broughton. Although the identity of the murderer has never been discovered, the author claims to have found new evidence pointing to Sir Delves, and the second part of the book concentrates on the author’s investigations and his interviews with surviving participants in the drama, both in Kenya and in the United Kingdom.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Mischief_(novel)#cite_note-goodreads-4)

## Film adaptation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=White_Mischief_(novel)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Film adaptation")]

_[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_, released in 1987, was directed by [Michael Radford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Radford "Michael Radford"), and stars [Charles Dance](link_11), [Greta Scacchi](link_12) and [Joss Ackland](link_13).

**Sidney Edmond Jocelyn Ackland** (29 February 1928 – 19 November 2023) was an English actor who appeared in more than 130 film, radio and television roles.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-1) He was nominated for the [BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role](link_8) for portraying [Jock Delves Broughton](link_9) in _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_ (1987).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-2)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joss_Ackland&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Sidney Edmond Jocelyn Ackland was born in a basement flat in "then insalubrious" [North Kensington](link_5), London, on [29 February 1928](link_10),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-bfi-3) the son of Sydney Norman Ackland (died 1981), an Irish journalist who had been sent to England to live with an aunt by his parents for seducing their maid, but subsequently seduced his aunt's maid, Ruth Izod (died 1957), whom he married.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-6) The Acklands' basement flat was one of "a string of similar places" in which they lived, invariably with "one bedroom and the absolute bare essentials"; Ackland described his upbringing in the [Ladbroke Grove](link_11) area as being "very poor".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-8)

Initially educated at [Dame Alice Owen's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Alice_Owen [link_12]'s_School "Dame Alice Owen's School"), Ackland left aged fifteen to become an actor.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-9) Thus, Ackland was trained by [Elsie Fogerty](link_13) at the [Central School of Speech and Drama](link_7), then based at the [Royal Albert Hall](link_14), London.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-10)

Ackland and Rosemary Kirkcaldy were married on 18 August 1951, when Ackland was 23 and she was 22.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-scotsman-11) She was an actress and Ackland wooed her when they appeared on stage together in [Pitlochry](link_15), Scotland.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-12) The couple struggled initially as Ackland's acting career was in its infancy.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-scotsman-11) In 1954 they moved to [Lilongwe](link_16) in what was then [Nyasaland](link_17), now Malawi, where Ackland managed a [tea plantation](link_18) for six months[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-TelegraphObitRef-13) but, deciding it was too dangerous, they moved to [Cape Town](link_19), South Africa.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-scotsman-11) Though they both obtained steady acting jobs in South Africa, after two years they returned to England in 1957.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-scotsman-11)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Ackland#cite_note-bbcnews-14)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joss_Ackland&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

After attending London's Central School of Speech and Drama, he made his professional debut on stage at just 17 years old, starring in the 1945 production of _The Hasty Heart_. Ackland joined the [Old Vic](link_20), appearing alongside other notable actors including [Maggie Smith](link_21), [Judi Dench](link_22) and [Tom Courtenay](link_23). Ackland worked steadily in television and film in the 1960s and 70s.

**Join the Commons**  

If you don't have a Wikimedia Commons account yet, [create one](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:CreateAccount "Special:CreateAccount") - takes just a few moments!**Find historical sites**

Upload your photos through October under a free license.

**Wiki Loves Monuments** is an international photographic competition that invites the global community to document and preserve historic sites around the world on [Wikipedia](link_15) and other Wikimedia projects.

A 'monument' refers to a protected historic site that is recognized by a governmental body or other organization, such as a historical society. In the United States, this primarily consists of places listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](link_16), which is the United States federal government's official list of districts, sites, buildings, structures and objects deemed worthy of preservation for their historical significance. We also accept photos of historic sites that are recognized by tribal, state, and local governments, as well as historical societies and related organizations.

This year the United States is participating through the month of October. By sharing your photos under a [free license](link_17) that allows anyone to use them, you help document our history and share it with the rest of the world to enjoy through the internet, and get a shot at winning a prize! We will explain below how to participate, what you can win and what monument sites are eligible.

### Participate

Find a registered historic site and upload a photo you have taken of it to the Wikimedia Commons:

[Find a monument»](link_7)

[Create an account»](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:CreateAccount "Special:CreateAccount")

[Upload your photos!»](link_8)

### U.S. Prizes

1st: $500  
 2nd: $300  
 3rd: $200  
 4th–10th: $50 each  
  
Special Prizes  
 Most sites previously unillustrated: $100  
 Top 2 Native American site photos: $50 each  
 Top 2 UAV (drone) photos: $50 each  
See the Prize Categories section below for full details. Monetary prizes will be provided as a gift card of the winner's choice.

## Why participate?

![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/WLM-icon-edit-neg.svg/120px-WLM-icon-edit-neg.svg.png?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Help Wikipedia document historically significant buildings and historical sites.

![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/WLM-icon-camera-neg.svg/120px-WLM-icon-camera-neg.svg.png?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)A nice challenge to improve your photography skills.

![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/WLM-icon-prize-neg.svg/120px-WLM-icon-prize-neg.svg.png?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Compete for prizes in both the national and international competitions.

## Competition rules

There are a few rules for photos to participate in the United States contest.

*   Photos must be your own work.
*   Photos may have been taken at any time (including prior to this event), but must be uploaded during October 2026 to be included in the contest. The US contest formally begins October 1 in US Eastern time (UTC-4) and ends at the end of October 31 in Hawaii-Aleutian Standard Time (UTC-10).
*   During the upload process, you must release your photo under a free license that allows for re-use of the image ([CC BY-SA license](link_13) or similar) - see [Commons:Licensing](link_17) for more information.
*   Photos should be **[uploaded through this link](link_8)** in order to be properly tagged for the contest. 
    *   Experienced contributors may also bypass the portal and manually tag their images [per this guide](link_18).

*   The photo must feature a site that is identifiable and registered as a historical or cultural site by some authoritative organization (whether on the federal, tribal, state, or local levels). Examples would be the National Register of Historic Places or your local historical society. When you upload your work, be sure to provide the name of the historical site, any identifiers, and the list it is on.
*   Digital manipulations must not deceive the viewer. Correcting flaws, color adjustments, and other minor edits are acceptable.

Next to that, there are a few practical rules:

*   You should have an activated e-mail address on Wikimedia Commons, so that you can be contacted if you win.
*   If the photo gets deleted for any reason, it is automatically disqualified from the competition.
*   You are responsible for following local laws and regulations. 
    *   Do not trespass onto private property.
    *   Be especially careful and ensure you are following regulations when doing drone photography.
    *   Some locations may require a permit for photography.

At the end of the month, the national jury will evaluate the photographs and select winners. See the Prize Categories and Judging sections below for more details.

### Copyright notes

In the United States, you may freely take photos of buildings, but _not_ copyrighted artworks, sculptures, and signage. See [our page on freedom of panorama](link_19) for more information. Permanently installed artworks may be photographed if they were **installed before 1926**, or **installed before 1978 without a copyright notice**.

Check out [Cornell's guide](link_20) for more details and an easy-to-read table.

Applicable templates:

*   For public artwork installed **before 1926**, use {{[PD-US](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Template:PD-US "Template:PD-US")}} or {{[PD-US-expired](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Template:PD-US-expired "Template:PD-US-expired")}}.
*   For public artwork installed **between 1926 and 1977** inclusive, use {{[PD-US-no notice](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Template:PD-US-no_notice "Template:PD-US-no notice")}} or {{[PD-US-not renewed](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Template:PD-US-not_renewed "Template:PD-US-not renewed")}}.

## Prize Categories

Each year, we recognize our top-ten photos based on composition, technical quality, originality, and usefulness for Wikipedia:

*   1st: $500
*   2nd: $300
*   3rd: $200
*   4th-10th: $50 each

A participant may only place once in the top ten.

The top-ten photos are also submitted to the international competition.

### Special Categories

This year, we have additional prizes for the following categories:

*   Most sites photographed that were previously unillustrated: $100
*   Top two photos of Native American sites: $50 each 
    *   Eligible submissions include photos of recognized tribal properties, historic sites, cultural landmarks, archaeological sites, and monuments that are connected to Native American heritage.
    *   Please note, some Native American nations may require permits for taking photos.

*   Top two UAV (drone) photos: $50 each 
    *   Please ensure you follow laws and regulations when flying a drone. Photos in which the drone operator was violating regulations or creating a hazardous situation will be disqualified.

**Walter Charles Dance** (born 10 October 1946) is an English actor. He is known for playing intimidating, authoritarian characters and villains. Dance started his career on stage with the [Royal Shakespeare Company](link_8) (RSC) before appearing in film and television. For his services to drama he was appointed an [OBE](link_9) by [Queen Elizabeth II](link_10) in 2006.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dance#cite_note-1)

He made his feature film debut in the [James Bond](link_11) film _[For Your Eyes Only](link_12)_ (1981). He has since acted in a string of critically acclaimed period films such as _[Michael Collins](link_13)_ (1996), _[Gosford Park](link_14)_ (2001), _[The Imitation Game](link_15)_ (2014), _[Mank](link_16)_ (2020), and _[The King's Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_King [link_17]'s\_Man "The King's Man")_ (2021). # Trivia

## White Mischief

Edit

The producers wanted to fire [Trevor Howard](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0002145/?ref_=tttrv_tr) from this movie, due to his alcoholism, but [Sarah Miles](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0587234/?ref_=tttrv_tr) insisted he should stay.

Helpful•19 0

The BBC television drama, [The Happy Valley (1986)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0093694/?ref_=tttrv_tr), covering the same subject matter, was broadcast on September 6, 1987, within the same year of this movie debuting in theaters.

Helpful•12 0

The closing credits legal disclaimer reads: "The story of this film is inspired by events which took place in Kenya in 1940 and 1941. The film does not purport to be an accurate representation of either the characters concerned, or the events that took place."

Helpful•16 1

Only career nude scene for Jacqueline Pearce. She talked about her audition process for this film in a 1991 TV Zone interview. Her agent had called her saying the producer Mike Radford and casting director Mary Selway wanted to see her, but since the role required nudity, they also wanted to see her naked. Pearce said it was no problem. When she arrived for the audition, all she wore were black stockings, a pair of high heeled shoes, and a full length mink. She walked into Radford's office, dropped the mink, stood before him and Selway stark naked, and said, "What do you think of that lot?" Radford hired her on the spot.

Helpful•9 0

Many movie posters featured a long blurb that read: "In England they were the elite, but bound by rules of society. In Kenya there were no rules, only glamour, decadence . . . and murder."

Helpful•8 1

_**Last Action Hero**_ is a 1993 American [fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_film "Fantasy film")[action comedy film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_comedy_film "Action comedy film") directed and produced by [John McTiernan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McTiernan "John McTiernan") and co-written by [Shane Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Black "Shane Black") and [David Arnott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Arnott "David Arnott").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Action_Hero#cite_note-Last_Action_Hero-4) It is a satire of the action genre and associated clichés, containing several parodies of action films in the form of [films within the film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_within_a_film#Film_within_a_film "Film within a film").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Action_Hero#cite_note-5) The film stars [Arnold Schwarzenegger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Schwarzenegger "Arnold Schwarzenegger") as Jack Slater, a [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") police detective within the _Jack Slater_ action film franchise, while [Austin O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_O'Brien "Austin O'Brien") co-stars as Danny Madigan, a boy magically transported into the _Slater_ universe and [Charles Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dance "Charles Dance") as Mr. Benedict, a ruthless assassin from the _Slater_ universe who escapes to the real world. Schwarzenegger also served as the film's executive producer and plays himself as the actor portraying Jack Slater.

_**The Golden Child**_ is a 1986 American [dark fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_fantasy "Dark fantasy")[action comedy film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_comedy_film "Action comedy film") directed by [Michael Ritchie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ritchie_(film_director) "Michael Ritchie (film director)"). The film stars [Eddie Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Murphy "Eddie Murphy") as Chandler Jarrell, a Los Angeles social worker who is informed that he is "[The Chosen One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Chosen_One_(trope) "The Chosen One (trope)")", and is destined to save "The Golden Child", a kidnapped [Tibetan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_people "Tibetan people") boy with [mystical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysticism "Mysticism") powers who is said to be the [savior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvation "Salvation") of all humankind. Alongside Murphy, the film's cast includes [Charlotte Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Lewis "Charlotte Lewis") and [Charles Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dance "Charles Dance").

_The Golden Child_ was produced and distributed by [Paramount Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures "Paramount Pictures")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golden_Child#cite_note-Maslin-5) and grossed a total of $79,817,937 at the United States domestic box office.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golden_Child#cite_note-numbers-1)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golden_Child#cite_note-mojo-6)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Golden_Child&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

In a remote temple in Tibet, a young boy – the Golden Child – demonstrates his mystical powers to the [monks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monk "Monk") of the [temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple "Temple") by reviving a dead [eastern rosella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_rosella "Eastern rosella"), which becomes a constant companion and [familiar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Familiar_spirit "Familiar spirit"). A mysterious man, Sardo Numspa, has his men break into the temple, slaughter the monks, and abduct the boy.

A young woman, [Kee Nang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kee_Nang "Kee Nang"), watches a [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") TV show in which independent [social worker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_worker "Social worker") and [private detective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_detective "Private detective") Chandler Jarrell talks about a missing girl named Cheryll Mosley. Kee informs him of the kidnapping of the Golden Child and that he is the "chosen one" who will save the Child. Chandler does not take this seriously, even after a bird begins following him and he sees an [astral projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astral_projection "Astral projection") of the Child. The next day, Cheryll is found dead near an abandoned house smeared with Tibetan [graffiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graffiti "Graffiti") and a pot full of blood-soaked oatmeal. Kee reveals to Chandler that this house was a holding place for the Child and introduces him to Doctor Hong, a mystic expert, and Kala (a creature half dragon, half woman).

Chandler and Kee track down a [motorcycle gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outlaw_motorcycle_club "Outlaw motorcycle club"), the Yellow Dragons, which Cheryll had joined, and [Chinese restaurant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_restaurant "Chinese restaurant") owner Tommy Tong, a henchman of Numspa, to whom Cheryll had been "sold" for her blood, a way to make the Child vulnerable to earthly harm. However, Tong is killed by Numspa as a potential traitor. Still not taking the case too seriously, Chandler is drawn by Numspa into a [controlled dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucid_dream "Lucid dream"). Numspa presents his demands: the Ajanti Dagger (a mystic weapon capable of killing the Child) in exchange for the boy. Chandler agrees to help, and he and Kee spend the night together.

Chandler and Kee travel to [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet"), where Chandler is swindled by an [amulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amulet "Amulet") seller, later revealed as the High [Priest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priest "Priest") of the temple where the dagger is kept hidden (and, subsequently, Kee's father). To obtain the knife, Chandler has to pass a test: an [obstacle course](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstacle_course "Obstacle course") in a bottomless cavern whilst carrying a glass of water without spilling a drop. With luck and wits, he recovers the blade and brings it into the United States.

That night, Numspa and his henchmen attack Chandler and Kee. The Ajanti Dagger is lost to the villains, and Kee takes a crossbow bolt meant for Chandler, dying in his arms while confessing her love for him. Doctor Hong and Kala offer him hope: as long as the sun shines upon Kee, the Child might be able to save her. With the help of the Child's familiar, Chandler locates Numspa's hideout, retrieves the dagger with the help of Til, one of Numspa's men converted to good by the Child, and frees the boy. When

**Wiki Loves Monuments - United States Competition**  
A campaign to improve our coverage of U.S. historic and cultural sites  
throughout the month of October.

## Frequently Asked Questions

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Frequently Asked Questions")]

### Event Basics

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Event Basics")]

#### What is Wiki Loves Monuments?

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: What is Wiki Loves Monuments?")]

Wiki Loves Monuments is a public photo competition in which readers and contributors of Wikipedia are asked to take pictures of monuments from participating countries and to upload them to Wikimedia Commons. The contest was first organized in 2010 in the Netherlands and is nowadays organized in dozens of countries around the world. Wiki Loves Monuments has collected some 2 million photos over the past years that can be used on Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons, and is recognized by the Guinness Book of World Records as the largest photography competition in the world.

#### What counts as a "monument" in the United States?

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: What counts as a \"monument\" in the United States?")]

Eligible sites are those that appear on authoritative heritage lists. This includes the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Register_of_Historic_Places_listings "en:United States National Register of Historic Places listings"), as well as lists from various government agencies, state and local historic societies, city preservation boards, and other recognized authorities.

In short: if it's formally recognized on a reliable list of historic or cultural sites, it qualifies.

#### When does the contest run?

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: When does the contest run?")]

In the United States, the contest runs each year from **October 1 through October 31**. Uploads must be made during this window to be eligible for prizes (but the photos can be from any point in time, not just October!).

Some other countries run their Wiki Loves Monuments campaigns in September, or in between the two months.

#### Who organizes the contest?

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Who organizes the contest?")]

The U.S. edition is put together by volunteers from the Wikimedia community in the United States. The international competition is coordinated by a separate Wiki Loves Monuments international team, which provides the tools and infrastructure needed to run the contest smoothly across dozens of countries.

#### Do I have to be a professional photographer?

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Do I have to be a professional photographer?")]

Not at all. Wiki Loves Monuments is open to everyone with all levels of photography experience.

### Uploading

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Uploading")]

#### How do I submit a photo for Wiki Loves Monuments?

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: How do I submit a photo for Wiki Loves Monuments?")]

For most contributors to Wiki Loves Monuments in the United States, we ask them to upload photos via our custom upload portal, located at **[wikilovesmonuments.us/upload](https://wikilovesmonuments.us/upload/)**. This helps us properly tag and categorize images, and also provides some notices to users uploading photos of potentially copyrighted subjects (historical markers, sculptures, etc).

You can also "manually" submit your photos by following [this guide](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/Manual_Tagging "Commons:Wiki Loves Monuments 2026 in the United States/Manual Tagging") to add the WLM template and categories, either during or after the upload process (as long as the photo is uploaded during the month of October 2026).

#### How many photos can I submit?

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: How many photos can I submit?")]

There is no limit. You can upload one photo or a thousand!

#### What if I have photos from years ago?

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: What if I have photos from years ago?")]

That's fine! We accept photos taken at any point of time. They just need to be uploaded during the month of October to be eligible for the contest.

#### What about people in the photos?

[[edit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Commons:Wiki_Loves_Monuments_2026_in_the_United_States/FAQ&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: What about people in the photos?")]

_**The Object of Beauty**_ is a 1991 [comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_film "Comedy film")[crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_film "Crime film")–[drama film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(modern_genre) "Drama (modern genre)") directed by [Michael Lindsay-Hogg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Lindsay-Hogg "Michael Lindsay-Hogg") and starring [John Malkovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Malkovich "John Malkovich") and [Andie MacDowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andie_MacDowell "Andie MacDowell").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Object_of_Beauty#cite_note-The_Object_of_Beauty-3)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Object_of_Beauty&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Jake and Tina have taken up residence in a London hotel, living way beyond their means. He is a [commodities broker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodity_broker "Commodity broker") whose shipment of cocoa beans is tied up by a Third World country's revolution. She is a woman with extravagant tastes who is still technically married to Larry, her first husband.

The two of them are so broke that when it comes time to pay for a dinner at the hotel, Jake hands a credit card to the waiter and prays that it won't be canceled. A pair of hotel executives, Mercer and Swayle, repeatedly make attempts to confront Jake and Tina about their growing unpaid bill.

Only one object stands between the couple and total insolvency. That is a tiny sculpture by Henry Moore that was given to Tina by her husband as a gift. But just as she and Jake hatch a scheme to pretend the object is stolen and collect the insurance on it, a deaf housekeeper, Jenny, decides to steal it for herself.

After she steals it Tina and Jake get upset. Then Jenny's brother decides to take it and sell it, but nobody will buy it and he ends up losing it. Jake and Tina argue, he goes to Joan (Tina's best friend) and they end up sleeping together. Next day Jenny searches with her brother and find the statue in a heap of rubble. Jenny returns it then steals it again and when the insurance company comes she hands it over. Jake and Tina auction it off later and are able to resolve their debt with the hotel and continue to go on vacation.

There is a _Jekyll and Hyde_ joke, Lindsay-Hogg directed "The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde", a [TV movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_movie "TV movie"), for [Nightmare Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightmare_Classics "Nightmare Classics").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

British baronet (1883–1942)

This British surname is [double-barrelled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-barrelled_name#British_tradition "Double-barrelled name"), being made up of multiple names. It should be written as _Delves Broughton_, not _Broughton_.

**Sir Henry John Delves Broughton, 11th Baronet**, [DL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Lieutenant "Deputy Lieutenant") (10 September 1883 – 5 December 1942), was a British baronet who is chiefly known for standing trial for the murder of [the 22nd Earl of Erroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josslyn_Hay,_22nd_Earl_of_Erroll "Josslyn Hay, 22nd Earl of Erroll"). The event was the basis of the film _[White Mischief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White\_Mischief\_(film) "White Mischief (film)")_ and of the British television drama _[The Happy Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Happy\_Valley "The Happy Valley")_, both from 1987.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jock_Delves_Broughton&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Born at [Doddington Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doddington_Hall,_Cheshire "Doddington Hall, Cheshire") in [Doddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doddington,_Cheshire "Doddington, Cheshire"), [Cheshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire"), 'Jock' Delves Broughton attended the [Royal Military College, Sandhurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Military_College,_Sandhurst "Royal Military College, Sandhurst"), and was commissioned a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_lieutenant "Second lieutenant") in the [Irish Guards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Guards "Irish Guards") on 10 December 1902.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-1) He came into the baronetcy upon the death of his father in April 1914. He had married Vera Edyth Griffith-Boscawen on 8 July 1913; their daughter, Rosamond, married [The 15th Lord Lovat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Fraser,_15th_Lord_Lovat "Simon Fraser, 15th Lord Lovat") in 1938.

On the outbreak of the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"), as a [captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(British_Army) "Captain (British Army)") in the 1st Battalion [Irish Guards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Guards "Irish Guards"), he was due to sail with his men, but was taken ill and had to be replaced.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-3) He was forced to sell off most of the 34,000 acres (140 km 2) of the family estate in the 1930s to pay gambling debts.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-4) In the late 1920s and early 1930s, he was part of a consortium which owned the Ensbury Park Race Course in [Kinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinson "Kinson"), [Dorset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorset "Dorset"), now a part of [Bournemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bournemouth "Bournemouth"). In 1939, he was suspected of insurance fraud after the theft of his wife's pearls and some paintings, on which he claimed the insurance.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-whitemischief-5) Months after he and Vera divorced, Delves Broughton married [Diana Caldwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_Caldwell "Diana Caldwell") in [Durban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durban "Durban"), [Natal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natal_(province) "Natal (province)"), [Union of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_South_Africa "Union of South Africa"), on 5 November 1940, and the couple moved to the [Colony and Protectorate of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_and_Protectorate_of_Kenya "Colony and Protectorate of Kenya").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-6)

## Murder trial

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jock_Delves_Broughton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Murder trial")]

[Lord Erroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josslyn_Hay,_22nd_Earl_of_Erroll "Josslyn Hay, 22nd Earl of Erroll") was found shot in the head in his car at a crossroads outside [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") on 24 January 1941. He and the Delves Broughtons were part of the so-called [Happy Valley set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Valley_set "Happy Valley set") living in [Happy Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Valley,_Kenya "Happy Valley, Kenya"), [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-juanita-7)

Erroll's former lover, [Alice de Janzé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_de_Janz%C3%A9 "Alice de Janzé"), was initially viewed by the Happy Valley set as a suspect, but [Sir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir "Sir") Jock Delves Broughton – whose wife was very publicly carrying-on with Erroll – was arrested. He was acquitted at trial for lack of evidence, a conclusion that hinged on the identification of the murder weapon. Delves Broughton's pistol was a [Colt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colt's_Manufacturing_Company "Colt's Manufacturing Company") with 6 grooves, and Erroll was killed by a bullet with 5 grooves. No pistol was produced by [the Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crown "The Crown") or by the defence. Delves Broughton claimed that two of his pistols, a silver cigarette case and 10 or 20 shillings were stolen days before Erroll's death ([Superintendent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintendent_(police) "Superintendent (police)") Arthur Poppy, a senior officer in the [Kenya Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Police "Kenya Police"), claimed that Delves Broughton had stolen the guns from himself to give the impression that he had no .32 pistol at the time).

Additionally, the bullet that killed Erroll was fired by a pistol with clockwise rifling; Colts use anti-clockwise rifling. Another bullet fired at Erroll also had 5 grooves and clockwise turning. On 11 May 2007, _[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_ writer Christine Nicholls described taped evidence she claimed was definitive proof that Delves Broughton killed Erroll[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-8) and the writer Juanita Carberry said she had heard his confession to the crime.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-juanita-7)

## Aftermath

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jock_Delves_Broughton&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Aftermath")]

Delves Broughton was never accepted back into the Happy Valley set and returned to England alone, his wife having already taken another lover. In December 1942, a few days after his arrival, 59-year-old Delves Broughton was found dying from a [morphine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphine "Morphine") overdose at the [Adelphi Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britannia_Adelphi_Hotel "Britannia Adelphi Hotel"), [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool"). The inquest recorded a verdict of suicide while the balance of his mind was disturbed, in relation to illness following a back injury from a fall, the official reason for his return to England.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jock_Delves_Broughton#cite_note-10) The baronetcy passed to his son, [Sir Evelyn Delves Broughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_Delves_Broughton "Evelyn Delves Broughton"). After his death, his widow [Diana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_Caldwell "Diana Caldwell") remarried twice, the first time to the Happy Valley's wealthiest settler, Gilbert Colvile, and the second time to the [4th Baron Delamere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cholmondeley,_4th_Baron_Delamere "Thomas Cholmondeley, 4th Baron Delamere").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
This article is about the online encyclopedia. For Wikipedia's home page, see Main Page. For the history of Wikipedia, see History of Wikipedia. For the English-language Wikipedia, see English Wikipedia. For other uses, see Wikipedia (disambiguation).
Wikipedia

Wikipedia[e] is a free online encyclopedia written and maintained by a community of volunteer editors, known as Wikipedians, through open collaboration and the wiki software MediaWiki. Founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001, Wikipedia has been hosted since 2003 by the Wikimedia Foundation, an American nonprofit organization funded mainly by donations from readers.[1] Wikipedia is the largest and most read reference work in history.[2][3]

Initially available only in English, Wikipedia has grown to over 300 languages and is one of the world's most visited websites as of 2026. The English Wikipedia, with over 7 million articles, remains the largest of the editions, which together comprise more than 68 million articles and attract more than 1.5 billion unique device visits and 13 million edits per month (about five edits per second on average) as of April 2024.[4] As of December 2025, over 25% of Wikipedia's traffic comes from the United States, while Japan accounts for nearly 7%, and the United Kingdom, Germany, and Russia each represent around 5%.[5]

Wikipedia has been praised for its internal structure and culture, enabling the democratization of knowledge, and for its extensive coverage on various topics. The encyclopedia has also been criticized for systemic bias, such as a gender bias against women and a geographical bias against the Global South.[6][7] The reliability of Wikipedia was frequently criticized in the 2000s, but has received greater praise from the late 2010s onward.[2][8] Censorship of Wikipedia by national governments has ranged from censoring specific pages to the entire site, sometimes due to its criticism of the government, or for content considered blasphemous.[9][10][11] Wikipedia articles on breaking news are accessed as sources for up-to-date information by many.[12][13]

History
Main article: History of Wikipedia
Nupedia
Main article: Nupedia
Wikipedia founders Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger

Various collaborative online encyclopedias were attempted before Wikipedia's launch, but with limited success.[14] Wikipedia began as a complementary project for Nupedia, a free online English-language encyclopedia project whose articles were written by experts and reviewed under a formal process.[15] It was founded on March 9, 2000, under the ownership of Bomis, a web portal company. Its main figures were Bomis CEO Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger, editor-in-chief for Nupedia and later Wikipedia.[16][17] Nupedia was initially licensed under its own Nupedia Open Content License. Before Wikipedia was founded, Nupedia switched to the GNU Free Documentation License at the urging of Richard Stallman.[18] Wales is often credited with defining the goal of making a publicly editable encyclopedia,[19] while Sanger is credited with the strategy of using a wiki to reach that goal.[20] On January 10, 2001, Sanger proposed on the Nupedia mailing list to create a wiki as a "feeder" project for Nupedia.[21]

Launch and growth

Wikipedia was launched on January 15, 2001 (sometimes referred to as "Wikipedia Day"),[22] as a single English language edition with the domain name www.wikipedia.com,[23] and was announced by Sanger on the Nupedia mailing list.[19] The name, proposed by Sanger to forestall any potential damage to the Nupedia name,[24] originated from a blend of the words wiki and encyclopedia.[25][26] Wales stated that the idea for Wikipedia was influenced by the spontaneous order ideas associated with Friedrich Hayek and the Austrian School of economics after being exposed to these ideas by the libertarian economist Mark Thornton.[27][28] In particular, Wales was influenced by Hayek's essay The Use of Knowledge in Society stating it was "central" to his thinking about "how to manage the Wikipedia project".[28] Its integral policy of "neutral point of view" arose within its first year.[29] Otherwise, there were initially relatively few rules, and it operated independently of Nupedia.[19] Bomis originally intended for it to be a for-profit business.[30]

The Wikipedia home page on December 20, 2001[f]

Wikipedia gained early contributors from Nupedia, Slashdot postings, and web search engine indexing. Language editions were created beginning in March 2001, with a total of 161 in use by the end of 2004.[31][32] Nupedia and Wikipedia coexisted until the former's servers were taken down permanently in 2003, and its text was incorporated into Wikipedia. The English Wikipedia passed the mark of 2 million articles on September 9, 2007, making it the largest encyclopedia ever assembled, surpassing the Yongle Encyclopedia made in China during the Ming dynasty in 1408, which had held the record for almost 600 years.[33]

Due to fears of commercial advertising and lack of control, users of the Spanish Wikipedia forked from Wikipedia to create Enciclopedia Libre in February 2002.[34] Wales then announced that Wikipedia would not display advertisements and changed Wikipedia's domain from wikipedia.com to wikipedia.org.[35][36]

After an early period of exponential growth,[37] the growth rate of the English Wikipedia in terms of the numbers of new articles and of editors appears to have peaked around early 2007.[38] The edition reached 3 million articles in August 2009. Around 1,800 articles were added daily to the encyclopedia in 2006; by 2013 that average was roughly 800.[39] A team at the Palo Alto Research Center attributed this slowing of growth to "increased coordination and overhead costs, exclusion of newcomers, and resistance to new edits".[37] Others suggested that the growth flattened naturally because articles that could be called "low-hanging fruit"—topics that clearly merit an article—had already been created and built up extensively.[40][41][42]

In November 2009, a researcher at the Rey Juan Carlos University in Madrid, Spain, found that the English Wikipedia had lost 49,000 editors during the first three months of 2009; in comparison, it lost only 4,900 editors during the same period in 2008.[43][44] The Wall Street Journal cited the array of rules applied to editing and disputes related to such content among the reasons for this trend.[45] Wales disputed these claims in 2009, denying the decline and questioning the study's methodology.[46] Two years later, in 2011, he acknowledged a slight decline, noting a decrease from "a little more than 36,000 writers" in June 2010 to 35,800 in June 2011. In the same interview, he also claimed the number of editors was "stable and sustainable".[47] A 2013 MIT Technology Review article, "The Decline of Wikipedia", questioned this claim, reporting that since 2007 Wikipedia had lost a third of its volunteer editors, and suggesting that those remaining had focused increasingly on minutiae.[48] In July 2012, The Atlantic reported that the number of administrators was also in decline.[49] In November 2013, New York magazine stated, "Wikipedia, the sixth-most-used website, is facing an internal crisis."[50] The number of active English Wikipedia editors has since remained steady after a long period of decline.[51][52]

On January 20, 2014, Subodh Varma reporting for The Economic Times indicated that not only had Wikipedia's growth stalled, it "had lost nearly ten percent of its page views last year. There was a decline of about 2 billion between December 2012 and December 2013. Its most popular versions are leading the slide: page-views of the English Wikipedia declined by twelve percent, those of the German version slid by 17 percent and the Japanese version lost 9 percent."[53] Varma added, "While Wikipedia's managers think that this could be due to errors in counting, other experts feel that Google's Knowledge Graphs project launched last year may be gobbling up Wikipedia users."[53] When contacted on this matter, Clay Shirky, associate professor at New York University and fellow at Harvard's Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society said that he suspected much of the page-view decline was due to Knowledge Graphs, stating, "If you can get your question answered from the search page, you don't need to click [any further]."[53] By the end of December 2016, Wikipedia was ranked the fifth most popular website globally.[54] As of January 2023, 55,791 English Wikipedia articles have been cited 92,300 times in scholarly journals,[55] from which cloud computing was the most cited page.[56]

Sister projects
Main article: Wikimedia project

Wikipedia has spawned several sister projects, which are also wikis run by the Wikimedia Foundation. These other Wikimedia projects include Wiktionary, a dictionary project launched in December 2002,[57] Wikiquote, a collection of quotations created a week after Wikimedia launched,[58] Wikibooks, a collection of collaboratively written free textbooks and annotated texts,[59] Wikimedia Commons, a site devoted to free-knowledge multimedia,[60] Wikinews, for collaborative journalism[61] (which was later shut down in 2026[62]), and Wikiversity, a project for the creation of free learning materials and the provision of online learning activities.[63] Another sister project of Wikipedia, Wikispecies, is a catalog of all species, but is not open for public editing.[64] In 2012, Wikivoyage, an editable travel guide,[65] and Wikidata, an editable knowledge base, launched.[66]

Milestones
Cartogram showing number of articles in the top 88 Wikipedias (as of March 2024). The size of the circles for Wikipedias that have less than a million articles is fixed and not proportional to the size of the Wikipedia. The smallest Wikipedia that made the cutoff is the Haitian Creole Wikipedia with 69K articles.[g]
The languages are roughly grouped by region:

     Northern Europe          Eastern Europe     Middle East     East Asia     Indian subcontinent     Sub-Saharan Africa     Central Asia     Caribbean

In January 2007, Wikipedia first became one of the ten most popular websites in the United States, according to Comscore Networks.[67] With 42.9 million unique visitors, it was ranked ninth, surpassing The New York Times (No. 10) and Apple (No. 11).[67] This marked a significant increase over January 2006, when Wikipedia ranked 33rd, with around 18.3 million unique visitors.[68] In 2014, it received 8 billion page views every month.[69] On February 9, 2014, The New York Times reported that Wikipedia had 18 billion page views and nearly 500 million unique visitors a month, "according to the ratings firm comScore".[70] As of March 2023, it ranked sixth in popularity, according to Similarweb.[71] Jeff Loveland and Joseph Reagle argue that, in process, Wikipedia follows a long tradition of historical encyclopedias that have accumulated improvements piecemeal through "stigmergic accumulation".[72][73]

On January 18, 2012, the English Wikipedia participated in a series of coordinated protests against two proposed laws in the United States Congress—the Stop Online Piracy Act (SOPA) and the PROTECT IP Act (PIPA)—by blacking out its pages for 24 hours.[74] More than 162 million people viewed the blackout explanation page that temporarily replaced its content.[75][76]

In January 2013, 274301 Wikipedia, an asteroid, was named after Wikipedia;[77] in October 2014, Wikipedia was honored with the Wikipedia Monument;[78] and, in July 2015, 106 of the 7,473 700-page volumes of Wikipedia became available as Print Wikipedia.[79] In April 2019, an Israeli lunar lander, Beresheet, crash landed on the surface of the Moon carrying a copy of nearly all of the English Wikipedia engraved on thin nickel plates; experts say the plates likely survived the crash.[80][81] In June 2019, scientists reported that all 16 GB of article text from the English Wikipedia had been encoded into synthetic DNA.[82]

On January 18, 2023, Wikipedia debuted a new website redesign, called "Vector 2022".[83][84] It featured a redesigned menu bar, moving the table of contents to the left as a sidebar, and numerous changes in the locations of buttons like the language selection tool.[84][85] The update initially received backlash, most notably when editors of the Swahili Wikipedia unanimously voted to revert the changes.[83][86]

Both Sanger and Wales gave public interviews in late 2025 about their reflections about the status and state of Wikipedia, leading up to its 25 years of operation on January 15, 2026; Wales appeared on the PBS television news show GZERO World interviewed by Ian Bremmer[87] and Sanger has appeared on the Fox News Channel, interviewed by Ashley Rindsberg.[88] Wales' book The Seven Rules of Trust was published in October 2025 by Penguin Random House. It was described by the publisher as a "sweeping reflection on the global crisis of credibility and knowledge" with the book examining the "rules of trust" that enabled the growth and success of Wikipedia.[89]

Impacts of generative AI on Wikipedia views
Further information: Artificial intelligence in Wikimedia projects

Since January 2024, the Wikimedia Foundation has reported a roughly 50 percent increase in bandwidth use from downloads of multimedia content across its projects. According to the foundation, this growth is largely attributed to automated programs, or "scraper" bots, that collect large volumes of data from Wikimedia sites for use in training large language models and related applications.[90]

In October 2025, the Wikimedia Foundation reported an estimated 8 percent decline in traffic as compared to the same month in 2024 in human page views. They speculated that it reflects the growing use of generative AI and social media for finding information.[91][92]

Collaborative editing
Differences between versions of an article are highlighted.
Restrictions

Due to Wikipedia's increasing popularity, some editions, including the English version, have introduced editing restrictions for certain cases. For instance, on the English Wikipedia and some other language editions, only users with 10 edits that have an account that is four days old may create a new article.[93] On the English Wikipedia, among others, particularly controversial, sensitive, or vandalism-prone pages have been protected to varying degrees.[94] A frequently vandalized article can be "semi-protected" or "extended confirmed protected", meaning that only "autoconfirmed" or "extended confirmed" editors can modify it.[95] A particularly contentious article may be locked so that only administrators can make changes.[96] A 2021 article in the Columbia Journalism Review identified Wikipedia's page-protection policies as "perhaps the most important" means at its disposal to "regulate its market of ideas".[97] Wikipedia has delegated some functions to bots. Such algorithmic governance has an ease of implementation and scaling, though the automated rejection of edits may have contributed to a downturn in active Wikipedia editors.[98] Bots must be approved by the community before their tasks are implemented.[99]

In certain cases, all editors are allowed to submit modifications, but review is required for some editors, depending on certain conditions. For example, the German Wikipedia maintains "stable versions" of articles which have passed certain reviews.[100] Following protracted trials and community discussion, the English Wikipedia introduced the "pending changes" system in December 2012.[101] Under this system, new and unregistered users' edits to certain controversial or vandalism-prone articles are reviewed by established users before they are published.[102] However, restrictions on editing may reduce editor engagement as well as efforts to diversify the editing community.[103]

Articles related to the Israeli–Palestinian conflict are placed under extended-confirmed protection.[104] Editors also can make only one revert per day across the entire field and can be banned from editing related articles. These restrictions were introduced in 2008.[105] In January 2025, the Arbitration Committee introduced the "balanced editing restriction", which requires sanctioned users to devote only a third of their edits to articles related to the Israeli–Palestinian conflict even when no misconduct rules have been violated.[106][107]

Review of changes
Wikipedia's editing interface

Although changes are not systematically reviewed, Wikipedia's software provides tools allowing anyone to review changes made by others. Each article's History page links to each revision.[h][108] On most articles, anyone can view the latest changes and undo others' revisions by clicking a link on the article's History page. Registered users may maintain a "watchlist" of articles that interest them so they can be notified of changes.[109] There are a variety of different 'patrols' on Wikipedia,[110] including "New pages patrol" a patrol where newly created articles are checked for glaring issues.[111]

In 2003, economics PhD student Andrea Ciffolilli argued that the low transaction costs of participating in a wiki created a catalyst for collaborative development, and that features such as allowing easy access to past versions of a page favored "creative construction" over "creative destruction".[112]

Vandalism
Main article: Vandalism on Wikipedia

Any change that deliberately compromises Wikipedia's integrity is considered vandalism. The most common and obvious types of vandalism include additions of obscenities and crude humor, but it can also include advertising and other types of spam.[113] Sometimes editors commit vandalism by removing content or entirely blanking a given page. Less common types of vandalism, such as the deliberate addition of plausible but false information, can be more difficult to detect. Vandals can introduce irrelevant formatting, modify page semantics such as the page's title or categorization, manipulate the article's underlying code, or use images disruptively.[114]

American journalist John Seigenthaler (1927–2014), subject of the Seigenthaler biography incident

Obvious vandalism is generally easy to remove from Wikipedia articles; the median time to detect and fix it is a few minutes.[115][116] However, some vandalism takes much longer to detect and repair.[117]

In the Seigenthaler biography incident, an anonymous editor introduced false information into the biography of American political figure John Seigenthaler in May 2005, falsely presenting him as a suspect in the assassination of John F. Kennedy.[117] It remained uncorrected for four months.[117] Seigenthaler, the founding editorial director of USA Today and founder of the Freedom Forum First Amendment Center at Vanderbilt University, called Wikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales and asked whether he had any way of knowing who contributed the misinformation. Wales said he did not, although the perpetrator was eventually traced.[118][119] After the incident, Seigenthaler described Wikipedia as "a flawed and irresponsible research tool".[117] The incident led to policy changes at Wikipedia for tightening up the verifiability of biographical articles of living people.[120]

Disputes and edit warring
Main article: Disputes on Wikipedia

Wikipedia editors often have disagreements regarding content, which can be discussed on article Talk pages. Disputes may result in repeated competing changes to an article, known as "edit warring".[121][122] It is widely seen as a resource-consuming scenario where no useful knowledge is added,[123] and criticized as creating a competitive[124] and conflict-based editing culture associated with traditional masculine gender roles.[125][126] Research has focused on, for example, impoliteness of disputes,[127][128] the influence of rival editing camps,[129][130] the conversational structure,[131] and the shift in conflicts to a focus on sources.[132][133]

Taha Yasseri of the University of Oxford examined editing conflicts and their resolution in a 2013 study.[134][135] Yasseri contended that simple reverts or "undo" operations were not the most significant measure of counterproductive work behavior at Wikipedia. #### [A worthwhile and sexy retelling of a famous murder-mystery case.](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0094317/reviews/?featured=rw0955505&ref_=tt_ururv_c_1_hd)

Circa World War II a grisly - but rich- old buffer and his far-too-young-for-him wife enjoy the high life in Kenya's Happy Valley. However their happiness proves sadly short lived. Based on a famous true life case.  
  
Interesting approach to the "central" crime-celeb subject. While many would have plunged straight in to the murder-mystery to get the movie off with a bang - not here. This is a lesson in restraint.   
  
This film seems to view the crime of secondary importance to atmosphere and the establishment of character and order. This is probably wise, because the mystery part of the crime is rather weak and one-sided. Especially in the manner the story is told.   
  
(While tying to be true to the facts there is more nodding and winking going on here than in a New York gay bar!)  
  
You can't complain about production values and acting, they are only of the very first order. Charles Dance was an actor born in to the wrong age - if the studio system had got a hold of him they could have turned him in to a superstar. He doesn't have enough to do here - but he does this "cad" act well enough.  
  
Kenya is made to look like heaven on earth - if you are white and well off that is. Here life is one big party with plenty of sun, sea and sex - with an army of cheap black labour to do any real work.  
  
The gin and tonic set form their own little England allowing the sex games to go on a bit further than at home because there are no prying eyes.  
  
If any movie showcased Scacchi's ample prime-time charms is this one. I don't know if the lady is a naturist in real life, but she never looks that bothered about whether she is wearing clothes or not. Her classy English accent further convinces you that if any woman was worth killing over it is her.   
  
(In interviews she talks about the audience getting tired of seeing her breasts!)  
  
Watching the film is rather like watching the film Titanic. You realize that everything you see is going to be destroyed, while those on the screen sail on without a care in the world.   
  
If the central crime had been more interesting and more ambiguous I might have enjoyed it more. A clear case of a film being rather weighed down by being based on facts rather than having the freedom of total fiction.
